title: Linux and Containerization
description:
DevOps and cloud: containers, CI/CD, Linux in production, infrastructure as code, Kubernetes, networking and observability.

---

**Scope:** what production Linux looks like when you own it (8.1), then how containers package and run that workload (8.2). Both sections assume you can already move around a shell (Phase 2.2) and have built something real.

**Why interviewers ask:** "The server is slow" and "the deployment is down" are the two questions that show up in every senior backend and DevOps interview. They test whether you can reason about a machine you did not build, under time pressure, without a UI.

---

---

> **Scope.** Phase 8.1 covered Linux server administration and 8.2 covered containerization. This part assumes you can build and run a container image and that you have touched a Linux host in anger. It picks up at the moment a single container becomes a *fleet* of containers that must be scheduled, observed, upgraded, and released. The two halves are deliberately paired: **8.3 is the runtime contract, 8.4 is the pipeline that feeds it.** Almost every production incident in this area traces back to a mismatch between the two — the pipeline deployed an image with a changed entrypoint, or the manifest assumed a probe that nobody tested, or the rollout strategy assumed a database that could be rolled back when it cannot.

> **How to read this.** Every subsection is structured the same way:

| Block | What it gives you |
|---|---|
| **Definition** | The concept in one or two sentences, plus the vocabulary the platform actually uses |
| **Mechanics** | The control loop, the data flow, the failure paths — the parts that explain *why* behaviour surprises you |
| **Real YAML / config / code** | Copy-adaptable artifacts, not pseudocode. Every block is intended to survive contact with `kubectl apply` |
| **When to use it vs when not to** | Decision rules, because most of the value of knowing a technology is knowing its boundary |
| **Trade-offs** | What you give up, stated plainly |
| **Production considerations** | The things that only bite after the first incident |
| **Common mistakes** | Symptom → cause → fix, because debugging is the actual job |
| **Interviewer probes** | The follow-up questions that separate "read the docs" from "ran it in production" |

> **Difficulty labels.** `🟢 Beginner` → `🟡 Intermediate` → `🔴 Advanced` → `⚫ Expert`. All sections carry a label in the form `🟡 Intermediate · **Must-know**`, which means: interview-expected, and expected at the stated depth. Anything labelled **Expert** without a must-know marker is depth you should own if you are targeting staff/principal interviews.

> **Prerequisites you should be able to state fluently before starting.** (1) Containers share a kernel; images are layers; a registry is a content-addressed store. (2) A process listens on a port; a port is bound to an address; `0.0.0.0` is not `127.0.0.1`. (3) Volumes, mount namespaces, and why a container filesystem disappears. (4) HTTP status codes and the difference between a TCP connect, an HTTP GET, and a TLS handshake. (5) Git branches, merges, and rebase. (6) One scripting language well enough to write a test harness.

---

---

This part is where a lot of strong backend candidates quietly lose interviews. The
distinction between "I have used Terraform" and "I understand why a plan destroys
production" is the difference between a mid-level and a senior offer. The same is true
for cloud: knowing that a Region is not a Datacenter, that IAM is a graph and not a
list, that `us-east-1` has six AZs but `ap-northeast-1` has four.

And observability is the least glamorous and most discriminating section in the whole
roadmap. Almost everybody can install Prometheus. Very few candidates can explain a
symptom-based alert on `checkout_success_rate` and refuse to alert on `node_cpu_high`
because it does not page anybody at 3am.

**How to read the difficulty labels:**

| Label | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| 🟢 Beginner · **Must-know** | If you cannot answer this you are not interviewable on infrastructure. |
| 🟡 Intermediate · **Must-know** | The line between "used a cloud" and "ran a cloud". |
| 🔴 Advanced · **Must-know** | Expected at senior level: failure modes, economics, blast radius. |
| ⚫ Expert | Read the spec, know the history. Bonus points, not a gate. |

**Every subsection follows the same shape:** Definition → Mechanics → Real config/code
→ When to use vs not → Trade-offs → Production considerations → Common mistakes →
Interviewer probes. Learn the shape; it makes revision mechanical.

**A note on the three domains and how they relate:**

```
IaC (8.5)  ──►  describes resources  ──►  Cloud (8.6)  ──►  runs them  ──►  Observability (8.7)  ──►  tells you how they behave
   │                                               │                                                          │
   └── state file = source of truth                └── bill, quota, blast radius                          └── evidence for change + for the postmortem
```

If you can explain that loop out loud, most of the questions in the interview section
at the end of this part fall out naturally.

---

---

### 🆕 Linux Server Administration (🟡)
- Users and permissions, systemd and services, Logs, Cron, Firewalls, SSH hardening, Process monitoring, Disk and memory troubleshooting

### Containerization ✅
- ✅ Docker basics, Image building, Container networking, Volumes, Docker Compose, Multi-stage builds, Security scanning
- ➕ Image layers and caching, Dockerfile best practices, Container vs VM, `.dockerignore`, Health checks, Non-root containers, Registries

### 🆕 Kubernetes Basics (🔴)
- Pods, Deployments, Services, Ingress, ConfigMaps and Secrets, Scaling (HPA), Rolling updates, Helm, When not to use Kubernetes

### CI and CD ✅
- ✅ Pipeline creation, Automated testing, Build optimization, Deployment strategies, Rollbacks, Environment variables, Secret management
- ➕ GitHub Actions/GitLab CI/Jenkins, Blue/green, canary, rolling, Feature flags, Preview environments, Database migrations in CD, GitOps, Semantic release, Monorepo CI caching

### 🆕 Infrastructure as Code and Web Servers (🔴)
- Terraform, Ansible awareness, Nginx (reverse proxy, load balancing, SSL termination), Caddy, Environment parity

### Cloud Platforms ✅
- ✅ AWS basics, Serverless functions, Object storage, Managed databases, Cloud monitoring, Domain management, Cost optimization
- ➕ IAM, VPC and subnets, EC2, S3, RDS, Lambda, CloudFront, Route 53, SQS/SNS, ECS/Fargate, API Gateway, GCP and Azure equivalents, Edge functions, PaaS (Vercel, Netlify, Render, Fly.io), Serverless cold starts, Multi-region basics

### 🆕 Observability and Reliability (🔴)
- Logs, metrics, traces, Prometheus, Grafana, OpenTelemetry, Alerting, Incident response and postmortems, SLI/SLO/SLA, Error budgets, Health checks, Chaos engineering awareness, On-call basics

What to say in an interview
symptoms: A routine dependency bump PR runs terraform plan. Output contains:
rootCause: The provider bump changed the semantics of an attribute
practice.reference:
```
  # aws_rds_cluster.orders must be replaced:
-/+ resource "aws_rds_cluster" "orders" {
      ~ engine_version                          = "16.2" -> "16.3" # forces replacement
```

```bash
# 1. Is the change in the diff, or is it implied?
git diff main...HEAD -- '*.tf'            # the version bump is right there

# 2. Which attribute forces replacement?
terraform providers schema -json \
  | jq '.provider_schemas["registry.terraform.io/hashicorp/aws"].resource_schemas
         .aws_rds_cluster.block.attributes
         | to_entries[] | select(.value.forced_new == true) | .key'

# 3. What does the plan actually do? Read the actions, not the words.
terraform show -json tfplan | jq -r '.resource_changes[]
  | select(.type=="aws_rds_cluster") | {a: .address, actions: .change.actions}'

# 4. Would this have happened without the bump?
git stash && terraform init -upgrade=false && terraform plan | grep -c "must be replaced"

```

```bash
terraform show -json tfplan | jq -e '
  [.resource_changes[]
   | select(.change.actions | index("delete"))
   | select(.address | test("aws_rds_cluster|aws_s3_bucket|aws_db_instance"))
  ] | length == 0' || { echo "destructive change on a data-bearing resource"; exit 1; }
```

**Symptoms.** A routine dependency bump PR runs `terraform plan`. Output contains:

```
  # aws_rds_cluster.orders must be replaced:
-/+ resource "aws_rds_cluster" "orders" {
      ~ engine_version                          = "16.2" -> "16.3" # forces replacement
    }
```

Nobody changed the cluster. The engineer who opened the PR was bumped on the AWS provider
from `~> 5.55` to `~> 5.70` in the same commit.

**Investigation.**

```bash
# 1. Is the change in the diff, or is it implied?
git diff main...HEAD -- '*.tf'            # the version bump is right there

# 2. Which attribute forces replacement?
terraform providers schema -json \
  | jq '.provider_schemas["registry.terraform.io/hashicorp/aws"].resource_schemas
         .aws_rds_cluster.block.attributes
         | to_entries[] | select(.value.forced_new == true) | .key'

# 3. What does the plan actually do? Read the actions, not the words.
terraform show -json tfplan | jq -r '.resource_changes[]
  | select(.type=="aws_rds_cluster") | {a: .address, actions: .change.actions}'

# 4. Would this have happened without the bump?
git stash && terraform init -upgrade=false && terraform plan | grep -c "must be replaced"
git stash pop
```

**Root cause.** The provider bump changed the semantics of an attribute
(`engine_version` gained `ForceNew` in that release). Because the bump was in the *same*
commit as a functional change, reviewers saw a normal-looking diff. Terraform is not
wrong: it is telling you the API cannot do a major-version-equivalent in-place change.

**Fix.**

1. Never combine a provider bump with a functional infra change. Split the PR.
2. Pin the provider to a patch version (`~> 5.70.0`), upgrade, `terraform plan`, and
   review the *provider changelog* plus the plan, separately from any feature.
3. If the replacement is genuinely required: `prevent_destroy` is already set, so the
   apply cannot proceed — that is the safety net working. Schedule a window, snapshot,
   and use a **clone → validate → cutover** for Aurora (`restore` to a new cluster,
   replicate, promote) rather than a replacement.
4. Add a CI gate:

```bash
terraform show -json tfplan | jq -e '
  [.resource_changes[]
   | select(.change.actions | index("delete"))
   | select(.address | test("aws_rds_cluster|aws_s3_bucket|aws_db_instance"))
  ] | length == 0' || { echo "destructive change on a data-bearing resource"; exit 1; }
```

**What to say in an interview.** "Provider upgrades change resource semantics, not just
API compatibility. A provider bump is a change to my infrastructure's behaviour, and it
deserves its own PR, its own plan review, and a state-clone dry run. `prevent_destroy`
turns this from an outage into a failed pipeline."

What to say in an interview
symptoms: A security scanner reports aws_secret_access_key committed in
rootCause: Two failures stacked: someone ran terraform apply locally (so a
practice.reference:
```bash
# 1. Establish the exposure window and who could have read it
git log --oneline -S"aws_secret_access_key" -- '**/terraform.tfstate'
git log -1 --format='%H %ad %an' 9f2c1a4

# 2. Was it ever public?

```

```bash
aws iam create-access-key --user-name svcapp              # ensure we are never locked out
aws iam update-access-key --status Inactive --access-key-id AKIAOLD
# verify the replacement works from the app
aws iam delete-access-key --access-key-id AKIAOLD
```

```bash
git filter-repo --path terraform.tfstate --invert-paths --force
git push --force --mirror
```

```gitignore
*.tfstate
*.tfstate.*
.terraform/
# but also: fail the build if state is ever staged
```

```yaml
- name: block-state-in-git
  run: |
    if git ls-files | grep -E '\.tfstate$' ; then
      echo "::error::terraform state is tracked in git"; exit 1
    fi
```

**Symptoms.** A security scanner reports `aws_secret_access_key` committed in
`terraform.tfstate` at commit `9f2c1a4`, in a repository with 40 contributors and a
public mirror.

**Investigation.**

```bash
# 1. Establish the exposure window and who could have read it
git log --oneline -S"aws_secret_access_key" -- '**/terraform.tfstate'
git log -1 --format='%H %ad %an' 9f2c1a4

# 2. Was it ever public?
gh api repos/:owner/:repo --jq '{private: .private, created: .created_at}'

# 3. Does the current state still contain it?
terraform show -json | jq -r '.values.root_module.resources[]
  | select(.type=="aws_iam_user") | .values | {name, keys: (.access_key // "n/a")}'

# 4. Blast radius from the cloud side, not from the repo
aws cloudtrail lookup-events \
  --lookup-attributes AttributeKey=EventName,AttributeValue=CreateAccessKey \
  --start-time 2026-01-01T00:00:00Z | jq -r '.Events[].CloudTrailEvent|fromjson
  | {user: .userIdentity.arn, ip: .sourceIPAddress, at: .eventTime}'
aws iam list-access-keys --user-name svcapp
```

**Root cause.** Two failures stacked: someone ran `terraform apply` locally (so a
`terraform.tfstate` existed in the working directory) and the `.gitignore` did not
exclude state, so a later `git add -A` committed it. And the secret was a *long-lived*
IAM key, so it was directly usable rather than needing role assumption.

**Fix, in order.**

1. **Rotate first, clean second.** Removing it from git does not un-leak it.

```bash
aws iam create-access-key --user-name svcapp              # ensure we are never locked out
aws iam update-access-key --status Inactive --access-key-id AKIAOLD
# verify the replacement works from the app
aws iam delete-access-key --access-key-id AKIAOLD
```

2. Migrate the identity to a role (instance profile / task role) so there is no long-lived
   key to leak.
3. Scrub the working tree and force-push the branch, but treat it as cosmetic:
```bash
git filter-repo --path terraform.tfstate --invert-paths --force
git push --force --mirror
```
4. Rewrite history properly with `git filter-repo` including the `.gitignore` fix, and
   coordinate because it invalidates every existing clone.
5. **The real fix:** make it impossible.

```gitignore
*.tfstate
*.tfstate.*
.terraform/
# but also: fail the build if state is ever staged
```

```yaml
- name: block-state-in-git
  run: |
    if git ls-files | grep -E '\.tfstate$' ; then
      echo "::error::terraform state is tracked in git"; exit 1
    fi
```
6. Add `sensitive = true`, `ephemeral = true` for write-only variables, and Secrets
   Manager for everything else, so state has nothing valuable in it.

**What to say in an interview.** "Rotation, not scrubbing. Git history is immutable and
was mirrored, so the value must be assumed compromised. Then I remove the ability to
repeat it: role-based access, no local applies, a CI check that fails if a `.tfstate`
path is tracked, and a `.gitignore` that is itself tested."

practice.title: Scenario 3 — Latency spikes every 90 seconds, exactly
practice.afterTopic: Reliability patterns: retries, timeouts, circuit breakers, bulkheads, hedging
items: What to say in an interview
symptoms: p99 latency oscillates between 80ms and 2.4s with a period of roughly 90
rootCause: The new pool's max_lifetime was 60s with a MaxIdleTime of 60s and
practice.reference:
```bash
# 1. Is it our service or an upstream?
#    Compare our server-side histogram with the ALB's TargetResponseTime
curl -gs 'localhost:9090/api/v1/query' \
  --data-urlencode 'query=histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by (le) (rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])))'
curl -gs 'localhost:9090/api/v1/query' \
  --data-urlencode 'query=histogram_quantile(0.99, aws_application_load_balancer_target_response_time_maximum[5m])'
# Server-side p99 is fine, ALB-side is not  -> the time is spent between the two,
# or in the socket hand-off.

# 2. Look for a periodic collaborator: pool metrics
curl -gs 'localhost:9090/api/v1/query' \
  --data-urlencode 'query=max_over_time(db_pool_wait_duration_seconds_count[5m])'

# 3. Correlate with the exact spike times
curl -gs 'localhost:9090/api/v1/query' \
  --data-urlencode 'query=rate(db_pool_connections_in_use[30s])'
```

```go
db.SetConnMaxLifetime(30 * time.Minute)     // far longer than the spike period
db.SetConnMaxIdleTime(5 * time.Minute)      // > the traffic gap, not = it
db.SetMaxIdleConns(50)                      // >= peak concurrent per host
db.SetMaxOpenConns(60)                      // < Postgres max_connections - reserved
db.SetConnMaxIdleTime(5 * time.Minute)
```

**Symptoms.** p99 latency oscillates between 80ms and 2.4s with a period of roughly 90
seconds. CPU is flat at 35%. Errors are zero. Started after a deploy that added a
connection pool.

**Investigation.**

```bash
# 1. Is it our service or an upstream?
#    Compare our server-side histogram with the ALB's TargetResponseTime
curl -gs 'localhost:9090/api/v1/query' \
  --data-urlencode 'query=histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by (le) (rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])))'
curl -gs 'localhost:9090/api/v1/query' \
  --data-urlencode 'query=histogram_quantile(0.99, aws_application_load_balancer_target_response_time_maximum[5m])'
# Server-side p99 is fine, ALB-side is not  -> the time is spent between the two,
# or in the socket hand-off.

# 2. Look for a periodic collaborator: pool metrics
curl -gs 'localhost:9090/api/v1/query' \
  --data-urlencode 'query=max_over_time(db_pool_wait_duration_seconds_count[5m])'

# 3. Correlate with the exact spike times
curl -gs 'localhost:9090/api/v1/query' \
  --data-urlencode 'query=rate(db_pool_connections_in_use[30s])'
```

**Root cause.** The new pool's `max_lifetime` was 60s with a `MaxIdleTime` of 60s and
`MaxIdleConnsPerHost` of 1. Every 60s all connections were closed at once; the next
burst of requests had to open new TCP+TLS connections to Postgres. Under TLS that is
5–20ms each, and with `MaxIdleConnsPerHost: 1` they serialised behind each other — a
classic 90-second sawtooth. The extra 2.3s came from `wait_timeout` being shorter than
the deploy's `ReadTimeout`.

**Fix.**

```go
db.SetConnMaxLifetime(30 * time.Minute)     // far longer than the spike period
db.SetConnMaxIdleTime(5 * time.Minute)      // > the traffic gap, not = it
db.SetMaxIdleConns(50)                      // >= peak concurrent per host
db.SetMaxOpenConns(60)                      // < Postgres max_connections - reserved
db.SetConnMaxIdleTime(5 * time.Minute)
```
Also enable jitter on `ConnMaxLifetime` if the driver supports it, so connections do not
all expire together. Verify with a 10-minute soak test watching
`db_pool_connections_in_use` and `db_pool_wait_duration_seconds`.

**What to say in an interview.** "A perfectly periodic spike is almost never random. I
differenced my server-side latency from the load balancer's, which localises the time,
then I looked for anything on the same period. Pool lifetimes are a very common source
because idle-connection reaping is periodic by design, and `MaxIdleConnsPerHost: 1`
turns the reconnection into a serial queue."

practice.title: Scenario 4 — 502 Bad Gateway on every deploy, only in production
practice.afterTopic: Reliability patterns: retries, timeouts, circuit breakers, bulkheads, hedging
items: The ALB target group's deregistration_delay.timeout_seconds was left at the default
The ECS task definition had no stopTimeout, so SIGTERM was followed by SIGKILL
What to say in an interview
symptoms: CI is green. Every deploy produces ~40 seconds of 502s for 3–5% of
rootCause: Two-part, and staging did not reproduce it because staging had
practice.reference:
```bash
# 1. ECS task state timeline during a deploy
aws ecs describe-services --services acme-prod/orders \
  --query 'services[0].deployments[].{status:status,desired:desiredCount,running:runningCount}'

# 2. ALB target draining config (this is the usual culprit)
aws elbv2 describe-target-group-attributes \
  --target-group-arn "$TG" \
  --query 'Attributes[?contains(Key,`deregistration`)]'
# If deregistration_delay is 0 or 5s, this is the bug.

# 3. Compare with the request duration distribution
curl -gs localhost:9090/api/v1/query \
  --data-urlencode 'query=histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by (le) (rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])))'
# If p99 is 20s and deregistration is 5s, in-flight requests die at deploy time.

# 4. Does the app handle SIGTERM?
kubectl logs <old-pod> --previous | grep -i "signal\|shutdown\|graceful"
```

```
aws elbv2 modify-target-group-attributes \
  --target-group-arn "$TG" \
  --attributes Key=deregistration_delay.timeout_seconds,Value=60

aws ecs update-service --service acme-prod/orders \
  --task-definition "$(aws ecs describe-task-definition \
     --task-definition orders:$(aws ecs list-task-definitions \
     --family-prefix orders --sort DESC --max-items 1 \
     --query 'taskDefinitionArns[0]' --output text | cut -d: -f2))"

# Kubernetes equivalent
lifecycle:
  preStop:
    exec: { command: ["sleep", "10"] }     # let the endpoint controller deregister
terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 45          # > drain time
```

**Symptoms.** CI is green. Every deploy produces ~40 seconds of 502s for 3–5% of
requests, then everything recovers. Never happens in staging (which deploys the same
image).

**Investigation.**

```bash
# 1. ECS task state timeline during a deploy
aws ecs describe-services --services acme-prod/orders \
  --query 'services[0].deployments[].{status:status,desired:desiredCount,running:runningCount}'

# 2. ALB target draining config (this is the usual culprit)
aws elbv2 describe-target-group-attributes \
  --target-group-arn "$TG" \
  --query 'Attributes[?contains(Key,`deregistration`)]'
# If deregistration_delay is 0 or 5s, this is the bug.

# 3. Compare with the request duration distribution
curl -gs localhost:9090/api/v1/query \
  --data-urlencode 'query=histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by (le) (rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])))'
# If p99 is 20s and deregistration is 5s, in-flight requests die at deploy time.

# 4. Does the app handle SIGTERM?
kubectl logs <old-pod> --previous | grep -i "signal\|shutdown\|graceful"
```

**Root cause.** Two-part, and staging did not reproduce it because staging had
`terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 0` and a *shorter* deregistration delay, so there was no
window during which requests could be killed (the pool there drains instantly because
traffic is tiny).

1. The ALB target group's `deregistration_delay.timeout_seconds` was left at the default
   0 (or set to 5) while requests have a p99 of 20s. The target was removed from the
   pool the instant it went out of service.
2. The ECS task definition had no `stopTimeout`, so SIGTERM was followed by SIGKILL
   almost immediately, and the app had no in-flight drain.

**Fix.**

```
aws elbv2 modify-target-group-attributes \
  --target-group-arn "$TG" \
  --attributes Key=deregistration_delay.timeout_seconds,Value=60

aws ecs update-service --service acme-prod/orders \
  --task-definition "$(aws ecs describe-task-definition \
     --task-definition orders:$(aws ecs list-task-definitions \
     --family-prefix orders --sort DESC --max-items 1 \
     --query 'taskDefinitionArns[0]' --output text | cut -d: -f2))"

# Kubernetes equivalent
lifecycle:
  preStop:
    exec: { command: ["sleep", "10"] }     # let the endpoint controller deregister
terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 45          # > drain time
```

**What to say in an interview.** "502-at-deploy is almost always a drain problem, not a
code problem. The fix is a chain of three timeouts that must be ordered correctly:
deregistration delay ≥ longest request, `stopTimeout`/grace period ≥ drain time, and a
preStop pause so the load balancer learns about the shutdown before the process stops
accepting. Staging did not show it because its drain window was proportionally longer
than its request duration — a parity gap I would now test explicitly."

---

practice.title: Scenario 5 — S3 objects 403 after enabling CloudFront
practice.afterTopic: Reliability patterns: retries, timeouts, circuit breakers, bulkheads, hedging
items: The bucket policy allowed Principal: "*" for s3:GetObject, but Block Public
The cache policy included the Authorization (or Origin) header in the cache key
What to say in an interview
symptoms: After putting CloudFront in front of an S3 bucket, direct S3 URLs still
rootCause: Two separate issues, which is why it looked confusing:
practice.reference:
```bash
# 1. Is it the bucket policy or the origin identity?
#    CloudFront with an OAC signs as the OAC principal, not as "Principal: *"
aws cloudfront get-origin-access-control --id "$(aws cloudfront list-origin-access-controls \
  --query 'OriginAccessControlList.Items[0].Id' --output text)" \
  --json 2>/dev/null || aws cloudfront list-origin-access-control-configs

# 2. Bucket policy: is the OAC/service principal allowed, and is BlockPublicAccess on?
aws s3api get-public-access-block --bucket acme-static
aws s3api get-bucket-policy --bucket acme-static | python3 -m json.tool

# 3. Does the *cache policy* forward Authorization/Origin headers to the origin?
#    If the cache key includes Authorization but the origin expects it absent (or the
#    reverse), the OAC signature becomes invalid for cached objects -> 403 after
#    the TTL expires.

# 4. What does CloudFront report?
aws cloudtrail lookup-events \
  --lookup-attributes AttributeKey=EventName,AttributeValue=GetObject \
  --start-time -2h | jq -r '.Events[].CloudTrailEvent | fromjson
  | select(.eventSource=="s3.amazonaws.com") | {ip: .sourceIPAddress, ua: .userAgent}'
# CloudFront edge IPs => request reached the bucket. No S3 log => it never did.
```

```hcl
resource "aws_cloudfront_origin_access_control" "main" {
  name                              = "oac"
  origin_access_control_origin_type = "s3"
  signing_behavior                   = "always"
  signing_protocol                  = "sigv4"
}

data "aws_iam_policy_document" "bucket" {
  statement {
    sid     = "AllowCloudFrontOAC"
    effect  = "Allow"
    actions = ["s3:GetObject"]
    resources = ["${aws_s3_bucket.static.arn}/*"]

    principals {
      type        = "Service"
      identifiers = ["cloudfront.amazonaws.com"]
    }
    # Narrow to THIS distribution; a wildcard Service principal lets any distribution
    # (including someone else's) read your bucket.
    condition {
      test     = "StringEquals"
      variable = "AWS:SourceArn"
      values   = [aws_cloudfront_distribution.main.arn]
    }
  }
}
```

**Symptoms.** After putting CloudFront in front of an S3 bucket, direct S3 URLs still
work, but CloudFront returns `HTTP 403: The request could not be satisfied`. The bucket
policy allows `GetObject` to `*`. Cached assets serve fine for an hour, then 403.

**Investigation.**

```bash
# 1. Is it the bucket policy or the origin identity?
#    CloudFront with an OAC signs as the OAC principal, not as "Principal: *"
aws cloudfront get-origin-access-control --id "$(aws cloudfront list-origin-access-controls \
  --query 'OriginAccessControlList.Items[0].Id' --output text)" \
  --json 2>/dev/null || aws cloudfront list-origin-access-control-configs

# 2. Bucket policy: is the OAC/service principal allowed, and is BlockPublicAccess on?
aws s3api get-public-access-block --bucket acme-static
aws s3api get-bucket-policy --bucket acme-static | python3 -m json.tool

# 3. Does the *cache policy* forward Authorization/Origin headers to the origin?
#    If the cache key includes Authorization but the origin expects it absent (or the
#    reverse), the OAC signature becomes invalid for cached objects -> 403 after
#    the TTL expires.

# 4. What does CloudFront report?
aws cloudtrail lookup-events \
  --lookup-attributes AttributeKey=EventName,AttributeValue=GetObject \
  --start-time -2h | jq -r '.Events[].CloudTrailEvent | fromjson
  | select(.eventSource=="s3.amazonaws.com") | {ip: .sourceIPAddress, ua: .userAgent}'
# CloudFront edge IPs => request reached the bucket. No S3 log => it never did.
```

**Root cause.** Two separate issues, which is why it looked confusing:

1. The bucket policy allowed `Principal: "*"` for `s3:GetObject`, but Block Public
   Access was enabled on the account, so public access is denied regardless — CloudFront
   needs an explicit grant to the **CloudFront distribution** (OAC) as principal.
2. The cache policy included the `Authorization` (or `Origin`) header in the cache key
   *and* forwarded it to the origin. On a miss, the OAC signature is computed correctly
   and the request works. On a hit... it worked too, for an hour. So the real
   contributor to "works then 403s" was the **1-hour default TTL** on cached 200s plus
   the S3 key rotation: objects re-signed/invalidated at a schedule stopped being
   reachable.

**Fix.**

```hcl
resource "aws_cloudfront_origin_access_control" "main" {
  name                              = "oac"
  origin_access_control_origin_type = "s3"
  signing_behavior                   = "always"
  signing_protocol                  = "sigv4"
}

data "aws_iam_policy_document" "bucket" {
  statement {
    sid     = "AllowCloudFrontOAC"
    effect  = "Allow"
    actions = ["s3:GetObject"]
    resources = ["${aws_s3_bucket.static.arn}/*"]

    principals {
      type        = "Service"
      identifiers = ["cloudfront.amazonaws.com"]
    }
    # Narrow to THIS distribution; a wildcard Service principal lets any distribution
    # (including someone else's) read your bucket.
    condition {
      test     = "StringEquals"
      variable = "AWS:SourceArn"
      values   = [aws_cloudfront_distribution.main.arn]
    }
  }
}
```

Then, for public assets, do **not** forward `Authorization` to the origin and do not
include it in the cache key. Verify with `curl -I` on a cache miss (`Cache-Control:
no-cache` request) and a hit.

**What to say in an interview.** "CloudFront with OAC changes the principal: requests are
signed as the OAC, so `Principal: "*"` plus Block Public Access is a guaranteed 403. The
correct grant names `cloudfront.amazonaws.com` scoped by `AWS:SourceArn` to my
distribution. And 'it works then it does not' usually means caching: a request-level
header difference between the miss and the hit paths, or simply TTL vs key rotation."

---

```bash
# 1. Where is the memory? (head chunks vs. query churn)
curl -s localhost:9090/metrics | grep -E 'tsdb_head_series|tsdb_head_chunks'
```


```go
// Per-customer data belongs in logs/traces, not in metric labels.
log.Info("checkout.completed",
    "customer_id", customerID, "tenant_tier", tier, "total_cents", cents)
// and for queries that need "per tenant", use a coarse label:
```

```promql

```

**Symptoms.** Prometheus is OOM-killed every 6–12 hours. Grafana queries time out.
`up` is fine. Disk usage is normal.

**Investigation.**

```bash
# 1. Where is the memory? (head chunks vs. query churn)
curl -s localhost:9090/metrics | grep -E 'tsdb_head_series|tsdb_head_chunks'

# 2. Who added the series?
curl -gs localhost:9090/api/v1/series \
  --data-urlencode 'match[]={__name__=~".+"}' --data-urlencode 'start=...&end=...' \
  | jq -r '.[].__name__' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -20

# 3. Label-value distribution on the worst metric
curl -gs localhost:9090/api/v1/label/label_name/values \
  | jq -r '.data[]' | head -50
# Values that look like ids/urls/uuids are the problem

# 4. Which metric name has the most distinct label sets?
curl -gs localhost:9090/api/v1/query \
  --data-urlencode 'query=topk(10, count by (__name__) ({__name__=~".+"}))' \
  | jq -r '.data.result[] | "\(.metric.__name__) \(.value[1])"'
```

**Root cause.** A new release added `customer_id` as a label on
`http_requests_total` (intending "per-customer latency"). With 40k MAU and ~400 active
customers per minute, that is ~576k new series per minute, and Prometheus keeps the
series alive for 5 minutes of staleness, so the active series count exploded from 12k to
several million. Head chunk memory is the failure mode.

**Fix, immediately.**

```yaml
# prometheus.yml — drop at scrape time so the TSDB never sees the bad series
metric_relabel_configs:
  - source_labels: [customer_id]
    regex: ".+"
    action: labeldrop        # cheap, safe, keeps the metric usable
  # or, if the metric is not needed at all:
  - source_labels: [__name__]
    regex: "http_requests_total_by_customer"
    action: drop
```

Then fix the instrumentation properly:

```go
// Per-customer data belongs in logs/traces, not in metric labels.
log.Info("checkout.completed",
    "customer_id", customerID, "tenant_tier", tier, "total_cents", cents)
// and for queries that need "per tenant", use a coarse label:
metric.WithLabelValues(serviceName, route, method, status, tier)
```

If per-tenant metrics are a genuine requirement, they belong in a system built for high
cardinality (a metrics backend with per-tenant pricing, or logs queried with Athena/Loki
where a `GROUP BY customer_id` costs you nothing per label).

Add a guard so it cannot recur:

```promql
# alert on growth, before OOM
prometheus_tsdb_head_series > 500000
# and a daily review of series-per-metric
topk(20, count by (__name__) ({__name__=~".+"}))
```

**What to say in an interview.** "Cardinality, not volume. A label whose values are
bounded by your user count is a rate multiplier on your TSDB memory. The rule I enforce
is: labels are dimensions you group by, and any unbounded value goes to logs or traces.
I also monitor `prometheus_tsdb_head_series` and alert on growth, and I add a
`labeldrop` rule as a fast mitigation without a deploy."

items: Reservations must be budgeted: the sum of all reservations must leave headroom under
Move the batch fan-out to SQS with concurrency set on the *consumer*, not the
Reduce the duration of the slow function (18s average is a mis-shaped lambda):

What to say in an interview
symptoms: AWS/Lambda Throttles spikes between 14:50 and 15:10 UTC daily. p99

```bash
# 1. Concurrency vs reserved concurrency
curl -gs localhost:9090/api/v1/query --data-urlencode \

# If this is exactly 1000, the account's *unreserved* pool is exhausted.

curl -gs localhost:9090/api/v1/query --data-urlencode \

# 3. Reserved concurrency per function

  {name:FunctionName, reserved:ReservedConcurrentExecutions,
   memory:MemorySize, timeout:Timeout}' --output table

# 4. Is it invocations, or one very slow invocation holding the slot?

```

```yaml
# Batch instead of one invocation per account
BatchSize: 10
MaximumBatchingWindowInSeconds: 5
```

```promql
aws_lambda_concurrent_executions_max / 1000 > 0.7
```

**Symptoms.** `AWS/Lambda` `Throttles` spikes between 14:50 and 15:10 UTC daily. p99
latency for the affected route goes from 90ms to 1.4s. No deploys in that window.

**Investigation.**

```bash
# 1. Concurrency vs reserved concurrency
curl -gs localhost:9090/api/v1/query --data-urlencode \
  'query=max_over_time(aws_lambda_concurrent_executions_max[1h])'
# If this is exactly 1000, the account's *unreserved* pool is exhausted.

# 2. Which function? (dimension = function name)
curl -gs localhost:9090/api/v1/query --data-urlencode \
  'query=sum by (function_name) (aws_lambda_throttles[5m])'

# 3. Reserved concurrency per function
aws lambda list-functions --query 'Functions[*].
  {name:FunctionName, reserved:ReservedConcurrentExecutions,
   memory:MemorySize, timeout:Timeout}' --output table

# 4. Is it invocations, or one very slow invocation holding the slot?
curl -gs localhost:9090/api/v1/query --data-urlencode \
  'query=avg by (function_name) (aws_lambda_duration_average[5m])'
```

**Root cause.** Two functions had `ReservedConcurrentExecutions = 1000` and `500`
respectively. The account's unreserved pool is 1,000 minus the sum of all reservations;
with 1,500 reserved, **every other function in the account had zero unreserved
concurrency** and threw throttles instantly the moment a scheduled batch job started at
14:55 (a report generator that fans out over 30 accounts).

**Fix.**

1. Reservations must be budgeted: the sum of all reservations must leave headroom under
   1,000 (e.g. cap each team at 60% of its measured peak and total at 60% of 1,000).
2. Move the batch fan-out to SQS with concurrency set on the *consumer*, not the
   function, or to a Fargate worker.
3. Reduce the duration of the slow function (18s average is a mis-shaped lambda):

```yaml
# Batch instead of one invocation per account
BatchSize: 10
MaximumBatchingWindowInSeconds: 5
```
4. Alert on reservation headroom:

```promql
aws_lambda_concurrent_executions_max / 1000 > 0.7
```

**What to say in an interview.** "Reserved concurrency is both a cap and a claim on the
account's shared 1,000 unreserved pool. Over-reserving does not give you more
concurrency; it takes it away from everyone else and makes their throttles instantaneous
and invisible. I budget reservations centrally and alert on the ratio."

---

practice.afterTopic: Reliability patterns: retries, timeouts, circuit breakers, bulkheads, hedging
items: Rotate both, in the correct order, with a dual-credential window:
For the *master* user, let RDS own it: manage_master_user_password = true, which
Make rotation not require a deploy. Read secrets at runtime and cache them with a
Restart-strategy consequence: because task definitions read secrets at start, a
What to say in an interview
symptoms: Every application task restarted at 09:02 and immediately failed readiness
rootCause: The application user svcapp was created with a password stored in
practice.reference:
```bash
# 1. Is the secret actually correct now, and when did it change?
aws secretsmanager get-secret-value --secret-id prod/orders/db \
  --query '{version: VersionId, created: CreatedDate}'
aws secretsmanager describe-secret --secret-id prod/orders/db \
  --query '{rotated: LastRotatedDate, changed: LastChangedDate}'

# 2. What does the app read? (task definition caches the secret at task start)
aws ecs describe-task-definition --task-definition orders:47 \
  --query 'taskDefinition.containerDefinitions[0].secrets'

# 3. Is the RDS master user password also rotated, and are they the SAME user?
aws rds describe-db-clusters --db-cluster-identifier orders-prod \
  --query 'DBClusters[0].{master:MasterUsername, managed:ManageMasterUserPassword}'

# 4. Connect manually with the value from the secret
PGPASSWORD=$(aws secretsmanager get-secret-value --secret-id prod/orders/db \
  --query SecretString --output text | jq -r .password) \
  psql -h orders.cluster-endpoint -U svcapp -d orders -c 'select 1'
```

```sql
-- Postgres: add the new password alongside the old for a transition period
ALTER USER svcapp WITH PASSWORD 'new';
-- (Postgres does not support two passwords; use a second role during rotation)
CREATE ROLE svcapp_next LOGIN PASSWORD 'new';
GRANT svcapp TO svcapp_next;                 -- inherit the existing grants
-- 1. update the secret + redeploy  2. verify  3. drop the old role
```

```go
type secretCache struct {
    mu sync.RWMutex
    val string
    expires time.Time
    ttl time.Duration
}
func (c *secretCache) Get(ctx context.Context) (string, error) { /* refresh from
    Secrets Manager when expired; on rotation, new pods and refreshed caches converge */ }
```

**Symptoms.** Every application task restarted at 09:02 and immediately failed readiness
with `FATAL: password authentication failed for user "svcapp"`. The Secrets Manager
secret was rotated at 09:01 as part of routine rotation. New tasks fail; tasks started
before 09:01 work.

**Investigation.**

```bash
# 1. Is the secret actually correct now, and when did it change?
aws secretsmanager get-secret-value --secret-id prod/orders/db \
  --query '{version: VersionId, created: CreatedDate}'
aws secretsmanager describe-secret --secret-id prod/orders/db \
  --query '{rotated: LastRotatedDate, changed: LastChangedDate}'

# 2. What does the app read? (task definition caches the secret at task start)
aws ecs describe-task-definition --task-definition orders:47 \
  --query 'taskDefinition.containerDefinitions[0].secrets'

# 3. Is the RDS master user password also rotated, and are they the SAME user?
aws rds describe-db-clusters --db-cluster-identifier orders-prod \
  --query 'DBClusters[0].{master:MasterUsername, managed:ManageMasterUserPassword}'

# 4. Connect manually with the value from the secret
PGPASSWORD=$(aws secretsmanager get-secret-value --secret-id prod/orders/db \
  --query SecretString --output text | jq -r .password) \
  psql -h orders.cluster-endpoint -U svcapp -d orders -c 'select 1'
```

**Root cause.** The application user `svcapp` was created with a password stored in
Secrets Manager, and rotation updated **the Secrets Manager value only** — the actual
Postgres role password was never changed. The mismatch was invisible until a task
restarted, because the running processes still held the *old* password in their
environment and Postgres had never changed.

**Fix.**

1. Rotate both, in the correct order, with a dual-credential window:

```sql
-- Postgres: add the new password alongside the old for a transition period
ALTER USER svcapp WITH PASSWORD 'new';
-- (Postgres does not support two passwords; use a second role during rotation)
CREATE ROLE svcapp_next LOGIN PASSWORD 'new';
GRANT svcapp TO svcapp_next;                 -- inherit the existing grants
-- 1. update the secret + redeploy  2. verify  3. drop the old role
```

2. For the *master* user, let RDS own it: `manage_master_user_password = true`, which
   gives you an Aurora master secret that RDS rotates for you, and never put it in
   Terraform state.
3. **Make rotation not require a deploy.** Read secrets at runtime and cache them with a
   TTL shorter than the rotation interval (e.g. 15 min), so a rotation propagates without
   a restart:

```go
type secretCache struct {
    mu sync.RWMutex
    val string
    expires time.Time
    ttl time.Duration
}
func (c *secretCache) Get(ctx context.Context) (string, error) { /* refresh from
    Secrets Manager when expired; on rotation, new pods and refreshed caches converge */ }
```
4. Restart-strategy consequence: because task definitions read secrets at start, a
   credential change without a rotation-safe app is an outage. This is a design finding,
   not an operational one.

**What to say in an interview.** "Rotation has to touch both sides, and it has to be
observable. The dangerous property here is that the outage only appears on restart, so
the failure is delayed from the cause — which is why I would add a canary that reads
the secret and authenticates as part of readiness, and move to RDS-managed master
credentials so this class of drift cannot exist."

---

Add a correctness SLI that is not HTTP-based:
Reconcile the SLO against *external* signals: support ticket rate per 1,000 orders as
Add a synthetic checkout with a scripted payment decline and assert the HTTP status.
What to say in an interview
symptoms: The availability SLI reads 99.99% and error-budget alerts have never
rootCause: The service returned 200 OK with a body like
practice.reference:
```bash
# 1. Check the SLI query's failure definition
curl -gs localhost:9090/api/v1/query --data-urlencode \
  'query=sum by (status, error_type, route) (rate(http_requests_total{service="orders"}[1d]))'
# status="200" but error_type="payment_declined" -> the SLI is technically correct and
# semantically wrong.

# 2. What does the app return for a business failure?
curl -s -X POST https://api.example.com/v1/checkout -d '{...}' -i | head -1
curl -s -X POST https://api.example.com/v1/checkout -d '{...}' -i | grep -i 'x-error'

# 3. Does the SLI exclude the failing population?
curl -gs localhost:9090/api/v1/query --data-urlencode \
  'query=sum by (scrape) (rate(http_requests_total[1d]))'
# If one "scrape" value dominates, your exclusion is filtering real traffic.
```

```promql
- record: orders:business_outcome:success_ratio_1h
  expr: |
    sum(rate(checkout_outcome_total{outcome="success"}[1h]))
      / sum(rate(checkout_outcome_total[1h]))
```

**Symptoms.** The availability SLI reads 99.99% and error-budget alerts have never
fired. But the weekly support report says ~3% of checkout attempts failed for users, and
internal testing reproduces a "failed" checkout that returns HTTP 200.

**Investigation.**

```bash
# 1. Check the SLI query's failure definition
curl -gs localhost:9090/api/v1/query --data-urlencode \
  'query=sum by (status, error_type, route) (rate(http_requests_total{service="orders"}[1d]))'
# status="200" but error_type="payment_declined" -> the SLI is technically correct and
# semantically wrong.

# 2. What does the app return for a business failure?
curl -s -X POST https://api.example.com/v1/checkout -d '{...}' -i | head -1
curl -s -X POST https://api.example.com/v1/checkout -d '{...}' -i | grep -i 'x-error'

# 3. Does the SLI exclude the failing population?
curl -gs localhost:9090/api/v1/query --data-urlencode \
  'query=sum by (scrape) (rate(http_requests_total[1d]))'
# If one "scrape" value dominates, your exclusion is filtering real traffic.
```

**Root cause.** The service returned `200 OK` with a body like
`{"status":"failed","reason":"payment_declined"}` for every business-level failure —
including a PSP timeout it *should* have surfaced as a 5xx. The SLI, defined as
"non-5xx ratio", was measuring HTTP status codes and therefore measured exactly the wrong
thing. This is the most dangerous observability bug class: **the dashboard is green while
users fail**, because the metric measures the implementation rather than the experience.

**Fix.**

1. Fix the semantics first: **user-visible failure must be a 5xx** (or at least a
   distinguished, counted status). Distinguish:
   - `400/422` client validation (excluded from the SLI)
   - `402` payment declined by the *user's* provider (excluded, with a carve-out)
   - `502/503` upstream we depend on (counted as failure)
   - `500` our bug (counted as failure)
2. Add a **correctness SLI** that is not HTTP-based:

```promql
- record: orders:business_outcome:success_ratio_1h
  expr: |
    sum(rate(checkout_outcome_total{outcome="success"}[1h]))
      / sum(rate(checkout_outcome_total[1h]))
```
with `outcome` ∈ {`success`, `declined`, `timeout`, `error`}, emitted from the domain
code rather than the HTTP layer.
3. Reconcile the SLO against *external* signals: support ticket rate per 1,000 orders as
   a weekly input to the SLO review. A green SLO plus a rising ticket rate is a contradiction
   you must resolve, not average out.
4. Add a synthetic checkout with a scripted payment decline and assert the HTTP status.

**What to say in an interview.** "A 100% green SLO with rising support tickets is a
definition bug, not a victory. SLIs must be defined from the user's perspective, not
from the HTTP status code, and I cross-check the SLI against an independent signal. The
hardest part of reliability work is convincing people that a green dashboard and failing
users can coexist."

---

practice.title: Scenario 10 — Terraform apply hangs on a resource for 40 minutes
practice.afterTopic: Reliability patterns: retries, timeouts, circuit breakers, bulkheads, hedging
items: Never set apply_immediately = true in a module used by prod.
Schedule parameter changes: apply them, then let the maintenance window do the reboot;
Long Terraform timeouts are a symptom, not a fix:
Add a pre-apply check to the pipeline:
Use a schema-migration tool with its own locking for DDL, separate from Terraform.
What to say in an interview
symptoms: terraform apply for a routine change hangs at
rootCause: apply_immediately = true on the parameter group change triggered an
practice.reference:
```bash
# 1. What is the API actually doing? (do not wait for Terraform)
aws rds describe-db-clusters --db-cluster-identifier orders-prod \
  --query 'DBClusters[0].{status:Status, modifying:Status,
   engine:EngineVersion, storage:AllocatedStorage}'

aws rds describe-events --source-identifier orders-prod --duration 60 \
  | jq -r '.Events[] | "\(.Date) \(.Message)"'

# 2. Is something else holding a lock?
aws rds describe-db-parameters --db-cluster-identifier orders-prod  # pending reboot?
aws rds describe-db-clusters --db-cluster-identifier orders-prod \
  --query 'DBClusters[0].PendingModifiedValues'

# 3. Is there a long-running migration holding a lock?
aws rds-data execute-statement --resource-arn "$ARN" --database orders \
  --sql 'select pid, state, query, now()-query_start as duration
         from pg_stat_activity
         where state <> '"'"'idle'"'"' order by duration desc limit 10'
```

```hcl
resource "aws_rds_cluster" "main" {
  # Never let Terraform reboot prod during an apply
  apply_immediately           = false
  preferred_maintenance_window = "sun:04:30-sun:05:30"

  lifecycle {
    prevent_destroy = true
    ignore_changes  = [engine_version]   # only if upgrades are managed separately
  }
}

resource "aws_rds_cluster_parameter_group" "main" {
  parameter {
    name         = "log_min_duration_statement"
    value        = "500"
    # pending-reboot = change recorded, applied in the maintenance window
    apply_method = "pending-reboot"
  }
}
```

```hcl
resource "aws_rds_cluster" "main" {
  timeouts { create = "3h" update = "3h" delete = "3h" }
}
```

```bash
# No long-running queries, no pending reboot, no maintenance-window-adjacent apply
aws rds describe-db-clusters --db-cluster-identifier orders-prod \
  --query 'DBClusters[0].PendingModifiedValues' | grep -q 'null' || {
    echo "pending RDS modifications; aborting apply"; exit 1; }
```

**Symptoms.** `terraform apply` for a routine change hangs at
`aws_db_instance.main: Still creating... [10m40s elapsed]`. Eventually fails with a
provider timeout. The RDS cluster has `deletion_protection = false` and
`apply_immediately = true`.

**Investigation.**

```bash
# 1. What is the API actually doing? (do not wait for Terraform)
aws rds describe-db-clusters --db-cluster-identifier orders-prod \
  --query 'DBClusters[0].{status:Status, modifying:Status,
   engine:EngineVersion, storage:AllocatedStorage}'

aws rds describe-events --source-identifier orders-prod --duration 60 \
  | jq -r '.Events[] | "\(.Date) \(.Message)"'

# 2. Is something else holding a lock?
aws rds describe-db-parameters --db-cluster-identifier orders-prod  # pending reboot?
aws rds describe-db-clusters --db-cluster-identifier orders-prod \
  --query 'DBClusters[0].PendingModifiedValues'

# 3. Is there a long-running migration holding a lock?
aws rds-data execute-statement --resource-arn "$ARN" --database orders \
  --sql 'select pid, state, query, now()-query_start as duration
         from pg_stat_activity
         where state <> '"'"'idle'"'"' order by duration desc limit 10'
```

**Root cause.** `apply_immediately = true` on the parameter group change triggered an
**instance reboot** during a business-hours apply, while the Terraform timeout (default
~20 minutes for RDS) was shorter than the reboot plus a `Modifying` state that also
required a parameter group apply to *pending-reboot* consumers. Terraform then retried
on its next run, and because the resource was mid-modification, the state recorded an
inconsistent view. A long-running analytics query on the writer extended the reboot
window past the timeout.

**Fix.**

```hcl
resource "aws_rds_cluster" "main" {
  # Never let Terraform reboot prod during an apply
  apply_immediately           = false
  preferred_maintenance_window = "sun:04:30-sun:05:30"

  lifecycle {
    prevent_destroy = true
    ignore_changes  = [engine_version]   # only if upgrades are managed separately
  }
}

resource "aws_rds_cluster_parameter_group" "main" {
  parameter {
    name         = "log_min_duration_statement"
    value        = "500"
    # pending-reboot = change recorded, applied in the maintenance window
    apply_method = "pending-reboot"
  }
}
```

Plus operational controls:

1. **Never set `apply_immediately = true`** in a module used by prod.
2. Schedule parameter changes: apply them, then let the maintenance window do the reboot;
   verify with `PendingModifiedValues` becoming empty.
3. Long Terraform timeouts are a symptom, not a fix:

```hcl
resource "aws_rds_cluster" "main" {
  timeouts { create = "3h" update = "3h" delete = "3h" }
}
```
4. Add a pre-apply check to the pipeline:

```bash
# No long-running queries, no pending reboot, no maintenance-window-adjacent apply
aws rds describe-db-clusters --db-cluster-identifier orders-prod \
  --query 'DBClusters[0].PendingModifiedValues' | grep -q 'null' || {
    echo "pending RDS modifications; aborting apply"; exit 1; }
```
5. Use a schema-migration tool with its own locking for DDL, separate from Terraform.

**What to say in an interview.** "Terraform's timeout is not a timeout for the cloud's
work. A 40-minute hang means the API call is doing something I did not anticipate — here,
a reboot triggered by `apply_immediately`. The fix is to move the disruptive action into
the maintenance window, keep `apply_immediately` off in shared modules, and treat a
Terraform timeout as a signal to go look at the provider API rather than to raise the
number."

practice.title: Scenario 11 — Autoscaling does not scale up fast enough, and the graph is confusing
practice.afterTopic: Reliability patterns: retries, timeouts, circuit breakers, bulkheads, hedging

What to say in an interview
symptoms: Traffic increases 5× over 4 minutes. p99 breaches the SLO for 6 minutes.
practice.reference:
```bash
# 1. How long from launch to healthy?
aws autoscaling describe-scaling-activities --auto-scaling-group-name orders-asg \
  --query 'Activities[-5:].[StartTime,StatusCode,Details]' --output table
# Launch → Pending:Wait → Pending:Proceed → Healthy: 3m40s

# 2. What is the boot sequence? (bake-in problem)
aws ecs describe-services --services acme-prod/orders \
  --query 'services[0].deployments[0].{circuitBreaker:deploymentCircuitBreaker,
     maxPercent:deploymentConfiguration.maximumPercent,
     minPercent:deploymentConfiguration.minimumHealthyPercent}'

# 3. Is the scaling policy CPU-based with a cooldown longer than the incident?
aws autoscaling describe-policies --auto-scaling-group-name orders-asg \
  --query 'ScalingPolicies[].{name:PolicyName, cooldown:Cooldown, step:StepAdjustments}'

# 4. Does the app need warm-up before it can serve efficiently?
#    (JIT, connection pool fill, cache cold, JVM/Go heap)
```

```hcl
resource "aws_appautoscaling_policy" "rps" {
  policy_type        = "TargetTrackingScaling"
  scalable_dimension = "ecs:service:DesiredCount"
  resource_id        = aws_appautoscaling_target.ecs.resource_id
  target_tracking_scaling_policy_configuration {
    target_value      = 250        # requests/min per task, from measured p50 cost
    scale_out_cooldown = 60
    scale_in_cooldown  = 300
    predefined_metric_specification {
      predefined_metric_type = "ALBRequestCountPerTarget"
      resource_label = "${aws_lb.main.arn_suffix}/${aws_lb_target_group.app.arn_suffix}"
    }
  }
}
```

```hcl
resource "aws_autoscaling_schedule" "predictive" {
  name              = "weekday-morning"
  scheduled_action  = aws_autoscaling_policy.scale_out.arn
  min_size          = 14
  max_size          = 40
  desired_capacity  = 14
  recurrence        = "0 8 * * MON-FRI"   # UTC; before the known ramp
}
```

**Symptoms.** Traffic increases 5× over 4 minutes. p99 breaches the SLO for 6 minutes.
The ASG graph shows desired capacity rising, but instances take 3–4 minutes to become
healthy. CloudWatch shows CPU at 95% the whole time.

**Investigation.**

```bash
# 1. How long from launch to healthy?
aws autoscaling describe-scaling-activities --auto-scaling-group-name orders-asg \
  --query 'Activities[-5:].[StartTime,StatusCode,Details]' --output table
# Launch → Pending:Wait → Pending:Proceed → Healthy: 3m40s

# 2. What is the boot sequence? (bake-in problem)
aws ecs describe-services --services acme-prod/orders \
  --query 'services[0].deployments[0].{circuitBreaker:deploymentCircuitBreaker,
     maxPercent:deploymentConfiguration.maximumPercent,
     minPercent:deploymentConfiguration.minimumHealthyPercent}'

# 3. Is the scaling policy CPU-based with a cooldown longer than the incident?
aws autoscaling describe-policies --auto-scaling-group-name orders-asg \
  --query 'ScalingPolicies[].{name:PolicyName, cooldown:Cooldown, step:StepAdjustments}'

# 4. Does the app need warm-up before it can serve efficiently?
#    (JIT, connection pool fill, cache cold, JVM/Go heap)
```

**Root cause.** Two compounding problems:

1. **The scaling signal was CPU with a 300-second cooldown.** Scale-out took 5 minutes
   to react after the cooldown expired — and the cooldown is meant to prevent thrashing,
   so it *by design* slows the response to a genuine spike.
2. **Boot time was 3m40s**: `startPeriod=45s` on the ECS health check plus a container
   image that ran migrations and warmed caches at boot, plus an ALB health check at
   15s × 3 thresholds. The instance was registered as serving almost immediately (target
   group health check passed on the first container health check returning 200 from a
   warm-up endpoint), then spent 3 minutes actually warming.

**Fix.**

1. **Scale on request rate, not CPU**, with a short cooldown:

```hcl
resource "aws_appautoscaling_policy" "rps" {
  policy_type        = "TargetTrackingScaling"
  scalable_dimension = "ecs:service:DesiredCount"
  resource_id        = aws_appautoscaling_target.ecs.resource_id
  target_tracking_scaling_policy_configuration {
    target_value      = 250        # requests/min per task, from measured p50 cost
    scale_out_cooldown = 60
    scale_in_cooldown  = 300
    predefined_metric_specification {
      predefined_metric_type = "ALBRequestCountPerTarget"
      resource_label = "${aws_lb.main.arn_suffix}/${aws_lb_target_group.app.arn_suffix}"
    }
  }
}
```
2. **Pre-warm capacity**: keep `min_count` high enough for a known baseline plus 20%, so
   growth starts from warm capacity.
3. **Reduce boot time** so replacement capacity is useful sooner:
   - Separate liveness (process) from readiness (warmed); register the target with
     readiness, not liveness. The ALB health check must point at `/readyz`.
   - Do migrations at *deploy* time (as a one-off task), not at container start.
   - Warm caches lazily/asynchronously and report readiness before warming if the app can
     serve partially.
4. **Predictive scaling** for known patterns (the 14:00 batch spike):

```hcl
resource "aws_autoscaling_schedule" "predictive" {
  name              = "weekday-morning"
  scheduled_action  = aws_autoscaling_policy.scale_out.arn
  min_size          = 14
  max_size          = 40
  desired_capacity  = 14
  recurrence        = "0 8 * * MON-FRI"   # UTC; before the known ramp
}
```
5. **Have the capacity you cannot predict** ready: on-demand base capacity above the
   minimum, so scale-out is not the only defence.

**What to say in an interview.** "Autoscaling is not a solution for a spike faster than
its reaction time; it is a solution for sustained growth. So the work is three-fold:
predict the predictable (schedules), react fast to the rest (request-rate target
tracking with a short cooldown), and make new capacity useful quickly (boot-time
budget). And keep enough warm baseline capacity that scaling is not the first line of
defence."

The log group had retentionInDays = 0 (never expire) because it was created by

What to say in an interview
symptoms: CloudWatch Logs invoice jumped from \$600 to \$3,400 in a month. Queries
practice.reference:
```bash
# 1. Volume by log group and stream
aws logs describe-log-groups --log-group-name-prefix /ecs/ --output json \
  | jq -r '.logGroups[] | "\(.logGroupName)\t\(.storedBytes)\t\(.retentionInDays)"' \
  | sort -k2 -n -r | head -20

# 2. Volume over time: which day, and which event type?
aws logs start-query --log-group-name /ecs/orders \
  --start-time $START --end-time $END \
  --query-string 'fields @timestamp, @message | stats count(*) by bin(1h) | sort by count(*) desc | limit 20' \

aws logs start-query --log-group-name /ecs/orders \

# 3. Retention configuration (a common accidental 0 = forever)
aws logs describe-log-groups --log-group-name-prefix /ecs/ --output json \
  | jq -r '.logGroups[] | select(.retentionInDays == 0) | .logGroupName'
```

```hcl
resource "aws_cloudwatch_log_group" "app" {
  name              = "/ecs/orders"
  retention_in_days = 14          # NEVER omit this: default is never expire
  kms_key_id        = aws_kms_key.logs.arn
}

resource "aws_cloudwatch_log_group" "audit" {
  name              = "/audit/orders"
  retention_in_days = 2555        # 7 years, compliance requirement, explicitly justified
  kms_key_id        = aws_kms_key.logs.arn
}
```

```python
# Configure noisy libraries explicitly — the single biggest volume lever
for noisy in ("urllib3", "httpx", "httpcore", "botocore", "asyncio", "aiomysql"):
    logging.getLogger(noisy).setLevel(logging.WARNING)

# Never log bodies at INFO
if response.status_code >= 400:
    log.warning("upstream_error", status=response.status_code,
                error_type=type(exc).__name__,     # not the whole exception + payload
                body_preview=response.text[:512])  # truncated, and only on error
```

```yaml
# Vector: drop and sample before it reaches the expensive index
sinks:
  console:
    inputs: [stdout]
    transforms:
      - name: drop_debug_samples
        type: sample
        rate: 20                # 20% of DEBUG records
        drop_on_abort: false
        exclude:
          - type: exclude_field
            name: level
            conditions: [ "level == \"error\"" ]   # never sample errors
      - name: redact
        type: redact
        fields:
          - match: '"authorization":"Bearer (.*?)"'
            replace: '"authorization":"Bearer [REDACTED]"'
      - name: drop_bulk_fields
        type: drop_fields
        fields: ["body", "response_payload", "sql"]
```

**Symptoms.** CloudWatch Logs invoice jumped from \$600 to \$3,400 in a month. Queries
time out. Log search is so slow that responders give up and use `kubectl logs` on a
guess.

**Investigation.**

```bash
# 1. Volume by log group and stream
aws logs describe-log-groups --log-group-name-prefix /ecs/ --output json \
  | jq -r '.logGroups[] | "\(.logGroupName)\t\(.storedBytes)\t\(.retentionInDays)"' \
  | sort -k2 -n -r | head -20

# 2. Volume over time: which day, and which event type?
aws logs start-query --log-group-name /ecs/orders \
  --start-time $START --end-time $END \
  --query-string 'fields @timestamp, @message | stats count(*) by bin(1h) | sort by count(*) desc | limit 20' \
  --output text
# then
aws logs start-query --log-group-name /ecs/orders \
  --query-string 'fields @message | filter @message like /?/ | stats count(*) by substr(@message,1,60) | sort by count(*) desc | limit 20' \
  --output text

# 3. Retention configuration (a common accidental 0 = forever)
aws logs describe-log-groups --log-group-name-prefix /ecs/ --output json \
  | jq -r '.logGroups[] | select(.retentionInDays == 0) | .logGroupName'
```

**Root cause.** Three compounding causes:

1. A new library version logged at INFO with **full HTTP response bodies** on every
   request, including a 2KB JSON payload per call: 40k requests/hour × 2KB.
2. The log group had `retentionInDays = 0` (never expire) because it was created by
   Terraform without the `retention_in_days` argument — invisible in the console until
   you look at "stored bytes".
3. No sampling: DEBUG logs from a dependency ran at 100% in production because the level
   was set by an env var default.

**Fix.**

```hcl
resource "aws_cloudwatch_log_group" "app" {
  name              = "/ecs/orders"
  retention_in_days = 14          # NEVER omit this: default is never expire
  kms_key_id        = aws_kms_key.logs.arn
}

resource "aws_cloudwatch_log_group" "audit" {
  name              = "/audit/orders"
  retention_in_days = 2555        # 7 years, compliance requirement, explicitly justified
  kms_key_id        = aws_kms_key.logs.arn
}
```

Application-side:

```python
# Configure noisy libraries explicitly — the single biggest volume lever
for noisy in ("urllib3", "httpx", "httpcore", "botocore", "asyncio", "aiomysql"):
    logging.getLogger(noisy).setLevel(logging.WARNING)

# Never log bodies at INFO
if response.status_code >= 400:
    log.warning("upstream_error", status=response.status_code,
                error_type=type(exc).__name__,     # not the whole exception + payload
                body_preview=response.text[:512])  # truncated, and only on error
```

Pipeline-side (so the app does not have to be perfect):

```yaml
# Vector: drop and sample before it reaches the expensive index
sinks:
  console:
    inputs: [stdout]
    transforms:
      - name: drop_debug_samples
        type: sample
        rate: 20                # 20% of DEBUG records
        drop_on_abort: false
        exclude:
          - type: exclude_field
            name: level
            conditions: [ "level == \"error\"" ]   # never sample errors
      - name: redact
        type: redact
        fields:
          - match: '"authorization":"Bearer (.*?)"'
            replace: '"authorization":"Bearer [REDACTED]"'
      - name: drop_bulk_fields
        type: drop_fields
        fields: ["body", "response_payload", "sql"]
```

Retention strategy: 14 days hot in CloudWatch (searchable, alerts, investigations) →
export to S3 → Athena for anything older, 400-day archive in Glacier for compliance.

**What to say in an interview.** "Log cost is an engineering problem with three levers:
stop emitting it (library levels and no payload logging), stop indexing it (a collector
with sampling and redaction), and stop storing it (explicit retention, plus a tiered
archive). And the reason I care about latency is that a log store nobody can query is
both expensive and useless — the cost is not the money, it is that responders fall back
to guessing during incidents."

questions.text: Explain the difference between Terraform state and your Git repository
questions.answer: Git holds the *declared intent*: the configuration, its history, who changed it and why. State holds the *observed reality*: for each declared resource, the provider's actual ID, its current attributes, and the dependencies Terraform resolved when it created it. They are different kinds of data with different lifecycles. Git is append-only and reviewed; state is a mutable binary-ish blob that changes on every apply, is locked during operations, and — critically — contains sensitive attributes in plaintext. The consequence people miss: because state is the only mapping from a logical address like aws_instance.web to i-0abc123, losing or corrupting state does not "lose the servers" — it makes Terraform believe those servers do not exist and try to create replacements. That is why state is backed up to versioned object storage, why it is encrypted, and why deleting it is an incident, not a cleanup. I would also say what state is *not*: not a source of truth about desired state (Git is), and not a backup mechanism (it is the most recent snapshot of what exists, not a point-in-time recoverable history of your data).

questions.text: What is drift, how do you detect it, and when is drift acceptable?
questions.answer: Drift is the gap between what Terraform recorded and what the provider API reports — usually because somebody changed something in the console, or because another system legitimately owns a field. Detection is terraform plan -refresh-only, run on a schedule in CI and posted as a diff; a clean plan is the only real proof of parity. Acceptable drift is when another controller legitimately owns that attribute: an autoscaler writing desired_capacity, a managed service writing its own status fields, Kubernetes controllers writing spec fields. In that case I declare ownership explicitly with a narrowly scoped ignore_changes — one attribute, never all — and I monitor the owner instead. Unacceptable drift is anything security- or data-related: a widened security group, a public bucket, a changed encryption setting. For those, the fix is not ignore_changes; it is removing console write access (SCP/permission boundary) so drift stops being possible, plus a plan to reconcile. The distinction I make in review: ignore_changes is a declaration of ownership, and using it to silence a real problem is how a security group stays open for a year.

questions.text: Your terraform plan shows -/+ on a resource. Is that safe?
questions.answer: Not automatically. -/+ means Terraform will destroy and recreate, because some attribute is ForceNew and the provider does not offer an in-place update. That has three classes of risk: identity (a new resource ID — an ENI gets a new private IP, a DNS record points at a new target), data (if the resource holds state you cannot recreate), and availability (the resource is genuinely gone for the duration of the replacement). So my answer is: read the plan's change.actions and the attribute that forces it, then decide by class. For an RDS cluster, changing the major version or a ForceNew parameter is a replacement, and I would use a clone-and-cutover, not a replacement. For a security group, replacement means traffic in flight sees a window with no rules. For an instance with an attached ENI, replacement means DNS staleness. The correct engineering response is layered: prevent_destroy for anything stateful (so an accidental apply fails at plan time), create_before_destroy where identity must persist, tests in a state-clone environment, and a change window with a snapshot. I would never raise the Terraform timeout to make a replacement "fit"; I would redesign it.

questions.text: Explain the AWS shared responsibility model, and where is the boundary for RDS?
questions.answer: The provider is responsible for security *of* the cloud — hardware, facility, hypervisor, host OS, physical network. The customer is responsible for security *in* the cloud — data, IAM policies, network configuration, and the guest OS on EC2. The interesting part, and what I would add unprompted, is that the boundary moves with the service, and for RDS it is narrower than people assume. AWS owns the host, storage, replication, and backup infrastructure. I still own the data, the schema, grants and roles, iam_auth, TLS settings, parameter group values (including anything with pending-reboot), extension versions, and every query. A managed database gives me patching and failover; it gives me nothing about whether my parameter group is sane. And there is no shared-responsibility escape from IAM: AWS owns the implementation of the IAM service, and I own every single policy in the account. Least privilege is entirely on me.

questions.text: How do you design least-privilege IAM for a service?
questions.answer: I treat it as a loop, not a setting. First, run the workload under a permissive role for a few days and read CloudTrail to learn what it actually calls. Then write a policy that grants exactly that, plus known planned needs, scoped by resource ARN — table, not *; bucket prefix, not bucket; a specific KMS key, not kms:*. Then wrap it in a fail-closed guardrail: an SCP or permission boundary so a mistake in the identity policy cannot exceed the ceiling. Then run Access Analyzer's "unused access" analysis for 30 days and delete what was never used, and repeat monthly. Two details that matter in review: conditions are where the real power is (aws:SourceVpce, aws:PrincipalOrgID, aws:SourceArn, s3:prefix), and the classic escalation is iam:PassRole combined with a service permission — Access Analyzer's policy validation now rejects that class by default, and I make sure it is on. For humans: SSO with short-lived sessions and MFA, never access keys. For workloads: roles everywhere — instance profiles, task roles — so there is no long-lived key on a machine to leak.

questions.text: What is the difference between a stateful and a stateless resource, and why does it change your deployment strategy?
questions.answer: Stateful means the resource holds data whose loss or duplication is user-visible: databases, queues, buckets, disks. Stateless means any instance can serve any request and losing one is uninteresting: web servers, caches, API replicas. The strategy difference is the tolerance for replacement. Stateless replacement is a non-event — start a new one, drain the old, delete it. Stateful replacement is a data event, which is why you want blue/green with replication, snapshots before changes, prevent_destroy, and a tested restore. The second difference is which side of the rollout can be rolled back. Stateless deploys roll forward/backward by swapping which instances are live. Stateful deploys roll forward by *contract-then-expand*: add a nullable column, dual-write, backfill, switch reads, drop the old. Destructive DDL cannot be rolled back, so it cannot be in the same deploy as the code that stops using the old column. The third, which people forget: statefulness determines your scale-down policy. A stateless tier can scale to zero or one; a stateful tier needs warm capacity because restoring or re-replicating from cold takes minutes during an incident.

questions.text: Walk me through an Nginx request lifecycle
questions.answer: A worker process accepts the connection, parses the request, matches server by SNI/Host and location by prefix/regex/exact, performs the TLS handshake if it is an ssl server, evaluates limit_req/limit_conn, selects an upstream server by the pool's algorithm, opens a connection to it (proxy_connect_timeout), sends the request with rewritten headers (proxy_http_version 1.1, Host, X-Forwarded-*), reads the response (proxy_read_timeout between reads, proxy_send_timeout for the request body), optionally buffers it to memory or disk, writes it to the client with add_headers applied, and logs with the timings. Two things I always mention because they are the most common bugs: proxy_pass with a trailing slash rewrites the URI, and proxy_set_header Connection "" is required (with keepalive in the upstream) or you get no connection reuse at all. And the concurrency arithmetic: worker_processes × worker_connections / 2 is the maximum concurrent proxied requests, because each one consumes a client socket and an upstream socket, and the LimitNOFILE in the systemd unit must match.

questions.text: You added a rate limit and throughput dropped. Why?
questions.answer: In order of likelihood: (1) I used delay instead of nodelay, so bursts are smoothed at the configured rate and every client pays up to burst/rate seconds of latency; (2) the zone is too small, so keys are evicted and the module's state churns — the error log says "could not allocate node in the shared zone", and eviction effectively *allows* traffic while doing it; (3) the key is $binary_remote_addr behind a CDN, so either everyone shares one bucket or, if I keyed on X-Forwarded-For without set_real_ip_from restricting who may set it, a client can rotate their header to bypass the limit entirely; (4) limit_req_status is still the default 503, so dashboards attribute throttling to the backend and someone "fixes" the backend. I would also note the cost angle: SQS-style request pricing makes polling the bill, so rate limiting interacts with your observability bill too.

questions.text: Explain HSTS and when preload is a bad idea
questions.answer: HSTS (Strict-Transport-Security) tells the browser to refuse plaintext HTTP to this host for max-age seconds. The risk is that it is a one-way door: once a browser has cached it, you cannot recall it from the client, and any legitimate plaintext HTTP to that host — a health-check poller on an http subdomain, an internal redirect, a legacy integration — fails until the header changes *and* the browser cache expires. includeSubDomains extends it to every subdomain, so one misconfigured internal host breaks everything beneath it. preload is stricter still: browsers require it to be at least a year, and submitting the domain to the preload list means users who have never visited it are also locked in. So the practice is to stage it: max-age=300, watch, then max-age=86400, then a year — and add includeSubDomains only after an inventory shows every subdomain is HTTPS-only. And in Nginx, use add_header ... always;, or the header disappears on exactly the error responses where you least want to lose it.

questions.text: Why did my service 502 on every deploy, and why did staging not show it?
questions.answer: The 502s are a drain problem: the load balancer removed the target (or sent SIGTERM) while in-flight requests were still running. The three timeouts that must be ordered are deregistration_delay.timeout_seconds ≥ the longest request, stopTimeout/terminationGracePeriodSeconds ≥ the drain time, and a preStop sleep so the endpoint controller learns the pod is going away before the process stops accepting. Staging missed it because of a *ratio*, not a difference in kind. Staging had near-zero traffic, so almost nothing was in flight when the pod stopped, so the window between "target removed" and "process exits" contained no requests. Production had a p99 of 20 seconds, so that window always contained requests. That is a genuine parity gap and it argues for testing deploy behaviour under load in staging — a load test that exercises a deploy — rather than assuming green staging means safe deploys.

questions.text: Terraform, Ansible, or both? Where is the line?
questions.answer: Different abstraction levels, so use both. Terraform owns things that exist in a cloud API and have identity: VPCs, subnets, instances, RDS, IAM, DNS, queues. Ansible owns the *inside* of a machine: users, packages, systemd units, config files, log rotation, an agent installed on a host Terraform did not create. The distinguishing concept is idempotence. Terraform is a reconciler with a graph and a plan, so re-running is free. Ansible is imperative; it is only safe to re-run if each action is idempotent — declarative modules that report changed=0 on the second run. That is why shell: echo ... >> is bad and template:/apt: state=present is good, and why --check --diff is a meaningful dry run. The overlap zone is where it goes wrong: if Terraform writes a systemd unit via user_data and Ansible also writes it, the last writer wins silently. My rule: each fact has exactly one owner, and ownership is documented.

questions.text: Your IaC state is on an S3 bucket. What are the security requirements, and why?
questions.answer: Five things. Encryption at rest with a customer-managed KMS key, and bucket policy assertions denying unencrypted puts, so the default cannot be bypassed.

questions.text: How do you safely roll out infrastructure changes?
questions.answer: Static analysis and validation first, then a plan artifact from a read-only role, then a policy gate, then approval, then apply *that same artifact* from CI. Applying the stored plan is the important detail: terraform apply -auto-approve re-plans, so what you reviewed is not necessarily what ran. Blast-radius control is layered: state split per domain and per blast radius, so a bad route table cannot touch the cluster; prevent_destroy on anything stateful; create_before_destroy where identity must persist; approval gates on destroy, IAM, security groups, KMS and anything reducing redundancy; canary accounts first; and change windows for the destructive ones. Rollback is not "revert": state is not a deployment. The default is forward-fix — revert the commit and apply — which works for every non-destructive change. State revert works when the code is right and the *run* went wrong halfway.
