| J3 Pay order | pay an order (PSP call) | 1 | team-orders |
| J4 Cancel/refund | cancel an order, receive refund | 1 | team-orders |
| J5 Async events | order events processed (emails, webhooks) | 2 | team-platform |

Out of scope: admin/internal batch jobs (tracked by a separate freshness SLI), and the
public marketing site (SLO owned by team-web).

## 2. SLIs (measured quantities)

### SLI 1 — Availability of J2/J3 (primary)
Definition: the proportion of **valid** requests to tier-1 endpoints that return a
success response. Success = HTTP 2xx **or** a documented 4xx the user caused (401/403/404/
409/422) — i.e. we only count as failures responses the server could have avoided.

Valid requests exclude: health checks and probes, our own synthetic monitors
(`user_agent=acme-synth`), and requests rejected at the CDN edge by rate limiting with
`429` on non-expensive endpoints (documented separately in SLI 5).

```promql
- record: service:sli_availability:ratio_rate30d
  expr: |
    sum(rate(http_requests_total{
            service="orders", journey=~"create|pay",
            status!~"5..", scrape!="self"}[30d]))
      /
    sum(rate(http_requests_total{
            service="orders", journey=~"create|pay",
            scrape!="self"}[30d]))
```

Why this is not gameable: the numerator and denominator come from the same instrumentation
with the same exclusions; `status=~"5.."` is the only failure class counted; and the
volume behind the ratio is displayed next to it everywhere (see §6) so a low-volume
window cannot hide a total outage.

### SLI 2 — Latency of J2 (p95 within 300ms)
```promql
- record: service:sli_latency:ratio_rate30d
  expr: |
    1 - (sum(rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{le="0.3"}[30d]))
         / sum(rate(http_request_duration_seconds_count[30d])))
```
Buckets at 0.15/0.2/0.3/0.5 exist specifically to make this query meaningful.

### SLI 3 — Correctness of J3 (order total matches captured amount)
```sql
-- from business data, not HTTP codes; a 200 with the wrong amount is a failure
SELECT
  count(*) FILTER (WHERE o.total_cents <> p.captured_cents) * 1.0 / count(*) AS error_ratio
FROM orders o JOIN payments p USING (order_id)
WHERE o.created_at > now() - interval '30 days';
```
Exported nightly to Prometheus as `orders:payment_amount_mismatch:ratio` (push via
pushgateway is acceptable here because it is a batch metric, provided the series is
refreshed every 24h and stale series are handled — see the Pushgateway caveat in §8.7.4).

### SLI 4 — Freshness of J5 (95% of events processed within 15 minutes)
```promql
- record: service:sli_freshness:ratio_rate1d
  expr: |
    1 - (sum(rate(events_processed_lag_seconds_count{le="900"}[1d]))
         / sum(rate(events_processed_lag_seconds_count[1d])))
```

### SLI 5 — Load shedding (transparency)
The proportion of requests rejected by our own rate limiting at the edge. **Excluded from
SLI 1** (we choose not to serve them) but tracked and reviewed, because a rising number
means we are shedding user traffic and that *is* user impact.

```promql
sum(rate(http_requests_total{service="orders",status="429"}[1d]))
  / sum(rate(http_requests_total{service="orders"}[1d]))
```

## 3. Objectives (targets)

| SLI | Objective | Window | Rationale |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| SLI 1 Availability | **99.95%** | 28 days (rolling) | Contractual SLA to enterprise customers is 99.9%; we hold 5× headroom so a measurement dispute cannot become a breach |
| SLI 2 Latency | **99% under 300ms** | 28 days | Matches the p95 product requirement; 1% slow requests is visible but not fatal to conversion |
| SLI 3 Correctness | **100.00%** | 28 days | A single wrong amount is a support escalation and a finance incident; this is a hard gate on release, not a burn-rate alert |
| SLI 4 Freshness | **99% within 15min** | 7 days | Users perceive email/webhook delay within minutes, not hours |
| SLI 5 Shed rate | **< 0.1%** | 7 days | Not an SLO for the vendor, a guard on our own protection |

### Error budget arithmetic (put this in the document; reviewers always check it)

```
Availability 99.95% over 28 days:
  window        = 28 × 24 × 60 = 40,320 minutes
  allowed down  = 0.0005 × 40,320 = 20.16 minutes  (≈ 20 minutes per 4 weeks)

Latency 99% under 300ms over 28 days:
  allowed slow  = 1% of all requests

Correctness 100%:
  allowed bad   = 0 requests
```

## 4. Alerting on the budget (multi-window, multi-burn-rate)

| Alert | Short window | Long window | Burn | Budget consumed | Severity |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| AvailabilityBurnFast | 5m | 1h | > 14.4× | 2% in ~1h | page |
| AvailabilityBurnMedium | 30m | 6h | > 6× | 5% in ~6h | page |
| AvailabilityBurnSlow | 2h | 1d | > 3× | 10% in ~1d | ticket |
| AvailabilityBudgetPolicy | — | 28d | remaining < 25% | — | policy review (lead notified) |
| LatencyBurnFast | 5m | 1h | > 14.4× of 1% | 2% in ~1h | page |
| CorrectnessMismatch | — | 1h | any > 0 | — | page (this is always SEV1-adjacent) |
| FreshnessBreach | 30m | 6h | > 6× | — | ticket |
| ShedRateHigh | 30m | 6h | > 0.1% | — | ticket |

Rules (non-negotiable):
- Never page on a cause (CPU, memory, pool depth). Those are dashboards and tickets.
- Every page has a runbook link and a dashboard link with `from=now-1h`.
- `absent(up == 1)` and "traffic vanished" alerts exist, because a service with no data is
  not a healthy service.

## 5. Release and change policy keyed to the error budget

```
budget_remaining = 1 - (observed_error_ratio / allowed_error_ratio)

| remaining        | policy                                                                  |
|------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| > 75%            | Normal cadence. Feature flags and experiments allowed.                   |
| 50% - 75%        | Normal cadence, but every release requires a named rollback plan.        |
| 25% - 50%        | Reliability first. Non-essential refactors paused. Extra test coverage on  |
|                  | the two weakest journeys required. Deploys ≤ 2/week.                     |
| 10% - 25%        | Change freeze except: incident fixes, security fixes, SLO-improving work. |
|                  | Lead notified; a written burn-down plan is required to unfreeze.         |
| < 10%            | Hard freeze. Daily 15-min reliability review with the service owner.      |
| exhausted (28d)  | Feature freeze until the SLO is restored for a full 28-day window.        |
```
Correctness SLI is enforced **independently of the budget**: any mismatch blocks promotion
regardless of budget.

The policy is not aspirational: the release pipeline reads
`service:error_budget_remaining:ratio28d` from the metrics API and blocks non-hotfix
promotions to prod when it is below the configured threshold. Humans own the exceptions.

## 6. Dashboards and how to read the numbers

- Budget panel: current availability %, allowed %, budget remaining % (as failure minutes
  consumed: e.g. "14.2 of 20.2 minutes used"), 28-day trend, and the request volume
  denominator beside every ratio.
- A ratio is *never* displayed alone. Every percentage panel shows `increase(...[window])`
  beneath it, because 99.9% of 30 requests is meaningless.
- Deploy markers on every chart so a budget burn can be attributed.

## 7. Current standing (filled in from the recording rules)

```
Availability (28d): 99.982%   -> budget remaining 36% (7.2 of 20.2 min used)
Latency (28d):      99.31% under 300ms
Correctness (28d):  100.000%
Freshness (7d):     99.7%
Shed rate (7d):     0.004%
Assessment: below the 50% threshold. Reliability work is prioritised this sprint.
```

## 8. Known limitations (state them; a review will find them anyway)

1. `status!~"5.."` treats a 200 with a wrong body as success — hence SLI 3 exists.
2. The 28-day window reacts slowly to a collapse; mitigated by the 5m/1h burn alert.
3. Cards are excluded from SLI 1 (a card decline is a PSP outage, not ours); this is a
   known carve-out with the enterprise contract attached.
4. If the PSP fails, SLI 1 breaches and the budget burns. That is intentional — we are
   still not serving orders — but it means we need a documented "PSP outage" policy
   (§9) for how we handle the budget after an external dependency burns it for us.

## 9. External dependency policy

When a third party (PSP) causes the SLO to be breached:
- Still count it in SLI 1 (users are affected).
- Do not page the whole company; page the owning team with a runbook that names the
  provider and links to their status page.
- After resolution, file an action item to define a **degraded mode** that reduces our
  burn (e.g. queue-and-retry with a 24h SLA instead of failing fast) and re-baseline the
  SLO discussion with the enterprise customer.
- If a single provider caused > 25% of the quarterly budget burn, that becomes a Q-level
  decision: multi-provider, or accept the burn with a documented risk acceptance.

## 10. Review

Quarterly, and after any SEV1. The review answers: is the objective still the right
target (too strict, too loose), are the SLI queries still valid after instrumentation
changes, is the budget policy being followed, and did any action item from a postmortem
change this document.
```

### Verification

```bash
# Every SLI query must return data and be ≤ 5s
for q in service:sli_availability:ratio_rate30d \
         service:sli_latency:ratio_rate30d \
         service:sli_freshness:ratio_rate1d; do
  curl -gs --data-urlencode "query=$q" localhost:9090/api/v1/query \
    | jq -e '.data.result | length > 0' || echo "SLI returns nothing: $q"
done

# The arithmetic must be reproducible
python3 -c "print(0.0005 * 28*24*60)   # 20.16 minutes allowed"

# The release policy must be enforced by the pipeline, not by memory
curl -s "$METRICS/api/v1/query?query=service:error_budget_remaining:ratio28d{service=\"orders\"}" \
  | jq -r '.data.result[0].value[1]'
```

### Interviewer follow-ups

1. **"Why 99.95% when the contract says 99.9%?"** — Because the SLO is an engineering
   target and the SLA is a promise; the 5× gap absorbs measurement error and dependency
   incidents without creating a breach of the contract.
2. **"Your PSP burned 60% of your budget. Now what?"** — Per §9: keep counting it, do not
   silently exclude it, and use the event to justify a degraded mode or multi-provider.
   Excluding external failures from an SLO that users feel is how teams talk themselves
   into 99.99% on a service that is actually 99.5%.
3. **"Who enforces the policy?"** — The pipeline, with named human owners for exceptions.
   A policy nobody enforces is a suggestion, and the first time it is bent is when the
   error budget stops meaning anything.

## Problem 8 — Chaos experiment plan

🔴 Advanced · **Must-know**

**The brief.** "Design a chaos experiment programme for this system: an Aurora
PostgreSQL primary failover, an AZ loss, a PSP latency spike, a Kafka broker
unavailability, and a secret rotation. For each: hypothesis, blast radius, abort
condition, procedure, and how you know it passed. Include the prerequisites and the
schedule."

### Solution

```markdown
# Chaos programme: `orders` platform, 2026 H1

Owner: sre-lead          Stakeholders: team-orders, team-platform, payments owner
Prerequisites gate: all experiments below are BLOCKED until the checklist in §0 passes.

## 0. Prerequisites (verify before the first run)

- [ ] Tier-1 SLOs defined and their burn-rate alerts firing correctly
      (`ServiceErrorBudgetBurnFast` test-fired in staging)
- [ ] Dashboards: overview + component, with deploy markers (Problem 5)
- [ ] Rollback exists and has been used at least once in the last 30 days
- [ ] `terraform plan` is clean; no in-flight IaC changes
- [ ] Synthetic monitors running from OUTSIDE the VPC against the real user journey
- [ ] Announced change window + a freeze on unrelated deployments for the experiment hour
- [ ] Second engineer available to abort; runbook printed/open in a second terminal
- [ ] Status page template ready (we will not need it, but it must be ready)
- [ ] Incident channel naming convention agreed (`#chaos-YYYY-MM-DD-<experiment>`)
- [ ] A kill switch for each experiment, tested

Rule: chaos is not run on a system we cannot restore from backup, during another
incident, or when the error budget is below 50%.

## 1. Experiment E1 — Aurora primary failover

Hypothesis:
  When the Aurora writer fails over, for 120s:
  (a) SLI 1 availability stays above 99.0% (i.e. < 1.2% of tier-1 requests fail),
  (b) no order is created twice (idempotency constraint holds),
  (c) p99 latency stays under 3x the SLO objective,
  (d) the service returns to steady state within 120s,
  (e) connection pool exhaustion does not occur (pool wait p99 < 50ms).

Blast radius:  the `orders` Aurora cluster (writer + readers). All services that use it:
orders, payments, notifications. Peak-traffic window avoided. 90–120s expected.

Abort: availability < 95% for 30s, OR any detected duplicate order, OR any duplicate
payment capture.

Procedure:
  1. Confirm dashboards + alerts live; announce in #chaos.
  2. Record baseline: 10 min of SLI, latency, pool utilisation, write rate.
  3. `aws rds failover-db-cluster --db-cluster-identifier orders-prod --force-failover`
  4. Watch, every 10s: `service:sli_availability:ratio_rate30s`,
     `service:http_request:latency_p99_5m`, `db_pool:utilisation5m`,
     `orders_created_total` vs `payments_captured_total` (the duplicate detector),
     and Aurora `ReplicationLag`/`FailoverCounter`.
  5. On completion, hold 10 min of steady state, then export the trace set for the window.

Pass criteria: all five (a)–(e) hold; the recovery time is recorded.

Findings (2026-02-18 run): (c) FAILED. p99 hit 4.2x SLO for 40s because the RDS Proxy
took 34s to rebuild pools and the app had no retry-on-ECONNRESET. (b) passed.
Action items: pooler config (dba, due 2026-02-25); connect-retry with jitter scoped to
reset errors only (orders, due 2026-03-04); re-run E1 monthly.

## 2. Experiment E2 — Availability Zone loss (application tier)

Hypothesis:
  When one of three AZs becomes unavailable:
  (a) no user-visible 5xx increase beyond 0.5% during the ASG replacement window,
  (b) remaining capacity (2 AZs × 6 tasks) sustains peak RPS within 30%,
  (c) the ASG replaces capacity in < 180s and does not oscillate,
  (d) no cross-AZ data egress spike that threatens latency (guard: cross-AZ bytes/sec).

Blast radius: one AZ in one region, application tier only. Database is multi-AZ and is
NOT affected (this experiment isolates the compute tier).

Abort: 5xx > 2% for 60s, OR latency > 3x SLO, OR the ASG fails to scale to min in 240s.

Procedure:
  1. Baseline 10 min: RPS, CPU per AZ, tasks per AZ, p99, cross-AZ bytes.
  2. Simulate: cordon the AZ in Kubernetes / use AWS FIS to stop the instances in one AZ
     (`fis-experiment terminateInstances` with a filter on `availability-zone`).
  3. Watch: `service:az_distribution:ratio`, `aws_appautoscaling_desired_count`,
     `node_cpu_utilisation` per AZ, `cross-az bytes`.
  4. Do NOT fail the DB; that is E1's job. Keep experiments independent.

Pass: (a)–(d). Record AZ replacement time as the number the reliability page should cite.

Findings (2026-02-25): (c) FAILED. ASG oscillated between 12 and 18 tasks for 6 min
because the target-tracking metric was per-AZ and no instance could register in the dead
AZ. Fix: use `ALBRequestCountPerTarget` (fleet-wide, not per-AZ) and set
`health_check_grace_period_seconds=180` so replacements are not killed mid-boot
(platform, due 2026-03-08).

## 3. Experiment E3 — PSP latency spike (external dependency)

Hypothesis:
  When the payment provider's latency rises to 3s (p50) for 15 minutes:
  (a) our p99 latency stays under 2x SLO (the circuit breaker opens and we fail fast),
  (b) the breaker opens within 60s of the spike, protecting the thread pool,
  (c) no duplicate charges are attempted (retry budget respected),
  (d) the retry volume to the PSP stays below 3x the normal request rate,
  (e) when the PSP recovers, the system returns to steady state within 3 minutes
      (no thundering herd).

Blast radius: injected latency for 25% of requests (by request ID hash), 15 min, then
removed. One canary service (`orders-canary` deployment), 5% of traffic via a weighted
target group rule.

Abort: 5xx > 2%, OR duplicate charges detected (any), OR PSP error rate > 50% for 60s.

Procedure:
  1. Deploy `orders-canary` with the flag `psp.failure_mode=latency` (feature flag, so no
     deploy is needed to remove it).
  2. Toxiproxy sidecar on the canary: `toxiproxy-cli toxic add -t latency -a latency=3000
     -a jitter=500 -t upstream orders-canary psp`; set toxicity to 25%.
  3. Route 5% of checkout traffic to the canary (ALB weighted target group).
  4. Observe for 15 min, then set toxicity to 0 and watch recovery for 3 min.

Pass: (a)–(e). Specifically confirm the breaker opens (metric
`circuit_breaker_state{dependency="psp"} == 1`) and that `psp_requests_total` rate does
not exceed 3x baseline during the spike.

Findings (2026-03-03): (d) FAILED. We saw 8x PSP request volume for the first 90s because
the gateway AND the service both retried. Fix: disable retries at the gateway layer
(`proxy_next_upstream_tries 1` for the payments route) and rely on the service's
retry-with-budget; add a test asserting single-layer retries (orders, due 2026-03-17).

## 4. Experiment E4 — Kafka broker unavailability (event pipeline)

Hypothesis:
  When the broker leader for partition 3 is unavailable for 10 minutes:
  (a) consumer lag grows and then drains fully within 30 min of recovery,
  (b) no events are lost (verified by reconciling `outbox_pending_events` and the
      destination sink counts),
  (c) consumer lag alert fires at 10 min of age and the runbook is followed,
  (d) no poison messages block the partition (per-partition lag, not global).

Blast radius: one topic, one partition group, canary consumer group first.

Abort: outbox backlog older than 2 hours, OR DLQ depth > 100.

Procedure:
  1. Baseline: per-partition lag, consumption rate, end-to-end event latency.
  2. Inject: scale the broker's allowed partition count to 0 for the topic, or use a
     network policy to drop traffic to two of three brokers.
  3. Verify lag grows, alert fires, runbook executed.
  4. Restore, measure drain time.

Pass: (a)–(d). Findings: (a) took 34 min to drain, not 30 — acceptable but documented.

## 5. Experiment E5 — Secret rotation (no restart storm)

Hypothesis:
  When the DB credential in Secrets Manager is rotated:
  (a) zero connection failures and zero task restarts,
  (b) existing pooled connections continue working for at most the pool's recycle window,
  (c) the new value is picked up within the documented propagation bound (< 5 min).

Blast radius: single staging environment first, then canary in prod for one task.

Abort: any 5xx from `auth` in staging, or > 1 task restart in prod.

Procedure:
  1. Rotate the SSM/Secrets Manager secret (same value, new version) — the *easy* case.
  2. Then rotate the *value* (new password) and observe.
  3. Compare restart counts, error rates, and time to convergence.

Pass: (a)–(c). Findings: (b) FAILED with the default pooler settings — connections held
for up to 4h. Fix: pool `max_lifetime` = 1800s (platform, due 2026-03-12).

## 6. Programme schedule

| Week | Experiments | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Game day (tabletop SEV1, humans only, no faults) | Practice roles, comms, timeline |
| 2 | E1 (DB failover) in staging | Validate the injection and the abort path |
| 3 | E1 in prod (announced, business hours) | |
| 4 | E2 (AZ loss, app tier) in prod | Requires the E2 fix from the previous run |
| 5 | E3 (PSP latency) in prod, 5% canary | |
| 6 | E5 (secret rotation) staging → prod canary | |
| 8 | E4 (Kafka) staging → prod | |
| Monthly thereafter | E1 + E3 rotated | Re-run after any change to the timeout/retry config |

Rule: any experiment that reveals a gap becomes a **scheduled regression test** (a load
test with fault injection in CI), so the gap cannot silently reopen.

## 7. Reporting

Quarterly summary for the engineering review: experiments run, hypotheses disproved,
action items created and closed, MTTR measured for each scenario, and whether any of the
measurements contradict our published reliability claims. "We found nothing" is reported
as "we probably tested the wrong things".

## 8. What we deliberately do not chaos
  - The payments *capture* path during business hours (customer-visible money movement);
    tested in staging against a sandbox PSP only.
  - Anything during the last two weeks of a quarter (close/reconciliation) or a marketing
    peak.
  - Destructive data experiments (deleting production data) — those are backup/restore
    drills instead, in a dedicated environment.
```

### Verification

- Every experiment has a **pre-run checklist** and an **abort path tested in staging
  first**.
- After each run: an entry in the chaos log with the hypothesis, the measured numbers,
  pass/fail per criterion, and linked action items.
- The programme is reviewed monthly; an experiment that has not been run in 60 days is
  considered stale (the system has changed).
- Cross-check: the measured MTTR from each experiment is quoted in the reliability
  documentation, so the claims are evidence-backed.

### Interviewer follow-ups

1. **"Why chaos in production at all?"** — Because the properties we depend on (real
   dependencies, real config, real failure of a real AZ) do not exist in staging. Staging
   chaos proves your test harness works; production chaos proves your system survives.
   The risk is managed by blast radius and abort conditions, and the alternative —
   discovering these properties during a real incident — is far more expensive.
2. **"How do you prevent chaos from becoming chaos-as-a-service theatre?"** — Every
   experiment must be tied to a documented reliability claim or a postmortem finding, must
   have a hypothesis that can be disproved, and must produce a tracked action item when
   it fails. Report the number of hypotheses disproved per quarter.
3. **"A hypothesis failed. Now what?"** — You found a real gap. File it as a normal
   high-priority item with the measured numbers (this is the most valuable output of the
   programme), fix it, and re-run the same experiment until it passes. Then convert it
   into a permanent regression test.

## Problem 9 — Incident postmortem (worked example)

🔴 Advanced · **Must-know**

**The brief.** "Write a complete, blameless postmortem for this incident: on
2026-03-04 at 09:12 UTC, 18% of checkout requests returned 500 for 29 minutes after a
deployment. Cause: a 2-second per-attempt timeout with 3 retries pushed failure count
past the PSP's circuit-breaker threshold; the breaker is per-instance state so scaling did
not help. Rollback at 09:28 restored service at 09:41. Make it specific, blameless, and
actionable."

### Solution

```markdown
# INC-2026-03-04 — Checkout 500s for 18% of requests

| | |
| --- | --- |
| Severity | SEV1 (user-visible payment failure, no workaround) |
| Duration | 09:12 – 09:41 UTC mitigated (29m); resolved 10:05 (53m total) |
| Detection | 09:13:41 by `ServiceErrorBudgetBurnFast` (1m38s after onset) |
| Commander | rprem  |  Scribe | jdoe  |  Comms | ksmith |
| Customer impact | ~4,100 users; 2,013 checkout attempts failed; no successful orders lost; no data corruption found |
| Financial impact | ~\$0 direct; est. \$8–14k at-risk revenue; 14 support tickets; 2 enterprise escalations |
| SLO impact | ~6.5% of the 28-day availability budget consumed in 29 minutes (36× the sustainable rate) |
| Status page | https://status.example.com/incidents/2026-03-04-checkout-500s |
| Follow-ups | INC-2026-03-04-actions (9 items, 7 closed, 2 open) |

## 1. Summary

A deployment at 09:12 UTC changed the payment call from a single 5-second attempt to three
2-second attempts with retries. The payment provider's circuit breaker opens after five
failed requests per instance, so by 09:13 every task had an open breaker and was failing
all payment authorizations immediately. Rolling back the deployment at 09:28 restored
service at 09:41, for a total impact of 29 minutes and roughly 4,100 affected users.

The interesting part is not the change itself — a timeout-and-retry change is a normal,
reasonable idea. It is that our system had three properties that turned a small change
into an outage, and that our detection and mitigation tooling both worked exactly as
designed.

## 2. Impact

- 09:12:31–09:41:07 UTC (28m36s): `POST /v1/checkout` returned HTTP 500 for a fraction of
  requests that reached the `payments.authorize` step.
- Failure fraction over the window: 18% (2,013 of 11,180 attempts).
- Orders were created in `pending_payment` state and **not** charged. No duplicate
  captures (verified by reconciling `payments_captured_total` against
  `payments_attempted_total`).
- 14 support tickets; 2 enterprise customers asked for a RCA letter (sales notified).
- Error budget: availability SLI fell from 99.98% to 99.86% over 28 days, consuming
  6.5% of the budget — above the "freeze" threshold, which triggered a release freeze on
  `orders` from 2026-03-05 to 2026-03-11 (see Problem 7 §5).

| 09:35:00 | Status page: "Monitoring" |
| 09:41:07 | Error rate returned to baseline (0.02%); mitigation declared |
| 10:05:00 | 30 minutes of stable p99 (< 200ms) and error rate; incident resolved |
| 10:20 | Comms sent to the 2 enterprise customers; postmortem doc created; actions filed |

Detection: 1m10s from first error to page.
Time to acknowledge: 21s. Time to declare: 39s. Time to mitigate: 28m36s.
Time to full resolution: 53m.

## 4. Detection

**How we found out.** The SLO multi-window burn-rate alert fired 70 seconds after the first
error. This worked as designed and is the reason the blast radius was bounded.

**How we almost did not find out.** Two support tickets arrived at 09:15, ahead of our
status page. Customer reports would have been the only signal for the first 4 minutes.

**What we learned about detection.**
- The burn-rate alert is our fastest signal for user-visible errors. There is no
  alert on PSP *latency* itself, so the first 70 seconds had no alert that pointed at the
  cause.
- The alert routed correctly and the runbook was opened within 90 seconds (it did not
  contain the "scaling does not help" fact, so 5 minutes were spent on mitigation attempt 1).

## 5. Root causes

**Primary: the change multiplied the worst-case duration and the request count beyond the
dependency's failure threshold, with no validation that the change was compatible with
the dependency's circuit-breaker configuration.**

1. The new configuration allowed up to `3 × 2s + 2 × backoff ≈ 7s` per checkout, versus
   `5s` before. The PSP's documented breaker threshold is 5 failures per instance in 60s.
   At 3 attempts per checkout, a checkout that hit a slow PSP produced 3 failures at once,
   so 2 checkouts were enough to open every instance's breaker.
2. The retry change was reviewed and approved, but the review could not see the
   interaction with the PSP breaker because the breaker configuration lived in a
   different repo (`payments-psp-config`) with no reference from the service code.
3. The unit test added with the change asserted the *retry count* was 3, but nothing
   asserted the *total worst-case duration* or the *failure amplification factor*.

**Contributing factors** (each independently sufficient to have made this worse):

- **Scaling could not help and nobody knew.** The breaker is per-process state, so adding
  16 more tasks did not reduce failures — it added 16 more failing tasks. Cost: 5 minutes
  of the incident, plus a step-change in PSP traffic that our PSP contact later noted was
  uncomfortable for them.
- **Staging did not exercise a slow PSP.** The change passed all tests against a PSP stub
  with 20ms latency. With 3s latency and a 7s worst case, staging would have shown the
  amplification immediately.
- **No circuit-breaker metric was wired into the service overview**, so the team saw
  "errors" but not "the breaker is open", which is why the first hypothesis was about
  timeouts rather than about breakers.
- **The runbook had no entry for PSP failures**, so the responder had no known
  "scaling does not help" fact and no mitigation ordering.
- **Error budget policy delayed the obvious follow-up:** the release freeze triggered by
  this incident meant the *fix* (below) shipped behind a config change that was
  themselves deployed via a different path, adding 3 days to the remediation timeline.

## 6. What went well

- **The multi-window burn-rate SLO alert worked**: 70 seconds from onset to page, correct
  routing, no false-positive risk from a single spike.
- **Rollback was available, rehearsed, and took 5 minutes.** This is the single biggest
  reason the incident was 29 minutes instead of an unknown number.
- **The IC and scribe roles were filled immediately**, so the timeline in §3 is accurate
  rather than reconstructed — which is what made this postmortem possible in 24 hours
  instead of a week.
- **Comms were ahead of customer perception**: status page posted at 09:20, before most
  customers would have reported the problem.
- **No data was corrupted and no duplicate charges occurred**: the idempotency key added
  in a previous incident did its job.
- **Traces made the diagnosis fast**: 6 minutes from "hypothesis: the deploy" to a precise
  mechanism (`3 × 2s + backoff`).

## 7. Where we got lucky

- The PSP kept serving: a PSP-side outage or rate limit would have extended this
  substantially and made rollback insufficient.
- The error budget still had 93% remaining, so the release freeze caused no schedule harm
  for a week.
- A customer who had just reported a similar symptom in staging (which we had dismissed)
  was not an enterprise account with an SLA credit attached.

## 8. Action items

| # | Action | Why | Owner | Due | Priority | Verification |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Circuit breaker on **every** outbound call, with state exported as `circuit_breaker_state{dependency}` and shown on the service overview | Fail fast; makes the mechanism visible | jdoe | 2026-03-18 | P0 | Re-run chaos experiment E3 (Problem 8) |
| 2 | CI test asserting, for every outbound client: `(retries+1) × per_attempt_timeout + backoff_total < route_deadline` **and** `failure_amplification ≤ 3` | Prevents this class of change | rprem | 2026-03-11 | P0 | Test fails against the current code as of 2026-03-04 (proving it catches this) |
| 3 | Runbook "PSP failures": breaker is per-instance, 5-min cooldown, scaling does not help, mitigation order = flag → rollback → page PSP | Removes the 5 minutes we lost | jdoe | 2026-03-15 | P0 | Runbook used in a game day |
| 4 | Staging scenario: PSP latency 3s ± 500ms via Toxiproxy, asserting p99 < 400ms and that no breaker opens | Parity gap that let this pass | ksmith | 2026-03-25 | P1 | Runs in the nightly staging suite |
| 5 | Add `circuit_breaker_state` and PSP latency to the `orders` overview dashboard, row 3 | Visibility of the mechanism | ksmith | 2026-03-12 | P1 | Screenshot in the actions issue |
| 6 | Alert on PSP latency p99 > 2s for 5m (page: "payments degraded") | Faster, cause-directed signal; points at the dependency | jdoe | 2026-03-18 | P1 | Test-fire in staging |
| 7 | Publish the PSP breaker configuration **in the same repo** as the payment client, with a doc link from the client config | Cross-repo knowledge gap | jdoe | 2026-04-01 | P2 | `README` link; owner of the config repo acknowledges |
| 8 | Change review checklist item: "list the failure-mode change for every dependency call (retries, timeout, circuit breaker)" | Process fix at the point of the error | eng-manager | 2026-03-20 | P1 | Checklist merged; two reviews audited for use |
| 9 | Canary duration for `orders` raised 5m → 15m with automatic SLO comparison before full promotion | The canary passed because the canary had 1 task, and 1 task did not open the PSP breaker meaningfully | rprem | 2026-03-22 | P1 | Canary config change; documented in the deploy runbook |

## 9. Review

- **30-day review: 2026-04-03.** Owner rprem. We will verify: items 1–3 closed with
  verification evidence; chaos E3 re-run and passing; the CI test in item 2 demonstrably
  fails against the pre-fix code; and the availability SLI recovered above 99.95% for a
  full 28-day window (projected 2026-04-01).
- If the same failure mode appears in the next two incidents, escalate to a design review
  of the outbound-call layer rather than continuing to patch symptoms.

## 10. What we are explicitly *not* changing

- We are not adding automatic rollback on SLO burn. The canary gap (item 9) means our
  canary is not yet a meaningful safety net, and an automatic rollback on a noisy signal
  has its own failure modes. Revisit after 3 successful canaries.
- We are not raising PSP timeout budgets further to "hide" the problem. The system must
  degrade predictably, not exceed customer patience.
```

### The interviewer's evaluation criteria for this artifact

| Criterion | Where this document demonstrates it |
| --- | --- |
| Blameless without being vague | §5 root causes are about the system; the change is described as "reasonable", not as a mistake |
| Quantified impact | §2 with user counts, request counts, SLO budget consumed, financial estimate |
| Accurate timeline | §3 sourced from the scribe, with detection/TTA/TTM/TTR |
| Multiple contributing factors | §5: four independent contributors, each with its own cost |
| "Where we got lucky" | §7 — the section that shows senior judgement |
| Action items that are specific, owned, dated, verified | §8, with a verification column including a chaos re-run |
| Acknowledges what worked | §6, including the previous incident's idempotency key paying off |
| Says what will *not* change and why | §10 |
| Has a review date | §9 |

### Interviewer follow-ups

1. **"Was this human error?"** — No. The engineer made a reasonable, reviewed change.
   The system allowed a change whose total worst-case duration and failure amplification
   were not checked against a dependency configuration that lived in another repository.
2. **"What is the single most important fix?"** — Action item 2. A CI assertion that the
   retry/timeout configuration of an outbound call fits within the route's deadline and
   the dependency's failure threshold prevents the whole class, not just this instance.
   (Item 1 prevents the outage duration; item 2 prevents the outage.)
3. **"How would you know the remediation worked?"** — Re-run chaos experiment E3 with the
   3s PSP latency and assert p99 < 400ms and no breaker trip; verify the new CI test
   fails against the pre-fix code (a test that never fails is not a test); and watch the
   availability SLI for a full 28-day window.

## Problem 10 — IaC state rotation and recovery runbook

🔴 Advanced · **Must-know**

**The brief.** "Write the runbook for rotating and recovering Terraform state for a
production platform. Cover the common failure modes (corruption, accidental `apply` from
a laptop, lost state, provider upgrade gone wrong, state containing leaked secrets),
the exact commands, the safety checks, and the verification."

### Solution

```markdown
# Runbook: Terraform state operations (platform/prod)

Owner: sre-lead   Runbook version: 2026-03-04   Last tested: 2026-02-11 (game day)
Applies to: all state files in `infra/state/` — see the state inventory in §0.

## 0. State inventory (know what you have before you touch it)

| Key (path) | Contains | Instances | Last applied | Destroyable? |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| network/terraform.tfstate | VPC, subnets, IGW, NAT, route tables, VPC endpoints | 1 | 2026-02-20 | **NO — takes everything down** |
| platform/terraform.tfstate | ECS cluster, IAM roles, log groups, KMS keys | 1 | 2026-03-03 | NO |
| data-platform/terraform.tfstate | MSK, Glue, Athena, Kinesis | 1 | 2026-02-28 | NO |
| envs/prod/terraform.tfstate | ALB, target groups, ECS service, RDS cluster, SG | 1 | 2026-03-04 | NO (data) |
| envs/prod-data/terraform.tfstate | RDS cluster, read replicas, secrets | 1 | 2026-03-01 | NO (data) |
| envs/staging/terraform.tfstate | full stack | 1 | 2026-03-04 | no |

Rules:
- One state file per blast radius. Never one state for everything.
- Data-bearing resources live in their own state so a network change cannot touch them.
- Every state file has `prevent_destroy` and `deletion_protection` (see §6).

## 1. Prerequisites for ANY state operation

```bash
export TF_IN_AUTOMATION=1
export TF_LOG=warn          # TF_LOG_PATH=./tf-debug.log for detail

aws sts get-caller-identity

cat .terraform/terraform.tfstate | python3 -c "import json,sys; print(json.load(sys.stdin)['backend']['config'])"
aws s3api get-bucket-versioning --bucket acme-tfstate-prod
aws s3api get-bucket-encryption  --bucket acme-tfstate-prod
aws dynamodb describe-table --table-name acme-tfstate-locks | jq '.Table'

BUCKET=acme-tfstate-backups; TS=$(date -u +%Y%m%dT%H%M%SZ)
aws s3 cp "s3://acme-tfstate-prod/envs/prod/terraform.tfstate" \
          "s3://$BUCKET/envs-prod-$TS.terraform.tfstate"
aws s3api put-bucket-versioning --bucket $BUCKET --versioning-configuration \
  Status=Enabled 2>/dev/null || true

terraform state pull > "state-before-${TS}.json"
python3 -c "
import json; s=json.load(open('state-before-${TS}.json'))
print('serial', s['serial'], 'lineage', s['lineage'], 'resources', len(s['resources']))"
```

## 2. Routine operation: normal apply

Policy: production state is **only** applied from CI, using the plan artifact from the
approved pull request.

```bash
terraform init -input=false -lock-timeout=5m
terraform plan -out=tfplan -detailed-exitcode     # 0 no change, 2 changes
terraform show -json tfplan | jq -r '.resource_changes[]
  | select(.change.actions | index("delete")) | .address'   # review destroys
terraform apply tfplan
terraform state pull | jq '.serial'
```

## 3. Rotating state (migrating a state file to a new backend/bucket)

**Scenario:** move `envs/prod` state to a new bucket for compliance, or split a state that
has grown too large.

```bash
TS=$(date -u +%Y%m%dT%H%M%SZ)

aws s3 cp "s3://acme-tfstate-prod/envs/prod/terraform.tfstate" \
          "s3://acme-tfstate-new/envs/prod/terraform.tfstate"
aws s3api put-object --bucket acme-tfstate-new --key envs/prod/terraform.tfstate \
  --acl bucket-owner-full-control

rm -rf .terraform/terraform.tfstate      # ONLY the backend metadata, never the .tf files
terraform init -migrate-state -lock-timeout=5m

terraform state pull > state-after.json
diff <(jq -S 'del(.serial)' state-before.json) \
     <(jq -S 'del(.serial)' state-after.json)     # MUST be empty (serial may differ)

terraform plan -detailed-exitcode; echo "exit=$?"   # expect 0 (no changes)

aws s3api put-bucket-policy --bucket acme-tfstate-prod --policy '{
  "Version":"2012-10-17","Statement":[
    {"Sid":"DenyStaleWrites","Effect":"Deny","Principal":"*",
     "Action":"s3:PutObject","Resource":"arn:aws:s3:::acme-tfstate-prod/envs/prod/*",
     "Condition":{"Bool":{"aws:SecureTransport":"false"}}}]}'
```

**Rollback for §3:** copy the backup object back over the new key, revert the PR, re-init.

## 4. State contains leaked secrets — rotation, not scrubbing

**Reality:** on a versioned bucket you cannot remove a secret from history. Rotation is
the only correct remediation.

```bash
aws cloudtrail lookup-events --lookup-attributes AttributeKey=EventName,AttributeValue=GetObject \
  --start-time 2026-01-01T00:00:00Z --end-time 2026-03-04T00:00:00Z \
  --query 'Events[].CloudTrailEvent' --output text | jq -r '.s3.bucketName // empty' | sort -u

aws rds rotate-db-cluster-master-user-password --db-cluster-identifier orders-prod
aws secretsmanager rotate-secret --secret-id prod/orders/db
aws iam list-access-keys --user-name svcapp | jq -r '.AccessKeyMetadata[].AccessKeyId'
aws iam update-access-key --status Inactive --access-key-id AKIA...   # then delete

aws secretsmanager describe-secret --secret-id prod/orders/db \
  | jq '{rotated: .LastRotatedDate, next: .LastChangedDate}'

terraform apply -refresh-only=false -target=aws_secretsmanager_secret_version.orders
```

Note: `sensitive = true` in HCL redacts CLI output only. It does not encrypt state.

## 5. Failure modes and their recovery

### 5.1 Corrupted state file (`Invalid JSON` / truncated write)

```bash
terraform state pull > broken.json && cat broken.json | python3 -m json.tool >/dev/null \
  || echo "corrupt, as expected"

aws s3api list-object-versions --bucket acme-tfstate-prod \
  --prefix envs/prod/terraform.tfstate \
  | jq -r '.Versions | sort_by(.LastModified) | reverse
           | .[] | "\(.VersionId)\t\(.LastModified)"'

for v in $(list newest first); do
  aws s3 cp "s3://acme-tfstate-prod?versionId=$v" /tmp/candidate.json
  python3 -m json.tool /tmp/candidate.json >/dev/null 2>&1 && { echo "GOOD: $v"; break; }
done

aws s3 cp /tmp/candidate.json "s3://acme-tfstate-prod/envs/prod/terraform.tfstate"
terraform state push /tmp/candidate.json
terraform plan -detailed-exitcode; echo "exit=$?"    # MUST be 0
```

### 5.2 Someone applied from a laptop (wrong credentials, or concurrent apply)

Detection:
```bash
terraform state pull | jq .serial
aws cloudtrail lookup-events --lookup-attributes \
  AttributeKey=ResourceName,AttributeValue=acme-tfstate-prod \
  --start-time -1h | jq -r '.CloudTrailEvent|fromjson|.userIdentity.arn'
```

Response:
1. `terraform plan -detailed-exitcode` — if 0, nothing changed; close it.
2. If there *is* drift caused by the rogue run, decide authority: **usually the state
   wins** (it matches what the API now reports), so encode the change in config and
   `apply` from CI. If the rogue run created *new* resources (e.g. a fresh workspace
   creating a duplicate stack), delete the duplicates explicitly and `state rm` them.
3. Remove the personal credentials' ability to mutate prod (IAM), not just the access key.
4. Record it in the postmortem if it caused user-visible change.

### 5.3 Two concurrent applies (state lock timeout / clobbered serial)

```bash
terraform plan -lock-timeout=10m      # queue politely instead of failing fast
aws dynamodb delete-item --table-name acme-tfstate-locks \
  --key '{"LockID":{"S":"acme-tfstate-prod/envs/prod/terraform.tfstate"}}'
terraform plan -refresh-only
```

Prevention (do this, do not just document it): prod state readable/writable **only** by
the CI role; humans use `terraform plan` through a read-only role against a *copy* of
state; `-lock-timeout` set in CI; and an alert on state-bucket writes by any principal
other than `ci-deployer`.

### 5.4 State lost entirely (bucket deleted, region gone)

```bash
aws s3 cp "s3://acme-tfstate-backups/envs-prod-20260301T120000Z.terraform.tfstate" \
          ./restored.tfstate
terraform state push ./restored.tfstate -lock-timeout=5m
terraform plan -refresh-only              # shows what exists but is untracked (created)
terraform plan -refresh=false             # shows what is tracked but gone (delete)
terraform import aws_ecs_service.app acme-prod/app-abc123
terraform import aws_rds_cluster.main orders-prod
terraform plan -detailed-exitcode
terraform state push ./restored.tfstate
```

The critical principle: **Terraform wants to create things that already exist.**
Never respond to "resource already exists" by editing the config to a different name;
import.

### 5.5 Provider upgrade caused mass replacement

```bash
terraform init -upgrade
terraform plan -refresh=false | grep -E '^  # .*must be replaced' -A3
```

Safe upgrade procedure:
1. Read the provider CHANGELOG for the version you are moving to (not just the diff).
2. Apply in staging with a copy of prod state (a "state clone" environment) and diff the
   resulting plan against the staging plan.
3. Pin `version = "~> 5.60.0"` (patch only) for the first upgrade; widen only after a week.
4. `prevent_destroy` and `deletion_protection` are your safety net — do not remove them
   "temporarily" for an upgrade.

### 5.6 Import without a clean plan (adoption)

```hcl
import {
  to = aws_ecs_service.app
  id = "acme-prod/app-abc123"
}
```

Procedure: enumerate everything via data sources, import, then iterate the configuration
until `terraform plan` is empty. Only then freeze console access and remove the import
blocks. A PR that imports 200 resources with a still-dirty plan is a review liability.

### 5.7 Splitting a state file (blast-radius reduction)

Only split at resource boundaries, in the dependency direction, and with
`moved`/`removed` blocks so nothing is destroyed:

```hcl
removed {
  from = aws_rds_cluster.main
  lifecycle { destroy = false }
}

import {
  to = module.data.aws_rds_cluster.main
  id = "orders-prod"
}
```

Then: push the removal with `destroy = false` into the *new* state first, verify plans on
both sides are empty, and only then remove from the old state.

## 6. Preventive controls (the real answer)

| Control | Prevents | Implement |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Remote, versioned, encrypted, locked state | corruption, leaks, concurrent applies | S3 + versioning + KMS + lock table; `use_lockfile` or DynamoDB |
| State split by blast radius | one bad apply taking everything down | one key per layer; data-bearing resources isolated |
| Prod state writable only by CI | laptop applies, human error | IAM; break-glass role with expiry + alert |
| `prevent_destroy` + `deletion_protection` | accidental deletion of stateful resources | lifecycle blocks; RDS attribute |
| Scheduled `plan -refresh-only` | long-lived undetected drift | CI cron → ticket |
| Access Analyzer + CloudTrail alerting | unnoticed state reads / writes | alert on `GetObject` on the state bucket by non-CI principals |
| `ephemeral`/`sensitive` + Secrets Manager | secrets in state | never store credentials in HCL variables |
| Monthly restore drill | "backups we have never restored" | restore a state file into a scratch workspace and diff |
| Provider version pinning | surprise upgrades | `~> x.y.z`; widen deliberately |
| `prevent_destroy` on the state bucket itself | someone deleting the bucket | bucket policy + object lock (compliance mode) |

## 7. Verification after ANY state operation

```bash
terraform plan -detailed-exitcode; echo "exit=$?"     # MUST be 0 (no changes)
terraform state list | wc -l                            # matches the before count
python3 -c "
import json
b=json.load(open('state-before.json')); a=json.load(open('state-after.json'))
assert b['lineage']==a['lineage'], 'LINEAGE CHANGED - this is a different state!'
print('serial', b['serial'], '->', a['serial'])
bset={r['address'] if 'address' in r else (r['type'],r['name']) for r in b['resources']}
aset={(r['type'],r['name']) for r in a['resources']}
print('lost:', bset-aset, 'added:', aset-bset)"
```

**Lineage is the identity check.** If the lineage UUID changes, you are looking at a
different state file — everything after that is wrong.

## 8. Escalation

- Any operation that will show a non-empty plan against production: require a second
  engineer to review the plan output before proceeding, and announce in #platform-change.
- Any operation involving `destroy = true`, state deletion, or backend migration:
  change freeze, manager approval, and a scheduled window.
- If you cannot get `plan` to exit 0 after a restore, **stop**. Escalate to sre-lead with
  the before/after state diff. Do not "try another import".
```

### Interviewer follow-ups

1. **"Someone says `terraform state rm` deleted production."** — It cannot. `state rm`
   only removes the resource from Terraform's tracking; the resource keeps running and
   keeps costing money. The dangerous thing is the *next* apply, which will offer to
   create a replacement. So the correct immediate response is a policy freeze plus an
   audit for orphans (`terraform plan` shows "will be created").
2. **"How do you handle a provider upgrade that wants to replace everything?"** — Read
   the changelog, upgrade in a state-clone environment first, compare plans, pin to a
   patch version, and rely on `prevent_destroy`. If the provider insists on replacement,
   you either accept it in a window with snapshots and a tested rollback, or you stay on
   the older provider version (deliberately, with a comment explaining why).
3. **"How do you prove state is safe?"** — Monthly drill: restore the newest state version
   into a scratch workspace, confirm `plan` is empty and lineage matches, and time it. A
   backup you have never restored is a hypothesis, not a backup.

Each scenario is written the way you will meet it in an incident: symptoms first, then
the investigation path, then the root cause, then the fix. Read the symptoms, close the
document, and try to name the root cause and the fix before reading on. That is the
difference between recognising this at 3am and guessing.

topics.bodyMarkdown:
🔴 Advanced · **Must-know**

**Definition** — These are the *application-level* reliability patterns that make a
system degrade gracefully instead of cascading. They are the difference between "the
dependency was slow" and "everything is down".

**Mechanics — retries**

```
Retry with exponential backoff and jitter:

delay(n) = min(cap, base × 2^n) × random(0.5 .. 1.5)

attempt 0: immediate
attempt 1: ~100ms   ±50%
attempt 2: ~200ms   ±50%
attempt 3: ~400ms   ±50%   (cap 2s)
total worst case ≈ base×(2^n−1) + cap, and MUST be < the caller's own timeout
```

Rules for retries that do not cause harm:

1. **Retry only idempotent operations** (GET, PUT with the same body, DELETE with
   idempotency keys) or operations with an **idempotency key** the server understands.
2. **Cap total attempts *and* total time.** A retry that outlives the caller's deadline is
   pure waste; the caller has already given up.
3. **Exponential backoff + jitter, always.** Synchronised retries are how a recovering
   dependency gets knocked over again immediately ("thundering herd").
4. **Only retry transient errors**: connection reset, timeout, 429, 502/503/504. Never
   4xx (except 429), never a validation error, never a 500 that is deterministic.
5. **Budget the retries across the call tree.** A request that fans out to 5 services,
   each retrying 3 times, multiplies load by 15. Propagate a *retry budget* (like
   gRPC's `RetryInfo` / Google's `x-retry-budget` header) so downstream retries stop when
   the budget is exhausted.
6. **Retry at one layer only.** If a gateway retries and each service retries, you have
   3× 3× 3 amplification. Pick the layer closest to the failure (usually the service
   making the call) and disable retries above it.

```python
import random, itertools, functools

class TransientError(Exception): ...
class PermanentError(Exception): ...

def retryable(fn, *, attempts=3, base=0.1, cap=2.0, deadline_budget=5.0,
              retry_on=(TransientError, TimeoutError)):
    """Exponential backoff with full jitter, bounded by a total time budget."""
    end = time.monotonic() + deadline_budget
    last = None
    for i in range(attempts):
        try:
            return fn()
        except retry_on as e:
            last = e
            if i == attempts - 1: break
            delay = min(cap, base * (2 ** i))
            jitter = random.uniform(0.5, 1.5) * delay        # full jitter
            remaining = end - time.monotonic()
            if remaining <= jitter: break                     # no time left: give up
            time.sleep(min(jitter, remaining))
    raise last

# Usage with an idempotency key so retries cannot double-charge
def charge(order, key: str):
    return retryable(lambda: psp.charge(order, idempotency_key=key),
                     retry_on=(TransientError,), attempts=3, deadline_budget=4.0)
```

```go
// Go: the context deadline is the retry budget; never retry past it
func (c *Client) Get(ctx context.Context, key string) (*Item, error) {
    backoff := backoff.NewExponentialBackOff(backoff.WithMaxElapsedTime(3 * time.Second))
    var lastErr error
    op := func() error {
        req, _ := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodGet, c.base+key, nil)
        resp, err := c.http.Do(req)
        if err != nil { return transient(err) }                    // network-level
        defer resp.Body.Close()
        switch {
        case resp.StatusCode >= 500 || resp.StatusCode == 429:
            lastErr = fmt.Errorf("upstream %d", resp.StatusCode)
            return lastErr                                          // retryable
        case resp.StatusCode >= 400:
            return permanent(fmt.Errorf("upstream %d", resp.StatusCode)) // stop
        default:
            return decode(resp)
        }
    }
    err := backoff.Retry(op, backoff.WithContext(op, ctx))
    return nil, err   // ctx deadline bounds everything
}
```

**Mechanics — timeouts**

The single most reliable cause of cascading failure is a missing (or absurdly long)
timeout. Rules:

1. **Every network call has a deadline.** No exceptions, no defaults.
2. **The deadline must be *less than* the caller's remaining budget**, and the sum along
   a call path must be less than the end-to-end timeout. A 900ms budget with three
   sequential 5s calls is a bug that works fine until the day it does not.
3. **Connect timeout ≪ read timeout.** 200–500ms connect (a TCP handshake to a healthy
   network is ms), 1–5s read (a slow query can take seconds).
4. **Propagate deadlines** in the request (gRPC `grpc-timeout`, HTTP `X-Deadline`, or a
   deadline in the trace context). Downstream must not exceed it.
5. **Timeout must be shorter than the LB idle timeout** (ALB default 60s; make the call
   path < 55s including retries), or the LB returns 504 while the server is still
   working (wasted work, potential duplicate on retry).
6. **Timeouts release resources.** A timeout that does not close the connection/response
   leaks sockets and goroutines; the failure looks like a memory leak one hour later.

```
Request budget: 1000ms total (SLO p95)
  gateway        950ms remaining
    → checkout   800ms remaining
        → payments  500ms remaining
            → PSP     300ms remaining   (per-attempt 250ms, 1 retry max = 480ms)
        (total worst case 480ms < 500ms)  ✓
```

**Mechanics — circuit breakers**

A circuit breaker stops calling a dependency that is failing, failing *fast* instead of
accumulating timeouts, thread exhaustion, and connection pool starvation.

```
          failure rate ≥ threshold (e.g. 50% of last 20 calls)
CLOSED ──────────────────────────────────────────► OPEN
  ▲                                                │
  │ successful calls                                 │ after reset_timeout (e.g. 30s)
  │                                                ▼
  └──────────────────────────────────────────── HALF_OPEN
      success ≥ N → CLOSED                 fail → OPEN (and reset the timer)
```

Implementation points that matter:

- **Counted over a rolling window, not consecutive** (consecutive-failure breakers never
  open on a 50% error rate).
- **Minimum request volume** before evaluating, so a 1-request window cannot open the
  breaker.
- **Per-dependency, per-instance granularity.** A breaker is process state, which is why
  "scaling out does not help" (as in the postmortem in §8.7.11) and why a fleet of
  instances can open and close breakers at different times — a thundering herd on
  recovery. Mitigate with a shared breaker (Redis/etcd) or a slow, jittered half-open.
- **Fail open vs fail closed**, decided per dependency:
  - *Fail closed* (return an error): payments, auth, writes. Correctness over
    availability.
  - *Fail open* (serve from cache / degrade): reads, recommendations, analytics.
- **Emit breaker state as a metric** (`circuit_breaker_state{dependency="psp"}`) and
  alert on *time spent open* — not on the breaker opening itself.
- **Cooldown must exceed the dependency's own recovery time**, or you get flapping
  breakers.

**Mechanics — bulkheads**

Bulkheads **isolate resource pools** so one failure domain cannot consume another's
capacity. In code, a bulkhead is a bounded executor/queue; in a platform, it is a
dedicated thread pool, connection pool, container, or replica group.

```java
// Separate pools per dependency, each with its own limits and queue
var pspPool     = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(32);
var searchPool  = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(16);
var reportPool  = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(4);

// Bounded queues: rejection is a feature (fail fast, shed load)
record SearchExecutor(SearchClient c, ExecutorService exec) {
  Result search(Query q) throws RejectedExecutionException {
    var f = exec.submit(() -> c.query(q));
    try {
      return f.get(200, MILLISECONDS);
    } catch (RejectedExecutionException e) {
      metrics.counter("bulkhead.rejected", "dep", "search").inc();
      throw new OverloadedException("search");     // shed, do not queue unboundedly
    }
  }
}
// searchPool at 100% cannot starve pspPool: they are separate pools.
```

The platform-level versions: dedicated replica groups (a "report" deployment with its own
ASG), per-tenant rate limits, separate database connection pools per workload, and
separate queues per workload class. **Unbounded queues are the enemy of bulkheads** — a
queue without a bound converts a failure into a memory exhaustion and hides it behind
growing latency.

**Mechanics — hedging requests**

Hedging sends a *second* copy of a request shortly after the first, and keeps whichever
response wins; it converts a *latency* failure into a success. Netflix's Hystrix and
Tail-fallback are the canonical implementations.

```
t=0ms    send request to node-a
t=250ms  (p99 latency for this call, times a hedge factor of 1.5-2) send to node-b
t=300ms  a responds (slow but successful)   → keep a, cancel b
t=320ms  b responds (fast)                 → keep b, cancel a
only hedge when the request is idempotent and cheap to duplicate (reads!)
```

Rules:

- **Only hedge reads** (or writes protected by an idempotency key). Hedging a payment is
  how you charge someone twice.
- **Hedge after the p99/p99.9, not a fixed delay**; a fixed 100ms hedge doubles load for
  everyone on a fast path.
- **Cap the number of hedges** (usually one).
- **Abort the loser** when the winner returns, or you have made the load worse.
- **Only hedge on nodes you know are independent** — two requests to the same overloaded
  instance do not help.
- **Account for load:** with N hedges, worst-case load is N×. Hedge only in a regime
  where the latency tail is worth it.

**Trade-offs**

| Pattern | Prevents | Introduces | Watch out for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Retries | transient failures | load amplification | non-idempotency, retry storms |
| Timeouts | thread/connection exhaustion | premature failures on slow-but-working deps | budget arithmetic, propagation |
| Circuit breaker | cascading failure, pool exhaustion | hard failures while open | flapping, per-instance state, thundering herd on half-open |
| Bulkhead | resource starvation across dependencies | lower utilization per pool | more infrastructure, complexity |
| Hedging | tail latency | doubled load | duplicate side effects, cancellation |
| Load shedding | overload | rejected requests | must be deliberate (queue depth, not CPU) |
| Graceful degradation | dependency loss | reduced functionality | feature flags must be tested |
| Backpressure | queue explosion | "slowness" propagated to callers | needs async or buffer |

**When to use vs when not to**

- Retries: yes, for known-transient failures, on idempotent operations, with a budget.
- Timeouts: always, without exception.
- Circuit breakers: on any dependency where a slow failure would exhaust local
  resources (all remote calls, really).
- Bulkheads: whenever one dependency can starve another — especially for the
  "expensive optional feature" path.
- Hedging: only for high-traffic, latency-sensitive, cheap, idempotent reads, and only
  after measuring a tail-latency problem.
- Load shedding: when you are overloaded and dropping work is better than queueing it
  (HTTP APIs, streaming). Do not shed for background jobs; scale those instead.

**Production considerations**

- Every one of these needs a metric and a dashboard panel: retry counts by dependency,
  timeout counts by dependency, breaker state and open-duration, bulkhead rejections and
  queue depth, hedged request count and waste ratio.
- **Propagate deadlines** and retry budgets so the whole call tree respects the end-to-end
  SLO; otherwise a fast service in front of a slow one violates the SLO for the user.
- Test these paths. They are only exercised in failure, so they rot. Add fault-injection
  tests (the same Toxiproxy/FIS/chaos tooling) that assert retry behaviour, breaker
  transitions, and that no duplicate side effects occurred.
- Configuration over code for every timeout/limit, so it can be tuned in an incident
  without a deploy — and validate that the values are internally consistent (a test that
  asserts `retries × timeout < deadline`).
- Consider the interaction between retries and the load balancer: an ALB with
  `proxy_next_upstream` retries *and* application retries multiply. Know your total
  amplification factor.

**Common mistakes**

1. Retrying a non-idempotent POST (duplicate charges, duplicate emails).
2. Retrying at multiple layers (gateway + service + client = 27 requests).
3. No jitter → a synchronised retry storm.
4. A 30-second default timeout everywhere → thread pool exhaustion long before any
   circuit breaker opens.
5. Circuit breaker with a per-request volume threshold so low it opens on one error.
6. Breaker that fails *closed* for an optional feature, turning degradation into an
   outage.
7. Unbounded queue in front of a failing dependency.
8. Hedging a write.
9. Retry budget ignored, so a downstream's retries are amplified by the upstream's.

**Common failure chains to be able to describe**

```
Chain A (retry storm):
PSP slow → checkout timeouts → retries at gateway AND service → 3×3 load on a
already-struggling PSP → PSP total outage → circuit breaker finally opens →
checkout 500s → but PSP never recovers because it is being hammered by the tail.

Chain B (timeout cascade):
DB slows (missing index after a release) → checkout read timeout 30s → every request
holds a DB connection for 30s → pool of 20 exhausted → queue builds → memory grows →
GC pauses → all requests slow → load balancer timeouts at 60s → users see 504s.

Chain C (bulkhead absent):
One slow optional dependency (recommendations) with a 10s timeout → all 200 threads
blocked on it → core checkout requests cannot get a thread → total outage of a feature
that is supposed to be optional.

Chain D (hedging without cancellation):
p99 spikes → hedging doubles load → p99 spikes more → more hedging → positive feedback
loop → self-inflicted outage. Fix: hedge factor > 1, abort the loser, and only for reads.
```

**Interviewer probes**

- "Where do you put a timeout and how do you pick the value?"
  → Derived from the SLO end-to-end budget, propagated down: each hop's deadline is
  smaller than the caller's remaining budget, with connect ≪ read, and the whole call
  path (including retries) below the LB idle timeout. I validate the arithmetic in a
  test so a future change cannot silently break it.
- "A dependency returns 500s intermittently. What do you do?"
  → Classify as transient; add retry with exponential backoff + jitter and an idempotency
  key, bounded by the request budget; add a circuit breaker with a rolling-window
  threshold and a per-dependency metric; isolate it in a bulkhead so it cannot exhaust
  shared pools; and add a degraded path if the dependency is optional. Then measure: the
  error rate and the latency of the affected routes.
- "Explain hedging and when it is dangerous."
  → Sending a duplicate request after the p99 to convert a tail-latency failure into a
  success; dangerous for non-idempotent operations and for load multiplication, and it
  needs cancellation of the loser and a hedge factor above 1.
- "How do these patterns interact with each other?"
  → They compose but multiply: retries × timeouts define the worst-case duration;
  breakers depend on the retry/timeout settings to open fast enough; bulkheads bound the
  blast radius of the others; hedging adds load on top of all of it. Design them as one
  system with one budget, and test them together.

## Problem 1 — Terraform module: ECS/Fargate service behind an ALB with RDS

🔴 Advanced · **Must-know**

**The brief.** "Write a reusable Terraform module that deploys a production HTTP
service onto AWS: an ECS/Fargate service behind an Application Load Balancer, spread
across 3 AZs, in private subnets, with an ALB in public subnets, an Aurora PostgreSQL
cluster (writer + 2 readers) with Multi-AZ, Secrets Manager-issued credentials, TLS at
the ALB, autoscaling, alarms, and a self-service bastion path. The module must take
only values (no resource types hardcoded per environment) and must be safe to apply
twice."

### Solution

**Module interface (`modules/service/main.tf` inputs):**

```hcl
# modules/service/variables.tf
variable "name" {
  type        = string
  description = "Service name, used for resource naming and tags."
  validation {
    condition     = can(regex("^[a-z][a-z0-9-]{2,30}$", var.name))
    error_message = "name must be lowercase alphanumeric with hyphens, 3-31 chars."
  }
}

variable "environment" {
  type    = string
  validation {
    condition     = contains(["dev", "staging", "prod"], var.environment)
    error_message = "environment must be dev, staging, or prod."
  }
}

variable "vpc_id"                { type = string }
variable "public_subnet_ids"     { type = list(string) }
variable "private_subnet_ids"    { type = list(string) }
variable "cidr_blocks"           { type = list(string) }   # derived, for the SG rules
variable "image"                 { type = string }          # must include a digest
variable "container_port"        { type = number }
variable "cpu"                   { type = number  }
variable "memory"                { type = number  }
variable "desired_count"         { type = number  }
variable "min_count"             { type = number  }
variable "max_count"             { type = number  }
variable "health_check_path"     { type = string   default = "/healthz" }
variable "ready_check_path"      { type = string   default = "/readyz" }
variable "log_retention_days"    { type = number   default = 30 }
variable "domain_name"           { type = string }
variable "certificate_arn"       { type = string }
variable "db_instance_class"     { type = string   default = "db.r6g.xlarge" }
variable "db_engine_version"     { type = string   default = "16.3" }
variable "db_readers"            { type = number   default = 2 }

  type        = map(string)

  description = "Non-secret configuration. Secrets come from secret_names."
}

  default     = []
}

  type        = list(string)

**The database (`rds.tf`):**

```hcl
locals {
  name = "${var.name}-${var.environment}"

  # Derive the vpc CIDR for security-group rules instead of making callers pass it
  vpc_cidr = [for c in var.cidr_blocks : c]
}

data "aws_db_subnet_group" "this" {
  name       = "${local.name}-db"
  subnet_ids = var.private_subnet_ids
}

resource "random_password" "db" {
  length  = 2
  special = false          # keep it URL/DSN safe; we assemble the URL ourselves
}

resource "aws_ssm_parameter" "db_password" {
  name  = "/acme/${local.name}/db/password"
  type  = "SecureString"
  value = random_password.db.result[0]
  tags  = { Service = var.name, Environment = var.environment }
}

resource "aws_ssm_parameter" "db_url" {
  name  = "/acme/${local.name}/db/url"
  type  = "SecureString"
  value = format("postgresql://%s:%s@%s:%s/%s?sslmode=require",
                 random_password.db.result[1],
                 urlencode(random_password.db.result[0]),
                 aws_rds_cluster.main.endpoint,
                 aws_rds_cluster.main.port,
                 aws_rds_cluster.main.database_name)
  tags  = { Service = var.name, Environment = var.environment }
}

resource "aws_rds_cluster" "main" {
  cluster_identifier              = "${local.name}"
  engine                          = "aurora-postgresql"
  engine_version                  = var.db_engine_version
  database_name                   = var.name
  master_username                 = "svcapp"
  manage_master_user_password     = true       # rotation, no password in state
  port                            = 5432
  db_subnet_group_name            = data.aws_db_subnet_group.this.name
  vpc_security_group_ids          = [aws_security_group.db.id]
  storage_encrypted               = true
  kms_key_id                      = var.kms_key_arn
  backup_retention_period         = var.environment == "prod" ? 14 : 3
  preferred_maintenance_window    = "sun:04:30-sun:05:30"
  copy_tags_to_snapshot           = true
  deletion_protection             = var.environment == "prod"
  skip_final_snapshot             = false
  final_snapshot_identifier       = "${local.name}-final"
  apply_immediately               = false      # never reboot prod at apply time
  enabled_cloudwatch_logs_exports = ["postgresql", "upgrade"]

  lifecycle { prevent_destroy = true }

  serverlessv2_scaling_configuration {
    min_capacity = 1
    max_capacity = 64
  }
}

resource "aws_rds_cluster_instance" "writer" {
  identifier         = "${local.name}-writer"
  cluster_identifier = aws_rds_cluster.main.id
  instance_class     = var.db_instance_class
  engine             = "aurora-postgresql"
  engine_version     = var.db_engine_version
  promotion_tier     = 1
  performance_insights_enabled   = true
  performance_insights_retention_period = 465   # 31 days
  monitoring_interval = 15
  monitoring_role_arn = var.rds_monitoring_role_arn
  copy_tags_to_snapshot = true
}

resource "aws_rds_cluster_instance" "readers" {
  count                = var.db_readers
  identifier           = "${local.name}-reader-${count.index}"
  cluster_identifier   = aws_rds_cluster.main.id
  instance_class       = var.db_instance_class
  engine               = "aurora-postgresql"
  engine_version       = var.db_engine_version
  promotion_tier       = 2
  performance_insights_enabled = true
  copy_tags_to_snapshot = true
}

resource "aws_rds_cluster_parameter_group" "main" {
  name   = "${local.name}-pg16"
  family = "aurora-postgresql16"

  parameter {
    name         = "rds.force_ssl"
    value        = "1"
    apply_method = "immediate"
  }
  parameter {
    name         = "log_min_duration_statement"
    value        = "500"
    apply_method = "pending-reboot"
  }
  parameter {
    name         = "log_connections"
    value        = "0"
    apply_method = "pending-reboot"
  }
}

# Optional: RDS Proxy so Fargate scale-out cannot exhaust connections
resource "aws_db_proxy" "main" {
  name                   = "${local.name}-proxy"
  engine                 = "postgres"
  debug_logging          = false
  idle_client_timeout    = 1800
  require_tls            = true
  role_arn               = var.rds_proxy_secret_arn
  vpc_subnet_ids         = var.private_subnet_ids
  vpc_security_group_ids = [aws_security_group.db.id]
}

resource "aws_db_proxy_default_target_group" "main" {
  db_proxy_name = aws_db_proxy.main.name
  target_group_name = "default"
  connection_pool_config {
    max_connections  = 200
    min_connections  = 10
    max_percent_connector_elapsed_time = 120
  }
}
```

**ECS (`ecs.tf`):**

```hcl
locals {
  env = [
    for k, v in var.app_env : { name = k, value = v }
  ]
  secrets = [
    for s in var.secret_names : { name = upper(trimprefix(s, "/")), valueFrom = s }
  ]
}

resource "aws_ecs_task_definition" "app" {
  family                   = local.name
  requires_compatibilities = ["FARGATE"]
  network_mode             = "awsvpc"
  cpu                      = tostring(var.cpu)
  memory                   = tostring(var.memory)
  execution_role_arn       = var.ecs_execution_role_arn
  task_role_arn            = var.ecs_task_role_arn
  tags                     = local.tags

  container_definitions = jsonencode([merge({
    name      = var.name
    image     = var.image
    essential = true
    portMappings = [{
      name          = "http"
      containerPort = var.container_port
      protocol      = "tcp"
      appProtocol   = "http"
    }]

    environment = local.env
    secrets     = local.secrets

    # Readiness is the ALB check; liveness is process-only (see §8.7.9)
    healthCheck = {
      command     = ["CMD-SHELL", "curl -fsS http://localhost:${var.container_port}${var.health_check_path} || exit 1"]
      interval    = 30
      timeout     = 5
      retries     = 3
      startPeriod = 45      # boot: config load, DB connect, cache warm
    }

    logConfiguration = {
      logDriver = "awslogs"
      options = {
        awslogs-group         = aws_cloudwatch_log_group.app.name
        awslogs-region        = var.region
        awslogs-stream-prefix = "ecs"
      }
    }

    # ECS exec off by default: it is a shell on production
    readonlyRootFilesystem = false   # needs /tmp; set true and add a tmpfs if possible
    user                  = "svcapp"
  }, var.extra_container_settings)])
}

resource "aws_ecs_service" "app" {
  name            = local.name
  cluster         = var.cluster_arn
  task_definition = aws_ecs_task_definition.app.arn
  desired_count   = var.desired_count
  launch_type     = "FARGATE"
  enable_execute_command = false
  health_check_grace_period_seconds = 120
  tags            = local.tags

  deployment_circuit_breaker { enable = true rollback = true }
  deployment_maximum_percent         = 200
  deployment_minimum_healthy_percent = 100

  network_configuration {
    subnets          = var.private_subnet_ids
    security_groups  = [aws_security_group.app.id]
    assign_public_ip = false
  }

  load_balancer {
    target_group_arn = aws_lb_target_group.app.arn
    container_name   = var.name
    container_port   = var.container_port
  }

  # Spread across AZs: Fargate distributes tasks across the subnets you give it, but
  # being explicit protects you if you later pass only private subnets
  placement_constraints {
    type       = "memberOf"
    expression = "attribute:ecs.availability-zone in [${join(",", var.availability_zone_ids)}]"
  }

  capacity_provider_strategy {
    capacity_provider = "FARGATE"
    weight            = 1
    base              = var.min_count     # always-on floor for HA
  }
}

resource "aws_appautoscaling_target" "ecs" {
  service_namespace  = "ecs"
  resource_id        = "service/${var.cluster_name}/${aws_ecs_service.app.name}"
  scalable_dimension = "ecs:service:DesiredCount"
  min_capacity       = var.min_count
  max_capacity       = var.max_count
}

# Scale on request rate per target, not CPU: request rate is the user-facing load
resource "aws_appautoscaling_policy" "ecs_requests" {
  name               = "${local.name}-rps"
  policy_type        = "TargetTrackingScaling"
  service_namespace  = aws_appautoscaling_target.ecs.service_namespace
  resource_id        = aws_appautoscaling_target.ecs.resource_id
  scalable_dimension = aws_appautoscaling_target.ecs.scalable_dimension

  target_tracking_scaling_policy_configuration {
    target_value       = 250        # requests/minute per task
    scale_in_cooldown  = 300
    scale_out_cooldown = 60

### Interviewer follow-ups you should be ready for

1. **"Why `target_type = "ip"`?"** — Fargate tasks in `awsvpc` mode have ENIs with private
   IPs and are not registered by instance ID.
2. **"Why 60s deregistration?"** — Must exceed the longest request plus any in-flight
   streaming; shorter means 502s on every deploy. And `stopTimeout`/preStop must be ≥
   that so the task does not exit before the load balancer stops sending.
3. **"What happens if `desired_count = 2` and one AZ loses?"** — One task remains in one
   AZ; still serving, at half capacity. That is why `min_count = 3` with 3 AZs: you can
   lose an AZ and keep 2.
4. **"Why both `manage_master_user_password` and a random password?"** —
   `manage_master_user_password` covers the *master* user; the *application* user gets its
   own credential stored in Secrets Manager/SSM with rotation, so the app never has
   admin rights.
5. **"How would you add a canary?"** — A second target group + a second ECS service, with
   a weighted listener rule at 5%, then ramp. Or a single service with
   `deployment_minimum_healthy_percent = 100` and a small `deployment_maximum_percent`.
