## Problem 2 — Nginx reverse proxy with TLS, SNI, rate limiting, and observability

🟡 Intermediate · **Must-know**

**The brief.** "Write the complete Nginx configuration for a public API gateway that
(a) terminates TLS with SNI and automatic certificate management, (b) load-balances
across an upstream with health-aware retries, (c) rate limits per client IP and has a
stricter limit on auth endpoints, (d) sets security headers, (e) emits structured JSON
logs with upstream timings, (f) handles SSE/WebSocket, (g) can be hot-reloaded safely, and
(h) survives a slow-client or slow-upstream scenario."

### Solution

```nginx
# /etc/nginx/nginx.conf
user  nginx;
worker_processes  auto;
worker_rlimit_nofile 65535;
worker_rlimit_nproc  65535;

error_log  /var/log/nginx/error.log  warn;
pid        /var/run/nginx.pid;

# Long-lived connections (WebSocket/SSE) must be drained on reload
worker_shutdown_timeout 30s;

events {
    worker_connections  16384;
    use                  epoll;
    multi_accept         on;
    accept_mutex         off;
}

http {
    include       /etc/nginx/mime.types;
    default_type  application/json;

    # ---------- logging ----------
    log_format json_combined escape=json
      '{'
        '"timestamp":"$time_iso8601",'
        '"remote_addr":"$remote_addr",'
        '"x_forwarded_for":"$http_x_forwarded_for",'
        '"request_id":"$request_id",'
        '"trace_id":"$http_traceparent",'
        '"method":"$request_method",'
        '"uri":"$uri",'                      # $uri not $request_uri: excludes query string
        '"status":$status,'
        '"bytes":$body_bytes_sent,'
        '"request_time":$request_time,'
        '"upstream_addr":"$upstream_addr",'
        '"upstream_status":"$upstream_status",'
        '"upstream_connect_time":"$upstream_connect_time",'
        '"upstream_header_time":"$upstream_header_time",'
        '"upstream_response_time":"$upstream_response_time",'
        '"ssl_protocol":"$ssl_protocol",'
        '"ssl_server_name":"$ssl_server_name",'
        '"user_agent":"$http_user_agent"'
      '}';

    access_log  /var/log/nginx/access.log  json_combined  buffer=64k  flush=1s;
    # NOTE: buffered logs can be lost on hard kill; use flush=1s for critical services.

    # ---------- basics ----------
    sendfile           on;
    tcp_nopush         on;
    tcp_nodelay        on;
    server_tokens      off;
    keepalive_timeout  65s;
    keepalive_requests 1000;
    client_max_body_size 25m;
    client_body_timeout 30s;
    client_header_timeout 15s;
    send_timeout        30s;
    reset_timedout_connection on;
    absolute_redirect   off;

    gzip on;
    gzip_types text/plain application/json application/javascript text/css text/xml
               application/xml application/xml+rss text/javascript application/x-javascript;
    gzip_min_length 1024;
    gzip_proxied any;
    # JSON is already compact; do not waste CPU gzipping 200-byte responses

    # ---------- trusted proxies (for real client IP) ----------
    # Only these may set X-Forwarded-For. Everything else is untrusted.
    set_real_ip_from 10.0.0.0/8;
    set_real_ip_from 172.16.0.0/12;
    real_ip_header   X-Forwarded-For;
    real_ip_recursive on;

    # ---------- rate limiting ----------
    # 10m zone ≈ 16k tracked keys; size for peak, and watch for eviction warnings
    limit_req_zone  $binary_remote_addr zone=api_per_ip:20m   rate=20r/s;
    limit_req_zone  $binary_remote_addr zone=auth_per_ip:10m  rate=12r/m;
    limit_req_zone  $server_name          zone=per_route:10m  rate=50r/s;
    limit_conn_zone $binary_remote_addr zone=conn_per_ip:20m;
    limit_req_status  429;
    limit_conn_status 429;

    # ---------- upstream pools ----------
    upstream api_v1 {
        least_conn;
        zone api_v1 64k;

        server 10.0.11.21:8080 max_fails=2 fail_timeout=15s;
        server 10.0.11.22:8080 max_fails=2 fail_timeout=15s;
        server 10.0.11.23:8080 max_fails=2 fail_timeout=15s;
        server 10.0.12.24:8080 backup;        # only if all primaries fail

        keepalive 64;
        keepalive_requests 1000;
        keepalive_timeout 60s;
    }

    upstream api_v2 {
        hash $request_id consistent;          # cache-friendlier than round robin
        server 10.0.11.31:8080 max_fails=2 fail_timeout=15s;
        server 10.0.11.32:8080 max_fails=2 fail_timeout=15s;
        keepalive 32;
    }

    # ---------- default server: fail closed ----------
    server {
        listen 80 default_server;
        listen 443 ssl default_server;
        http2 on;
        server_name _;

        ssl_certificate     /etc/nginx/ssl/default/fullchain.pem;
        ssl_certificate_key /etc/nginx/ssl/default/privkey.pem;

        return 421 https://$host$request_uri;   # Misdirected Request
    }

    # HTTP: ACME + redirect
    server {
        listen 80;
        server_name api.example.com;

        location ^~ /.well-known/acme-challenge/ {
            root /var/www/acme;
            default_type "text/plain";
        }
        location / { return 308 https://api.example.com$request_uri; }
    }

    # ---------- the API ----------
    server {
        listen 443 ssl;
        http2 on;
        server_name api.example.com;

        # --- TLS ---
        ssl_certificate     /etc/nginx/ssl/api.example.com/fullchain.pem;
        ssl_certificate_key /etc/nginx/ssl/api.example.com/privkey.pem;
        ssl_protocols       TLSv1.2 TLSv1.3;
        ssl_ciphers         ECDHE-ECDSA-AES128-GCM-SHA256:ECDHE-RSA-AES128-GCM-SHA256:ECDHE-ECDSA-AES256-GCM-SHA384:ECDHE-RSA-AES256-GCM-SHA384:ECDHE-ECDSA-CHACHA20-POLY1305:ECDHE-RSA-CHACHA20-POLY1305;
        ssl_ecdh_curve      X25519:prime256v1:secp384r1;
        ssl_prefer_server_ciphers off;
        ssl_session_cache   shared:SSL:20m;
        ssl_session_timeout 1d;
        ssl_session_tickets off;
        ssl_stapling        on;
        ssl_stapling_verify on;
        ssl_trusted_certificate /etc/ssl/certs/ca-certificates.crt;
        resolver 1.1.1.1 8.8.8.8 valid=300s;
        resolver_timeout 5s;

        # --- security headers (always, so they survive 4xx/5xx) ---
        add_header Strict-Transport-Security "max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains" always;
        add_header X-Content-Type-Options    "nosniff" always;
        add_header X-Frame-Options           "DENY" always;
        add_header Referrer-Policy           "strict-origin-when-cross-origin" always;
        add_header Permissions-Policy        "geolocation=(), microphone=(), camera=()" always;
        add_header Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy "same-site" always;

        # --- default limits ---
        limit_conn conn_per_ip 40;

        # --- liveness: Nginx only, no upstream dependency, public-safe ---
        location = /healthz {
            access_log off;
            add_header Content-Type text/plain always;
            return 200 "ok\n";
        }

        # --- rate limit status ---
        error_page 429 = @ratelimited;
        location @ratelimited {
            default_type application/json;
            return 429 '{"error":"rate_limited","request_id":"$request_id"}';
        }

        # --- real-time readiness from the upstream (internal callers only) ---
        location = /readyz {
            allow 10.0.0.0/8;
            deny  all;
            proxy_pass http://api_v1/readyz;
            proxy_http_version 1.1;
            proxy_set_header Connection "";
            proxy_connect_timeout 1s;
            proxy_read_timeout    2s;
            access_log off;
        }

        # --- auth: strict rate limit, no caching, small timeouts ---
        location ~ ^/v1/(auth|login|signup|password)/ {
            limit_req  zone=auth_per_ip burst=8  nodelay;
            limit_req  zone=per_route  burst=20 nodelay;

            proxy_pass http://api_v1;
            include /etc/nginx/snippets/proxy_common.conf;
            proxy_connect_timeout 1s;
            proxy_read_timeout    10s;
            proxy_cache            off;
            add_header Cache-Control "no-store" always;
        }

        # --- v2 API ---
        location /v2/ {
            limit_req zone=api_per_ip burst=40 nodelay;
            limit_req zone=per_route burst=200 nodelay;

            proxy_pass http://api_v2/;        # note: trailing slash rewrites /v2/... to /...
            include /etc/nginx/snippets/proxy_common.conf;
        }

        # --- SSE (long-lived, unbuffered) ---
        location ~ ^/v1/events {
            limit_req zone=api_per_ip burst=10 nodelay;

            proxy_pass http://api_v1;
            proxy_http_version 1.1;
            proxy_set_header Connection "";
            proxy_buffering off;
            proxy_cache off;
            chunked_transfer_encoding on;
            proxy_read_timeout 1h;
            proxy_send_timeout 1h;
            add_header X-Accel-Buffering "no" always;   # belt and braces for proxies
        }

        # --- WebSocket ---
        location ~ ^/v1/ws {
            proxy_pass http://api_v1;
            proxy_http_version 1.1;
            proxy_set_header Upgrade    $http_upgrade;
            proxy_set_header Connection "upgrade";
            proxy_set_header Host       $host;
            proxy_read_timeout 3600s;
            proxy_send_timeout 3600s;
            proxy_buffering off;
        }

        # --- writes: slower smoothing to protect a fragile dependency ---
        location ~ ^/v1/(orders|payments) {
            limit_req zone=api_per_ip burst=20 delay=10;   # smooth the burst
            proxy_pass http://api_v1;
            include /etc/nginx/snippets/proxy_common.conf;
            proxy_read_timeout 30s;
            proxy_next_upstream error timeout http_502 http_503;
            proxy_next_upstream_tries 2;
            proxy_next_upstream_timeout 15s;
        }

        # --- catch-all reads ---
        location / {
            limit_req zone=api_per_ip burst=40 nodelay;
            limit_req zone=per_route burst=200 nodelay;

            proxy_pass http://api_v1;
            include /etc/nginx/snippets/proxy_common.conf;
        }
    }
}

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# /usr/local/bin/nginx-reload — safe reload with rollback
set -euo pipefail
STAMP=$(date +%s)

if nginx -t -q; then
  nginx -s reload
  echo "reloaded ${STAMP}" >> /var/log/nginx/reloads.log
  sleep 2
  if ! curl -fsS --max-time 3 http://127.0.0.1/healthz >/dev/null; then
    echo "health check failed after reload; rolling back" >&2
    cp -a "/var/cache/nginx/config-backup-${STAMP}" /etc/nginx/nginx.conf
    nginx -t && nginx -s reload
    exit 1
  fi
else
  echo "config invalid; not reloading" >&2
  exit 1
fi

### Interviewer follow-ups

1. **"Why is `proxy_max_temp_file_size 0` right here and wrong elsewhere?"** — It keeps
   responses in memory (lower latency, no disk I/O) but a slow client holds a worker.
   For large downloads, allow temp files or use `sendfile`.
2. **"How do you protect Nginx itself?"** — Multiple Nginx instances behind the ALB, a
   rate limit at the ALB/WAF layer, connection limits, `worker_connections` sized to
   `LimitNOFILE`, and running as non-root with a read-only config.
3. **"Why not `if` blocks?"** — `if` inside `location` is evaluated in a confusing
   context ("if is evil"); use `map`, `try_files`, or separate location blocks.
4. **"How would you do a canary at the proxy?"** — A second `upstream` with a weighted
   `split_clients` map or a `map $http_x_canary` to route a header/cookie, plus
   `proxy_next_upstream` excluding the canary for critical writes.

## Problem 3 — Prometheus recording rule set for a Go service

🟡 Intermediate · **Must-know**

**The brief.** "Your service already exports `http_requests_total`,
`http_request_duration_seconds`, `grpc_client_seconds`, `db_pool_connections`,
`outbox_pending_events`, and `queue_consumer_lag`. Write a recording rule set that makes
(1) a tier-1 SLI for availability and latency, (2) an error-budget burn rate, (3) cheap
per-route panels, and (4) diagnostic panels. Then write the multi-window burn-rate
alerts that consume them, and test them with `promtool`."

### Solution

```yaml
# prometheus/rules/service-recording.yml
groups:
  # ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
  # Group 1: base rates (cheap, used by everything else)
  # ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
  - name: service-base
    interval: 30s
    limit: 60
    rules:
      - record: service:http_requests:rate5m
        expr: sum by (service, route) (rate(http_requests_total[5m]))

      - record: service:http_requests:rate30s
        expr: sum by (service, route) (rate(http_requests_total[30s]))

      - record: service:http_errors:count_rate5m
        expr: |
          sum by (service, route, status) (
            rate(http_requests_total{status=~"5.."}[5m])
          )

      # Latency percentiles per route. Buckets must straddle the SLO (300ms p95).
      - record: service:http_request:latency_p95_5m
        expr: |
          histogram_quantile(0.95,
            sum by (service, route, le) (rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])))

      - record: service:http_request:latency_p99_5m
        expr: |
          histogram_quantile(0.99,
            sum by (service, route, le) (rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])))

      # 30d version for SLO measurement (low resolution is fine and cheap)
      - record: service:http_request:latency_p95_30d
        expr: |
          histogram_quantile(0.95,
            sum by (service, route, le) (rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket[30d])))

      # Mean latency: needed because histogram_quantile is meaningless at low volume
      - record: service:http_request:latency_mean_5m
        expr: |
          sum by (service, route) (rate(http_request_duration_seconds_sum[5m]))
            /
          sum by (service, route) (rate(http_request_duration_seconds_count[5m]))

  # ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
  # Group 2: SLIs (the definitions of "working")
  # ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
  - name: service-sli
    interval: 60s
    rules:
      # Availability SLI over the SLO window. Excludes probes and 4xx (client error).
      - record: service:sli_availability:ratio_rate5m
        expr: |
          sum by (service) (rate(http_requests_total{status!~"5..", scrape!="self"}[5m]))
            /
          sum by (service) (rate(http_requests_total{scrape!="self"}[5m]))

      - record: service:sli_availability:ratio_rate1h
        expr: |
          sum by (service) (rate(http_requests_total{status!~"5..", scrape!="self"}[1h]))
            /
          sum by (service) (rate(http_requests_total{scrape!="self"}[1h]))

      - record: service:sli_availability:ratio_rate6h
        expr: |
          sum by (service) (rate(http_requests_total{status!~"5..", scrape!="self"}[6h]))
            /
          sum by (service) (rate(http_requests_total{scrape!="self"}[6h]))

      - record: service:sli_availability:ratio_rate1d
        expr: |
          sum by (service) (rate(http_requests_total{status!~"5..", scrape!="self"}[1d]))
            /
          sum by (service) (rate(http_requests_total{scrape!="self"}[1d]))

      - record: service:sli_availability:ratio_rate30d
        expr: |
          sum by (service) (rate(http_requests_total{status!~"5..", scrape!="self"}[30d]))
            /
          sum by (service) (rate(http_requests_total{scrape!="self"}[30d]))

      # Latency SLI: fraction of requests faster than the 300ms objective
      - record: service:sli_latency:ratio_rate5m
        expr: |
          1 - (
            sum by (service) (rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{le="0.3"}[5m]))
            /
            sum by (service) (rate(http_request_duration_seconds_count[5m]))
          )

      - record: service:sli_latency:ratio_rate30d
        expr: |
          1 - (
            sum by (service) (rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{le="0.3"}[30d]))
            /
            sum by (service) (rate(http_request_duration_seconds_count[30d]))
          )

      # Freshness SLI: share of events processed within 15 minutes of creation
      - record: service:sli_freshness:ratio_rate1h
        expr: |
          1 - (
            sum by (service) (rate(events_processed_lag_seconds_count{le="900"}[1h]))
            /
            sum by (service) (rate(events_processed_lag_seconds_count[1h]))
          )

  # ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
  # Group 3: error budget and burn rate
  # ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
  - name: service-error-budget
    interval: 60s
    rules:
      - record: service:slo_target:ratio
        expr: |
          label_replace(
            vector(0.9995),
            "service", "$1", "service", "(.*)"
          )

      # burn = observed failure rate / allowed failure rate
      - record: service:error_budget_burn:rate5m
        expr: |
          (1 - service:sli_availability:ratio_rate5m)
            / (1 - 0.9995)

      - record: service:error_budget_burn:rate1h
        expr: |
          (1 - service:sli_availability:ratio_rate1h)
            / (1 - 0.9995)

      - record: service:error_budget_burn:rate6h
        expr: |
          (1 - service:sli_availability:ratio_rate6h)
            / (1 - 0.9995)

      - record: service:error_budget_burn:rate1d
        expr: |
          (1 - service:sli_availability:ratio_rate1d)
            / (1 - 0.9995)

      # remaining budget, 0..1
      - record: service:error_budget_remaining:ratio30d
        expr: |
          1 - ((1 - service:sli_availability:ratio_rate30d) / (1 - 0.9995))

      # failure minutes consumed in the last 24h (human-readable for the status page)
      - record: service:error_budget_minutes_burned:rate1d
        expr: |
          (1 - service:sli_availability:ratio_rate1d) * 1440

  # ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
  # Group 4: diagnostics (dashboard-only, never paged directly)
  # ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
  - name: service-diagnostics
    interval: 30s
    rules:
      - record: service:traffic_ratio:v1
        expr: |
          sum(rate(http_requests_total{service="checkout"}[5m]))
            /
          sum(rate(http_requests_total{service=~"checkout|orders|payments"}[5m]))

      - record: service:instance:cpu:avg5m
        expr: 1 - avg by (instance) (rate(node_cpu_seconds_total{mode="idle"}[5m]))

      - record: service:instance:memory:used_ratio5m
        expr: |
          1 - (node_memory_MemAvailable_bytes
               / node_memory_MemTotal_bytes)

      # Saturation: connection pool utilisation
      - record: service:db_pool:utilisation5m
        expr: |
          sum by (service) (db_pool_connections_in_use)
            /
          sum by (service) (db_pool_connections_max)

      # Per-AZ spread: an imbalance means one AZ is unhealthy or the ASG is lopsided
      - record: service:az_distribution:ratio
        expr: |
          count by (service, zone) (up{job="service"})
            /
          count by (service) (up{job="service"})

      # Queue: age is the harm, depth is not
      - record: service:queue:oldest_age_seconds
        expr: queue_consumer_lag_seconds

      # Outbox: the durable publishing pattern; a stuck outbox is a silent data loss risk
      - record: service:outbox:oldest_pending_seconds
        expr: time() - (outbox_pending_events and on() (max by (service) (outbox_oldest_created_at)))

      # Dependency error rate (per outbound dependency)
      - record: service:dependency:error_ratio_5m
        expr: |
          sum by (service, dependency) (rate(http_client_requests_total{status=~"5.."}[5m]))
            /
          sum by (service, dependency) (rate(http_client_requests_total[5m]))

      # Deploy marker: a change() on build_info = a release happened
      - record: service:deploy:info
        expr: build_info

      - record: service:restart:rate1h
        expr: rate(node_boot_time_seconds[1h])   # proxy; better: k8s container restarts
```

# prometheus/rules/service-alerts.yml
groups:
  - name: service-slo-alerts
    rules:
      # ---------- fast burn: page ----------
      # 14.4x burn over 1h (long) AND 5m (short) => ~2% of a 30d budget in 1h
      - alert: ServiceErrorBudgetBurnFast
        expr: |
          service:error_budget_burn:rate1h{service=~"tier1-.+"} > 14.4
            and
          service:error_budget_burn:rate5m{service=~"tier1-.+"} > 14.4
        for: 2m
        labels:
          severity: page
          team: "{{ $labels.service }}"
          slo: availability
        annotations:
          summary: "{{ $labels.service }}: burning error budget 14.4x too fast"
          description: >-
            Availability over 1h is
            {{ $value | humanizePercentage }} against a 99.95% objective.
            Users are seeing errors right now. Expected recovery requires acting.
          impact: "User-visible failures on the tier-1 journey"
          dashboard_url: "https://grafana.internal/d/svc-overview?var-service={{ $labels.service }}&from=now-1h"
          runbook_url: "https://wiki.internal/runbooks/error-budget-burn"

      # ---------- medium burn: page ----------
      - alert: ServiceErrorBudgetBurnMedium
        expr: |
          service:error_budget_burn:rate6h{service=~"tier1-.+"} > 6
            and
          service:error_budget_burn:rate30s{service=~"tier1-.+"} > 6
        for: 15m
        labels: { severity: page, team: "{{ $labels.service }}" }
        annotations:
          summary: "{{ $labels.service }}: burning error budget 6x too fast"
          runbook_url: "https://wiki.internal/runbooks/error-budget-burn"

      # ---------- slow burn: ticket ----------
      - alert: ServiceErrorBudgetBurnSlow
        expr: service:error_budget_burn:rate1d{service=~"tier1-.+"} > 3
        for: 1h
        labels: { severity: ticket, team: "{{ $labels.service }}" }
        annotations:
          summary: "{{ $labels.service }}: error budget burn 3x for a day"
          dashboard_url: "https://grafana.internal/d/svc-budget?var-service={{ $labels.service }}&from=now-1d"

      # ---------- latency SLO: page ----------
      - alert: ServiceLatencySLOBurnFast
        expr: |
          (service:sli_latency:ratio_rate5m{service=~"tier1-.+"} > (1 - 14.4 * 0.005))
            and
          (service:sli_latency:ratio_rate30d{service=~"tier1-.+"} > (1 - 14.4 * 0.005))
        for: 5m
        labels: { severity: page, slo: latency }
        annotations:
          summary: "{{ $labels.service }}: p95 latency objective breached, burning 14.4x"
          dashboard_url: "https://grafana.internal/d/svc-latency?var-service={{ $labels.service }}&from=now-1h"

      # ---------- the alert nobody writes: the service vanished ----------
      - alert: ServiceMetricsMissing
        expr: absent(up{job="service", service=~"tier1-.+"} == 1)
        for: 5m
        labels: { severity: page }
        annotations:
          summary: "No scrape data for tier-1 service {{ $labels.service }}"
          runbook_url: "https://wiki.internal/runbooks/missing-metrics"

      - alert: ServiceTrafficVanished
        expr: |
          (service:http_requests:rate5m > 0.1)
            and
          (rate(http_requests_total[1h]) == 0)
        for: 15m
        labels: { severity: page }
        annotations:
          summary: "{{ $labels.service }} stopped receiving traffic"

  - name: saturation-tickets
    rules:
      # Cause-based => ticket. The harm (latency) has its own alert above.
      - alert: ServiceDbPoolSaturated
        expr: service:db_pool:utilisation5m > 0.85
        for: 20m
        labels: { severity: ticket, team: platform }
        annotations:
          summary: "{{ $labels.service }} DB pool above 85% for 20m"
          runbook_url: "https://wiki.internal/runbooks/db-pool"

      - alert: ServiceQueueBacklogGrowing
        expr: |
          service:queue:oldest_age_seconds > 600
            and
          deriv(service:queue:oldest_age_seconds[30m]) > 0
        for: 15m
        labels: { severity: ticket }
        annotations:
          summary: "{{ $labels.service }} queue age over 10m and still growing"

      - alert: ServiceOutboxStuck
        expr: service:outbox:oldest_pending_seconds > 3600
        for: 30m
        labels: { severity: ticket }
        annotations:
          summary: "{{ $labels.service }} outbox has unpublished events older than 1h"
          runbook_url: "https://wiki.internal/runbooks/outbox"

      # Monitoring health itself
      - alert: PrometheusScrapeTooSlow
        expr: scrape_duration_seconds{job="service"} > 8
        for: 10m
        labels: { severity: ticket, team: platform }
        annotations:
          summary: "Scrape taking >8s; dashboards may be stale"

### Interviewer follow-ups

1. **"Why 30s rule interval with a 15s scrape?"** — Recording rules at 2× the scrape
   interval are cheap and stable; a 1s interval just duplicates samples.
2. **"What is `deriv` good for?"** — Trend detection: `deriv(x[30m]) > 0` catches a growing
   backlog before it becomes a breach.
3. **"How do you decide the burn-rate thresholds?"** — From how long you need to detect
   versus how quickly you can respond. 14.4× ≈ 2% of a 30-day budget per hour, which for
   a 30-minute detection target gives roughly two consecutive windows of headroom.

## Problem 4 — OpenTelemetry-instrumented service (Go, HTTP + Postgres + Kafka)

🔴 Advanced · **Must-know**

**The brief.** "Instrument a Go HTTP service with OpenTelemetry so that (a) every inbound
request produces a trace, (b) outbound HTTP and Postgres calls become child spans, (c)
Kafka-produced and Kafka-consumed messages stay in the same trace, (d) span attributes
follow semantic conventions with no PII, (e) sampling is parent-based 5% head sampling,
and (f) logs carry the trace ID."

### Solution

```go
// internal/otel/otel.go
package otelx

import (
    "context"
    "os"

    "go.opentelemetry.io/contrib/instrumentation/github.com/gorilla/mux/otelmux"
    "go.opentelemetry.io/otel"
    "go.opentelemetry.io/otel/attribute"
    "go.opentelemetry.io/otel/exporters/prometheus"
    "go.opentelemetry.io/otel/exporters/otlp/otlptrace/otlptracegrpc"
    "go.opentelemetry.io/otel/propagation"
    sdkmetric "go.opentelemetry.io/otel/sdk/metric"
    "go.opentelemetry.io/otel/sdk/resource"
    sdktrace "go.opentelemetry.io/otel/sdk/trace"
    semconv "go.opentelemetry.io/otel/semconv/v1.26.0"
    "go.opentelemetry.io/otel/trace"
)

func Init(ctx context.Context, serviceName, version, env string) (func(context.Context) error, error) {
    res, err := resource.New(ctx,
        resource.WithFromEnv(),                                    // OTEL_RESOURCE_ATTRIBUTES
        resource.WithTelemetrySDK(),
        resource.WithAttributes(
            semconv.ServiceName(serviceName),
            semconv.ServiceVersion(version),
            semconv.DeploymentEnvironmentName(env),
            attribute.String("service.git.sha", os.Getenv("GIT_SHA")),
        ),
    )
    if err != nil {
        return nil, err
    }

    // W3C TraceContext + Baggage. Baggage only if you truly need cross-service
    // tenant/feature context, and never with secrets.
    propagator := propagation.NewCompositeTextMapPropagator(
        propagation.TraceContext{}, propagation.Baggage{},
    )

    // OTLP gRPC trace export (recommended default) + Prometheus for metrics
    traceExp, err := otlptracegrpc.New(ctx,
        otlptracegrpc.WithEndpoint(os.Getenv("OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT")),
        otlptracegrpc.WithInsecure(),
    )
    if err != nil {
        return nil, err
    }

    tp := sdktrace.NewTracerProvider(
        sdktrace.WithResource(res),
        sdktrace.WithSampler(sdktrace.ParentBased(sdktrace.TraceIDRatioBased(0.05))),
        sdktrace.WithBatcher(traceExp,
            sdktrace.WithBatchTimeout(5*time.Second),
            sdktrace.WithMaxExportBatchSize(512),
        ),
        // Guard against a chatty span blowing up the pipeline
        sdktrace.WithSpanLimits(sdktrace.SpanLimits{
            MaxAttributesPerSpan: 128,
            MaxEventsPerSpan:     128,
            MaxSpanLinks:         32,
        }),
    )

    otel.SetTracerProvider(tp)
    otel.SetTextMapPropagator(propagator)
    otel.SetErrorHandler(otel.ErrorHandlerFunc(func(err error) {
        slog.Error("otel error", "err", err)
    }))

    mp := sdkmetric.NewMeterProvider(sdkmetric.WithResource(res))
    otel.SetMeterProvider(mp)

    return func(ctx context.Context) error {
        ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(ctx, 10*time.Second)
        defer cancel()
        if err := tp.Shutdown(ctx); err != nil {
            return err
        }
        return mp.Shutdown(ctx)
    }, nil
}

// LogHandler injects trace context into slog so logs pivot to traces
func LogHandler(base slog.Handler) slog.Handler {
    return slog.HandlerFunc(func(ctx context.Context, r slog.Record) error {
        sc := trace.SpanContextFromContext(ctx)
        if sc.IsValid() {
            r.AddAttrs(
                slog.String("trace_id", sc.TraceID().String()),
                slog.String("span_id", sc.SpanID().String()),
                slog.Bool("sampled", sc.IsSampled()),
            )
        }
        return base.Handle(ctx, r)
    })
}
```

// cmd/api/main.go — manual instrumentation with correct attribute names
func main() {
    ctx := context.Background()
    shutdown, err := otelx.Init(ctx, "orders", buildVersion, env)
    defer shutdown(ctx)

    logger := slog.New(slog.NewJSONHandler(os.Stdout,
        &slog.HandlerOptions{Level: slog.LevelInfo})).With("service", "orders")
    slog.SetDefault(slog.New(otelx.LogHandler(logger)))

    // otelmux gives you: server spans, W3C extraction, route-based span names,
    // and status code -> span status mapping. Without it, `http.route` stays empty
    // and your dashboards show /orders/12345 as distinct series.
    mux := http.NewServeMux()
    mux.Handle("/v1/orders/", otelmux.NewHandler(ordersHandler, "v1.orders"))
    mux.HandleFunc("/healthz", func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
        w.WriteHeader(http.StatusOK) // deliberately untraced
    })

    srv := &http.Server{
        Addr:              ":8080",
        Handler:           mux,
        ReadHeaderTimeout: 5 * time.Second,
        ReadTimeout:       15 * time.Second,
        WriteTimeout:      30 * time.Second,
        IdleTimeout:       60 * time.Second,
    }

    go func() { // graceful shutdown so in-flight spans/export complete
        sig := make(chan os.Signal, 1)
        signal.Notify(sig, syscall.SIGTERM)
        <-sig
        ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 20*time.Second)
        defer cancel()
        srv.Shutdown(ctx) // waits for in-flight requests; spans end naturally
    }()

    logger.Info("starting", "addr", srv.Addr, "version", buildVersion)
    if err := srv.ListenAndServe(); err != nil && !errors.Is(err, http.ErrServerClosed) {
        logger.Error("server failed", "err", err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
}

// internal/orders/handler.go — a span with domain attributes (no PII)
func (h *Handler) CreateOrder(ctx context.Context, req CreateOrderRequest) (Order, error) {
    ctx, span := h.tracer.Start(ctx, "orders.create",
        trace.WithSpanKind(trace.SpanKindInternal),
        trace.WithAttributes(
            attribute.String("order.channel", req.Channel),      // bounded/enumerated
            attribute.Int("order.item_count", len(req.Items)),
            attribute.Int("order.total_cents", req.TotalCents),
            attribute.Bool("order.is_guest", req.Guest),
        ))
    defer span.End()

    // NEVER attribute.String("user.email", ...) or ids that are unbounded.
    // If you need per-customer correlation, hash into a low-cardinality attribute:
    attribute.String("user.tier", req.Tier)

    // Downstream calls create children automatically because ctx carries the span
    order, err := h.repo.Insert(ctx, req)
    if err != nil {
        span.RecordError(err)
        span.SetStatus(codes.Error, "insert failed")
        span.SetAttributes(
            attribute.String("error.type", fmt.Sprintf("%T", err)),
            attribute.Bool("error.retryable", errors.Is(err, repo.ErrTransient)),
        )
        // Transient failures are retried; count them on the span so a slow dependency
        // is visible even when the request succeeds
        return Order{}, fmt.Errorf("create order: %w", err)
    }

    span.SetAttributes(
        attribute.String("order.id", order.ID),   // high-cardinality OK in traces
        attribute.Int("order.id_hash", order.IDHash),
    )
    return order, nil
}

```go
// internal/events/producer.go — Kafka: propagate trace context in headers
func (p *Producer) Publish(ctx context.Context, topic string, key string, v any) error {
    // otelkafka's producer injects the trace context into Kafka headers automatically
    // when you use the instrumented client; manual version for clarity:
    carrier := propagation.MapCarrier{}
    otel.GetTextMapPropagator().Inject(ctx, carrier)

    msg := &kafka.Message{
        Topic: topic,
        Key:   []byte(key),
        Value: payload,
        Headers: []kafka.Header{
            {Key: "traceparent", Value: []byte(carrier.Get("traceparent"))},
            {Key: "tracestate",  Value: []byte(carrier.Get("tracestate"))},
            {Key: "baggage",     Value: []byte(carrier.Get("baggage"))},
        },
    }
    return p.writer.WriteMessages(ctx, msg)
}
```

```go
// internal/events/consumer.go — Kafka: extract and continue the trace
func (c *Consumer) run(ctx context.Context) error {
    for {
        m, err := c.reader.FetchMessage(ctx)   // NOT ReadMessage: manual commit
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        if err := c.handle(ctx, m); err != nil {
            slog.Error("event handling failed", "err", err, "topic", m.Topic,
                "partition", m.Partition, "offset", m.Offset)
            // Do not commit: redelivery is the retry. Bounded by max.poll + DLQ.
            continue
        }
        if err := c.reader.CommitMessages(ctx, m); err != nil {
            slog.Error("commit failed", "err", err)
        }
    }
}

func (c *Consumer) handle(ctx context.Context, m kafka.Message) error {
    // Extract the producer's context so the whole job is one trace tree
    carrier := propagation.MapCarrier{}
    for _, h := range m.Headers {
        carrier[h.Key] = string(h.Value)
    }
    remote := otel.GetTextMapPropagator().Extract(ctx, carrier)

    // context.root() detaches from the caller's context: a consumer's processing
    // should not accidentally inherit a cancelled request context.
    ctx, span := c.tracer.Start(context.withoutCancel(remote), "orders.handle",
        trace.WithSpanKind(trace.SpanKindConsumer),
        trace.WithAttributes(
            semconv.MessagingSystem("kafka"),
            semconv.MessagingDestinationName(m.Topic),
            semconv.MessagingOperationTypeReceive,
            semconv.MessagingKafkaMessageKey(string(m.Key)),
            semconv.MessagingMessageID(fmt.Sprintf("%s-%d-%d", m.Topic, m.Partition, m.Offset)),
        ))
    defer span.End()

    start := time.Now()
    err := c.processor.Process(ctx, m.Value)

    // Consumer lag as span duration context: this is how you find "the slow message"
    enqueue, _ := strconv.ParseInt(string(m.Headers[1].Value), 10, 64)
    span.SetAttributes(attribute.Int64("messaging.kafka.message.enqueue.time_ms",
        time.Since(time.UnixMilli(enqueue)).Milliseconds()))

    if err != nil {
        span.RecordError(err)
        span.SetStatus(codes.Error, "processing failed")
        return err
    }
    slog.InfoContext(ctx, "event handled",
        "topic", m.Topic, "duration_ms", time.Since(start).Milliseconds())
    return nil
}
```

### Interviewer follow-ups

1. **"Why head sampling if you have tail sampling?"** — Head sampling at 100% plus tail
   sampling needs the collector to buffer 100% of spans, which is expensive. The common
   production setup is 5–10% head sampling (cheap) *or* 100% head with aggressive tail
   policies. Do not run 100% head with a 5% tail policy and think you have "all errors
   sampled".
2. **"How do you debug a request that is slow in one region only?"** — Add
   `cloud.region`/`cloud.availability_zone` from `resourcedetection` (or
   `deployment.environment` for clusters) so you can filter; then compare spans filtered
   by that resource attribute to see which dependency span differs.
3. **"What happens to traces when the backend is down?"** — The batch exporter queues and
   drops after `max_queue_size`/`max_export_batch_size` limits; you will see
   `otelcol_exporter_send_failed_spans` and `otelcol_processor_dropped_spans` rise.
   Alert on those, and keep the queue sized for a realistic outage window.

## Problem 5 — Grafana dashboard specification

🟡 Intermediate · **Must-know**

**The brief.** "Specify two dashboards for the `orders` service: a one-screen *on-call
overview* and a deeper *component* dashboard. Specify every panel with its title as a
question, the query, the units, the thresholds, the intended decision, and where the data
comes from. Then say how you provision them and how you keep them in sync with the code."

### Solution

**Design rules applied**

| Rule | Consequence in this spec |
| --- | --- |
| Triage order | Row 1 "Is there user impact?", Row 2 "What is it?", Row 3 "Which dependency?", Row 4 "What changed?" |
| Titles are questions | "Are users seeing errors?" not "Error rate" |
| Consistent colour language | Red = user harm, orange = approaching, green = healthy. Never colour by metric type. |
| One screen | Overview ≤ 12 panels, 1 screen, 6h default range |
| Every panel has a decision attached | Each row has a `description` saying what you do with it |
| Every panel links to a runbook | Alerts link to a panel; panels link to runbooks |
| Deploy markers everywhere | `annotations` on every timeseries |
| Templated | `service`, `env`, `cluster`, `route` variables drive both dashboards |

---

**Dashboard 1 — `orders / on-call overview` (uid: `orders-overview`, tag `tier1`)**

Row 1 — "Is there user impact, and how bad?"

| # | Panel | Type | Query | Unit / thresholds | Decision it supports |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1.1 | "Are users seeing errors right now?" | Stat, red→orange→green, big number + sparkline | `service:sli_availability:ratio_rate5m{service="orders"}` | percentunit; red < 0.997, orange < 0.999, green ≥ 0.999 | If red: start the incident, open the channel, go to row 2 |
| 1.2 | "Is the error budget still healthy?" | Stat | `service:error_budget_remaining:ratio30d{service="orders"}` | percentunit, min 0 max 1; red < 0.25 | Decide whether to freeze releases *today*, not during the incident |
| 1.3 | "How fast are we burning it?" | Stat with colour | `service:error_budget_burn:rate1h{service="orders"}` | unit none, thresholds green < 1, orange < 3, red ≥ 6 | Fast burn = page-and-fix now; slow burn = plan the work |
| 1.4 | "Is latency within the SLO?" | Stat | `1 - service:sli_latency:ratio_rate30d{service="orders"}` | percentunit; red > 0.005 | Latency breaches need their own runbook |
| 1.5 | "How many requests are failing?" | Stat with secondary unit "req/s" and "last 1h" | `sum(rate(http_requests_total{service="orders",status=~"5.."}[5m]))` and `increase(...[1h])` | short, percentunit secondary | Blast radius for the status page |
| 1.6 | "How many replicas are serving?" | Stat | `sum(up{job="orders"})` vs expected (`count(up{job="orders"})`) | short; red if `up == 0` | Missing telemetry vs missing instances (§8.7.10) |

Row 2 — "What exactly is failing, and where?"

| # | Panel | Type | Query | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 2.1 | "Which routes are failing?" | Timeseries, stacked area | `sum by (route) (rate(http_requests_total{service="orders",status=~"5.."}[5m]))` | Start here to scope |
| 2.2 | "Which error types?" | Timeseries | `sum by (status, error_type) (rate(http_errors_total{service="orders"}[5m]))` | Requires an app-level counter with a bounded `error_type` label |
| 2.3 | "Is latency breaching per route?" | Timeseries, unit s, threshold 0.3 | `service:http_request:latency_p99_5m{service="orders"}` with a `p50` overlay | The p50/p99 gap tells you it is a tail problem |
| 2.4 | "Are we at capacity?" | Timeseries, unit short | `aws_appautoscaling_desired_count{service="orders"}` (or `ecs_desired_count`) with `max_count` as a max | "At max while burning budget" = capacity incident |
| 2.5 | "Are all AZs serving?" | Timeseries, unit percentunit | `service:az_distribution:ratio{service="orders"}` | 0.33/0.67/0.00 = an AZ problem, not a code problem |

Row 3 — "Which dependency is the problem?"

| # | Panel | Type | Query |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 3.1 | "Is the database pool near exhaustion?" | Timeseries + threshold 0.85 | `service:db_pool:utilisation5m{service="orders"}` |
| 3.2 | "Is the database itself slow?" | Timeseries | `histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by (le) (rate(pg_stat_statements_query_duration_seconds_bucket{service="orders"}[5m])))` and CloudWatch `SelectLatency` |
| 3.3 | "Is the cache hitting?" | Timeseries, percentunit | `sum by (outcome) (rate(cache_operations_total{service="orders"}[5m]))` normalised |
| 3.4 | "Are outbound dependencies failing?" | Timeseries | `service:dependency:error_ratio_5m{service="orders"}` |
| 3.5 | "Is the queue backing up?" | Timeseries, unit s | `service:queue:oldest_age_seconds{service="orders"}` with threshold 600 |
| 3.6 | "Is the outbox stuck?" | Stat | `service:outbox:oldest_pending_seconds{service="orders"}` (this is silent data loss risk) |

Row 4 — "What changed?"

| # | Panel | Type | Query / content |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 4.1 | "When did we last deploy?" | Table/annotation list | `build_info{service="orders"}` with `version` and `git_sha`, plus GitHub deploy links |
| 4.2 | "Recent deploys" | Text/links panel | Query GitHub Deployments API for the last 7 days |
| 4.3 | "Recent config/flag changes" | Annotations | `flags_changes_total{service="orders"}` increases |
| 4.4 | "Open alerts right now" | Alert list | Grafana alert list filtered to this service |

**Dashboard 2 — `orders / component & dependencies` (uid: `orders-component`)**

Row 1 — "What is the request mix?" (traffic is context for everything else)
- Requests/second by route (`service:http_requests:rate5m`)
- Traffic ratio by route as a share of all services (`service:traffic_ratio:v1`)
- Payload size p50/p95/p99
- Authenticated vs anonymous ratio

Row 2 — "What is the latency structure?"
- p50/p90/p95/p99 by route (4 lines, same colour family, unit `s`)
- Mean latency (because `histogram_quantile` is unreliable at low volume)
- Response time split by phase: handler vs database vs external call
  (`sum by (phase) (rate(http_server_phase_duration_seconds_sum[5m])) / count`)
- Tail: ratio of p99 to p50 (this single number explains most latency debates)

Row 3 — "What about the database?"
- Pool in-use / max / waiting (`db_pool_wait_duration_seconds_count`)
- Query p95/p99 by statement fingerprint (`pg_stat_statements` via `pg_exporter`)
- Rows scanned vs returned (`pg_stat_statements` `rows`), with threshold on scans/returned > 100
- Connection count vs `max_connections` with threshold at 0.8
- Transaction rate, rollback rate
- Replication lag (Aurora `ReplicationLag` / read replica `ReplicaLag`)

Row 4 — "What about the cache and the queue?"
- Cache hit ratio by operation
- Eviction rate (`evicted_keys_total`) — a burst here means the cache is too small
- Command latency p99 (`cmdstat_latency_seconds` from `redis_exporter`)
- Queue depth, oldest message age, consumer rate, consumer lag
- Dead-letter queue depth with a threshold at 1

Row 5 — "What about the platform?"
- CPU, memory, and network per instance, with instance name in the legend
- Container restarts (`increase(kube_pod_container_status_restarts_total[15m])`)
- OOM kills (`increase(kube_pod_container_status_last_terminated_reason{reason="OOMKilled"}[1h])`)
- GC pause p99 (Go), heap size, goroutine count
- File descriptors in use vs limit
- Network errors and drops

Row 6 — "What about traces and logs?"
- Top 10 slowest traces in the window (from Tempo via the `tracesToLogs`/`traceql` plugin
  or a saved query)
- Trace volume and error rate from the collector
  (`otelcol_exporter_sent_spans` / `dropped_spans`, `rate(span_calls_total)`)
- Log volume by level (`sum by (level) (rate(loki_log_lines[5m]))`) with a growth alert
- Exemplar-linked latency panel (click the p99 datapoint to jump to the trace)

```bash

# scripts/apply-dashboards.sh — run from CI after every service change
set -euo pipefail
: "${GF_URL:?}"
: "${GF_TOKEN:?}"       # a service account token with dashboards:write only

for f in dashboards/*.json; do
  name=$(jq -r .title "$f")
  if curl -fsS -H "Authorization: Bearer $GF_TOKEN" \
       "$GF_URL/api/dashboards/uid/$(jq -r .uid "$f")" >/dev/null 2>&1; then
    endpoint="db"                       # update
  else
    endpoint="db"                       # create (same endpoint, no uid => create)

    -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
    "$GF_URL/api/dashboards/$endpoint" --data-binary "@$f" \
  | jq -e '.id' >/dev/null || { echo "failed to apply $name" >&2; exit 1; }
  echo "applied: $name"
done

### Verification (this is what you demo in the interview)

1. **The 60-second test.** Give the interviewer the dashboard and the alert
   `ServiceErrorBudgetBurnFast`. In 60 seconds they should be able to answer: is there
   user impact, how much, which route, and which runbook to open.
2. **The empty-state test.** Delete a series (or set a variable to a service with no
   traffic) and confirm panels say "No data" rather than showing a misleading 0.
3. **The deploy-correlation test.** Jump the time range to an incident where a deploy
   caused a spike and confirm the annotation lines up.
4. **The link test.** Click every runbook link; every one must be live and current.
5. **The read-only test.** Confirm `editable: false` in production.

### Interviewer follow-ups

1. **"How do you prevent dashboard sprawl?"** — Two dashboards per service maximum
   (overview + component), templates instead of copies, and a review gate: every panel
   needs a decision it supports, otherwise it is deleted.
2. **"A dashboard shows 0 errors but users complain."** — The SLI excludes the failing
   route (wrong `route` label), the error is a 4xx (counted as client error), the failure
   is downstream of your metrics (edge/CDN), or the SLI is measured in a region nobody
   uses. Verify with the *raw* query and the user's `trace_id`.
3. **"How do you decide the overview's panels?"** — Take the last 10 alerts that paged you
   and write down which panel you opened first. Those are the panels. Remove everything
   else.

## Problem 6 — Cost-optimization exercise (with numbers)

🔴 Advanced · **Must-know**

**The brief.** "Here is a monthly AWS bill of \$14,200 for a B2B SaaS at 40k monthly
active users with an SLO of 99.9%. Find the money, propose changes with expected savings
and risk, and prioritise. Here is the breakdown:

```
$4,180  EC2 (autoscaling, 3 AZs, 8× m6i.2xlarge, On-Demand + Savings Plan)
$2,350  RDS (Aurora PostgreSQL writer db.r6g.2xlarge + 3 readers db.r6g.xlarge)
$1,610  NAT Gateways (4 × ~$97 + data processing)
$1,420  S3 (120 TB, all Standard, 90-day log retention, no lifecycle)
$  980  CloudFront (2.1 TB egress, static from S3 + API from ALB)
$  760  CloudWatch (metrics + 30-day log retention, 1,800 metric series)
$  640  Lambda (18M invocations, 512MB, avg 220ms)
$  520  ELB (ALB LCUs)
$  390  Route 53
$  310  KMS requests
$  330  ECR
$  240  ECS Fargate
$  520  Misc (EIP, snapshots, staging, support)
────────
$14,200
```

**Findings, with the reasoning you must be able to state out loud**

### Finding 1 — EC2: over-provisioned, on-demand-heavy (\$4,180 → ~\$2,300, save ~\$1,880)

Evidence gathered (do this *before* proposing anything):

```bash
# 30 days of actual usage per instance, not from a screenshot
aws cloudwatch get-metric-statistics --namespace AWS/EC2 --metric-name CPUUtilization \
  --dimensions Name=InstanceId,Value=i-0abc --statistics p95 p99 Maximum \
  --start-time 2026-02-01T00:00:00Z --end-time 2026-03-01T00:00:00Z \
  --period 3600 --region eu-west-1
```

| Metric | Observed | Capacity provided | Action |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| CPU p99 (business hours) | 41% | 100% | Right-size to `m6i.xlarge` (4 vCPU) — halves the cost of the On-Demand portion |
| CPU p95 overnight | 3% | 100% | Scale-in floor 3 → keep, but 1-hour scale-down |
| Memory p99 | 28% | 100% | Confirms CPU-bound, not memory-bound |
| EBS IOPS utilisation | 22% of 16k provisioned | — | gp2 → gp3 with 3,000 IOPS is cheaper than gp2 at this size |

Savings: 8 instances from `m6i.2xlarge` ($0.384/hr) to `m6i.xlarge` ($0.192/hr) =
\$8 × \$0.192 × 730 ≈ **\$1,121**. Plus move the non-prod 4 instances to Spot =
**\$760**. Risk: p99 CPU at 41% means halving capacity puts p99 near 82%; instead size to
`m6i.xlarge` with headroom and enable target-tracking on requests-per-target, and
right-size **after** one week of measurement. Realistic saving: **\$1,100–1,500**, and it
must be validated against the latency SLO for two weeks.

### Finding 2 — NAT Gateways: four of them carrying S3 and CloudFront traffic (\$1,610 → ~\$310, save ~\$1,300)

The bill line is dominated by data processing, not hourly cost:

```
NAT hourly:      4 × \$0.045 × 730  = \$131
NAT processing:  ~14 TB × \$0.045/GB = ... (dominant)
```

Two structural problems:

1. **S3 and DynamoDB traffic is going out through NAT.** Add gateway and interface VPC
   endpoints; S3 gateway endpoints are **free** and remove the NAT hop entirely.
2. **Four NAT gateways** when there are three private subnets per environment × two
   environments = six. Consolidation is possible but reduces AZ redundancy — keep
   one-per-AZ for prod, and **schedule non-prod NAT off outside hours** (or put non-prod
   in a single NAT).

```hcl
resource "aws_vpc_endpoint" "s3" {
  vpc_id            = module.network.vpc_id
  service_name      = "com.amazonaws.eu-west-1.s3"
  vpc_endpoint_type = "Gateway"
  route_table_ids   = [for k, rt in module.network.private_route_tables : rt.id]
}

resource "aws_vpc_endpoint" "dynamodb" {
  vpc_id            = module.network.vpc_id
  service_name      = "com.amazonaws.eu-west-1.dynamodb"
  vpc_endpoint_type = "Gateway"
  route_table_ids   = [for k, rt in module.network.private_route_tables : rt.id]
}

# Interface endpoints for high-volume AWS APIs (Savings: NAT processing on those calls)
resource "aws_vpc_endpoint" "ecr_api"     { service_name = "com.amazonaws.eu-west-1.ecr.api" }
resource "aws_vpc_endpoint" "ecr_dkr"     { service_name = "com.amazonaws.eu-west-1.ecr.dkr" }
resource "aws_vpc_endpoint" "sts"         { service_name = "com.amazonaws.eu-west-1.sts" }
resource "aws_vpc_endpoint" "secretsmanager" { service_name = "com.amazonaws.eu-west-1.secretsmanager" }
resource "aws_vpc_endpoint" "logs"        { service_name = "com.amazonaws.eu-west-1.logs" }
```

Expected: NAT processing from ~14 TB to ~1.5 TB → NAT line to **~\$350** (hourly + a
little processing). Saving **~\$1,260**. Risk: low, and it *improves* availability (no
dependency on the NAT AZ) and latency (no internet round trip).

### Finding 3 — S3: 120 TB of logs in Standard with 90-day retention (\$1,420 → ~\$430, save ~\$990)

Split the 120 TB by access pattern (this is the analysis that matters, not the average):

| Prefix | Volume | Accessed in last 30 days | Class | Cost/mo |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `logs/app/` | 74 TB | yes, daily (queries in the first week) | 7 days Standard → `logs-archive/` Glacier Flexible | ~\$310 |
| `logs/access/` | 34 TB | never queried after 7 days | 7 days Standard → Glacier Flexible 30d → Deep Archive 180d | ~\$95 |
| `backups/db/` | 9 TB | monthly restores | Deep Archive with PITR retained separately | ~\$20 |
| `media/uploads/` | 3 TB | hot, user-facing | stay Standard + CloudFront | ~\$70 |
| **Total** | 120 TB | | | **~\$495** |

Rules applied: lifecycle transitions with `StorageClass` at day 7/30, `noncurrent`
expiration at 30 days, `abort incomplete multipart` at 7 days, and a lifecycle policy on
the old-versioning bucket. Mind the IA minimum object size (128 KiB) and Deep Archive's
180-day minimum.

**Verification before deleting anything:** run 30 days of S3 access logs through Athena,
group by prefix, and confirm zero `GET`/`SELECT` requests for the deep prefixes in the
last 14 days. This is the step that turns "a guess" into a decision.

Saving: **~\$990**. Risk: low *for app logs you can still query from S3 via Athena*; make
sure the retention policy is written down, because log retention is often a compliance
requirement (this is the one place where cost can conflict with a legal obligation —
escalate rather than delete).

### Finding 4 — RDS: readers sized for a worst case that never happens (\$2,350 → ~\$1,700, save ~\$650)

| Finding | Evidence | Action |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Writer p99 CPU 38%, max 71% | CloudWatch | Keep class (a spike to 71% would hurt on a smaller writer) |
| Readers: p99 CPU 9%, `pg_stat_statements` shows most queries are index scans | Performance Insights | 3 readers → 2; saves \$0.121/hr × 730 = **\$353/mo** |
| Aurora Serverless v2 alternative | Load is spiky (day/night ratio 4:1) | Model it: 2 ACUs average vs 2 × db.xlarge constant. **Saving ~\$300/mo**, but a migration project, not a toggle |
| Graviton (`r6g`) | Already using r6g! | No saving available — good, previous work done |
| `io1`/`io2` Block Express on the writer? No, Standard | IOPS usage 22% | Already right |

Realistic: **\$350/mo now** (drop one reader, keep the writer), **\$650/mo** with a
Serverless v2 evaluation. Risk: low for the reader count (verify read traffic per replica
with `ReadIOPS`/`AuroraReplicaLag` first), medium for Serverless v2 (scaling lag and
per-second ACU billing).

### Finding 5 — Lambda: 18M invocations that could be 3M with batching (\$640 → ~\$210, save ~\$430)

The dominant cost is **request count**, not duration: 18M × \$0.20/M = \$3.60... so the
\$640 must come from duration and memory, plus one 512 MB function running long. Actions:

1. **Batch 10 events per invocation** with SQS `BatchSize: 10` and a 5-second batching
   window: 18M invocations → ~2M. Immediately saves the per-request cost and the cold
   start cost.
2. **Reduce memory** where the function is I/O-bound: 512 MB → 256 MB halves GB-second
   cost (and can make it *faster* if it was CPU-starved; check duration per MB).
3. **Move the long-running one** to a small Fargate service or step the workflow down:
   measured 1.8s average duration × 512 MB × 18M = a lot of GB-seconds. Lambdas with
   >1s average duration are usually a mis-shaped function.

Expected: **\$400–450 saved**. Risk: low; batching adds up to 5s of latency to an
asynchronous path, which is acceptable for notifications but not for a user-facing call.

### Finding 6 — CloudWatch: cardinality and retention (\$760 → ~\$420, save ~\$340)

```promql
topk(20, count by (__name__) ({__name__=~".+"}))
count by (job) (up)
prometheus_tsdb_head_series
```

Findings:
- 640 metric series are per-request-route with an unbounded `route` value (raw URLs
  containing order IDs). Fix: normalise to a route template in instrumentation and add a
  post-scrape `metric_relabel_configs` drop rule → series drop from 1,800 to ~900.
- Logs retained 30 days in CloudWatch at \$0.50/GB ingest+index. Move days 8–30 to S3
  (Athena-queryable) → **\$280 saved**.
- An unused `log_driver` capturing full stack traces from a library at INFO → **\$60**.

### Finding 7 — The small things that surprise people (\$240, save ~\$180)

```
EIPs attached but unused (2 prod + 3 staging):        \$21   -> release
Old AMIs (37 × 8GB, never referenced):               \$26   -> deregister
Unattached EBS volumes (18 × 40GB):                   \$30   -> snapshot+delete
RDS snapshots older than 90d kept "just in case" (9):  \$63   -> delete, PITR exists
Staging running 24/7 (4 instances + 1 db):           \$500   -> scheduled 07-19 UTC
Cross-AZ traffic spike after the NAT change:          \$0    -> already optimal
```

### Total

| Area | Current | Proposed | Saving | Risk | Effort |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| EC2 rightsize + Spot for non-prod | \$4,180 | \$2,600 | **\$1,580** | Medium | 2 weeks (measure first) |
| NAT + VPC endpoints | \$1,610 | \$350 | **\$1,260** | Low | 1 day |
| S3 lifecycle | \$1,420 | \$430 | **\$990** | Low | 2 days + compliance check |
| RDS readers | \$2,350 | \$2,000 | **\$350** | Low | 1 hour |
| Lambda batching + memory | \$640 | \$200 | **\$440** | Low | 1 day |
| CloudWatch series + log tiering | \$760 | \$420 | **\$340** | Low | 2 days |
| Waste cleanup | \$590 | \$150 | **\$440** | Low | 1 day |
| **Total** | **\$14,200** | **\$6,600** | **\$5,410 (38%)** | | |

### The follow-ups that make this a *senior* answer

1. **Tag before optimising.** Every dollar above is attributable only because tags existed.
   Enforce `owner`, `env`, `service`, `cost-center` at deploy time.
2. **Budgets and anomaly detection** so a regression is caught in days, not the next
   month: budget alarm at 80% of forecast, AWS Cost Anomaly Detection on EC2/S3/RDS.
3. **A weekly cost review** by the team that owns the tag, on the same dashboard as the
   SLOs, so cost and reliability are argued together rather than in silos.
4. **Reserve after rightsize.** Once the fleet is stable for 30 days at the *new* size,
   buy 1-year Compute Savings Plans (No Upfront) for the measured baseline. Do this
   **last**: committing to today's over-provisioned fleet wastes the saving.
5. **What I deliberately did *not* do**, and why — this is the part that distinguishes a
   senior answer:
   - Did not delete a 9 TB database snapshot: it is the only physical backup outside PITR,
     and PITR only covers 35 days.
   - Did not cut metrics or logs below what the SLO and debugging require; I re-tiered
     instead, and I would rather pay \$420/mo for the ability to diagnose an incident.
   - Did not reduce replicas below 3 (one per AZ): the SLO is 99.9% and the AZ-failure
     story depends on it.
   - Did not move to Spot for prod; Spot interruption during a traffic peak is a worse
     outcome than the saving.

## Problem 7 — SLO and error-budget document

🔴 Advanced · **Must-know**

**The brief.** "Write the SLO document for the `orders` service: the user journeys, the
SLIs with exact queries, the objectives, the error budget arithmetic, the release policy
keyed to the budget, the alert thresholds, and the review cadence."

### Solution

```markdown
# SLO document: `orders` service

Owner: team-orders (Slack #team-orders, on-call rota "orders-primary")
Last reviewed: 2026-03-04   Next review: 2026-06-04 (quarterly) or after any SEV1
Status page: https://status.example.com  |  Dashboards: [overview] [budget] [component]

## 1. User journeys in scope

| Journey | What the user does | Tier | Owner |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| J1 Browse orders | list/search orders | 2 | team-orders |
| J2 Create order | cart -> submit -> order created | 1 | team-orders |
| J3 Pay order | pay an order (PSP call) | 1 | team-orders |
| J4 Cancel/refund | cancel an order, receive refund | 1 | team-orders |
| J5 Async events | order events processed (emails, webhooks) | 2 | team-platform |

Out of scope: admin/internal batch jobs (tracked by a separate freshness SLI), and the
public marketing site (SLO owned by team-web).

## 2. SLIs (measured quantities)

### SLI 1 — Availability of J2/J3 (primary)
Definition: the proportion of **valid** requests to tier-1 endpoints that return a
success response. Success = HTTP 2xx **or** a documented 4xx the user caused (401/403/404/
409/422) — i.e. we only count as failures responses the server could have avoided.

Valid requests exclude: health checks and probes, our own synthetic monitors
(`user_agent=acme-synth`), and requests rejected at the CDN edge by rate limiting with
`429` on non-expensive endpoints (documented separately in SLI 5).

```promql
- record: service:sli_availability:ratio_rate30d
  expr: |
    sum(rate(http_requests_total{
            service="orders", journey=~"create|pay",
            status!~"5..", scrape!="self"}[30d]))
      /
    sum(rate(http_requests_total{
            service="orders", journey=~"create|pay",
            scrape!="self"}[30d]))
```

Why this is not gameable: the numerator and denominator come from the same instrumentation
with the same exclusions; `status=~"5.."` is the only failure class counted; and the
volume behind the ratio is displayed next to it everywhere (see §6) so a low-volume
window cannot hide a total outage.

### SLI 2 — Latency of J2 (p95 within 300ms)
```promql
- record: service:sli_latency:ratio_rate30d
  expr: |
    1 - (sum(rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{le="0.3"}[30d]))
         / sum(rate(http_request_duration_seconds_count[30d])))
```
Buckets at 0.15/0.2/0.3/0.5 exist specifically to make this query meaningful.

### SLI 3 — Correctness of J3 (order total matches captured amount)
```sql
-- from business data, not HTTP codes; a 200 with the wrong amount is a failure
SELECT
  count(*) FILTER (WHERE o.total_cents <> p.captured_cents) * 1.0 / count(*) AS error_ratio
FROM orders o JOIN payments p USING (order_id)
WHERE o.created_at > now() - interval '30 days';
```
Exported nightly to Prometheus as `orders:payment_amount_mismatch:ratio` (push via
pushgateway is acceptable here because it is a batch metric, provided the series is
refreshed every 24h and stale series are handled — see the Pushgateway caveat in §8.7.4).

### SLI 4 — Freshness of J5 (95% of events processed within 15 minutes)
```promql
- record: service:sli_freshness:ratio_rate1d
  expr: |
    1 - (sum(rate(events_processed_lag_seconds_count{le="900"}[1d]))
         / sum(rate(events_processed_lag_seconds_count[1d])))
```

### SLI 5 — Load shedding (transparency)
The proportion of requests rejected by our own rate limiting at the edge. **Excluded from
SLI 1** (we choose not to serve them) but tracked and reviewed, because a rising number
means we are shedding user traffic and that *is* user impact.

```promql
sum(rate(http_requests_total{service="orders",status="429"}[1d]))
  / sum(rate(http_requests_total{service="orders"}[1d]))
```

## 3. Objectives (targets)

| SLI | Objective | Window | Rationale |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| SLI 1 Availability | **99.95%** | 28 days (rolling) | Contractual SLA to enterprise customers is 99.9%; we hold 5× headroom so a measurement dispute cannot become a breach |
| SLI 2 Latency | **99% under 300ms** | 28 days | Matches the p95 product requirement; 1% slow requests is visible but not fatal to conversion |
| SLI 3 Correctness | **100.00%** | 28 days | A single wrong amount is a support escalation and a finance incident; this is a hard gate on release, not a burn-rate alert |
| SLI 4 Freshness | **99% within 15min** | 7 days | Users perceive email/webhook delay within minutes, not hours |
| SLI 5 Shed rate | **< 0.1%** | 7 days | Not an SLO for the vendor, a guard on our own protection |

### Error budget arithmetic (put this in the document; reviewers always check it)

```
Availability 99.95% over 28 days:
  window        = 28 × 24 × 60 = 40,320 minutes
  allowed down  = 0.0005 × 40,320 = 20.16 minutes  (≈ 20 minutes per 4 weeks)

Latency 99% under 300ms over 28 days:
  allowed slow  = 1% of all requests

Correctness 100%:
  allowed bad   = 0 requests
```

## 4. Alerting on the budget (multi-window, multi-burn-rate)

| Alert | Short window | Long window | Burn | Budget consumed | Severity |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| AvailabilityBurnFast | 5m | 1h | > 14.4× | 2% in ~1h | page |
| AvailabilityBurnMedium | 30m | 6h | > 6× | 5% in ~6h | page |
| AvailabilityBurnSlow | 2h | 1d | > 3× | 10% in ~1d | ticket |
| AvailabilityBudgetPolicy | — | 28d | remaining < 25% | — | policy review (lead notified) |
| LatencyBurnFast | 5m | 1h | > 14.4× of 1% | 2% in ~1h | page |
| CorrectnessMismatch | — | 1h | any > 0 | — | page (this is always SEV1-adjacent) |
| FreshnessBreach | 30m | 6h | > 6× | — | ticket |
| ShedRateHigh | 30m | 6h | > 0.1% | — | ticket |

Rules (non-negotiable):
- Never page on a cause (CPU, memory, pool depth). Those are dashboards and tickets.
- Every page has a runbook link and a dashboard link with `from=now-1h`.
- `absent(up == 1)` and "traffic vanished" alerts exist, because a service with no data is
  not a healthy service.

## 5. Release and change policy keyed to the error budget

```
budget_remaining = 1 - (observed_error_ratio / allowed_error_ratio)

| remaining        | policy                                                                  |
|------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| > 75%            | Normal cadence. Feature flags and experiments allowed.                   |
| 50% - 75%        | Normal cadence, but every release requires a named rollback plan.        |
| 25% - 50%        | Reliability first. Non-essential refactors paused. Extra test coverage on  |
|                  | the two weakest journeys required. Deploys ≤ 2/week.                     |
| 10% - 25%        | Change freeze except: incident fixes, security fixes, SLO-improving work. |
|                  | Lead notified; a written burn-down plan is required to unfreeze.         |
| < 10%            | Hard freeze. Daily 15-min reliability review with the service owner.      |
| exhausted (28d)  | Feature freeze until the SLO is restored for a full 28-day window.        |
```
Correctness SLI is enforced **independently of the budget**: any mismatch blocks promotion
regardless of budget.

The policy is not aspirational: the release pipeline reads
`service:error_budget_remaining:ratio28d` from the metrics API and blocks non-hotfix
promotions to prod when it is below the configured threshold. Humans own the exceptions.

## 6. Dashboards and how to read the numbers

- Budget panel: current availability %, allowed %, budget remaining % (as failure minutes
  consumed: e.g. "14.2 of 20.2 minutes used"), 28-day trend, and the request volume
  denominator beside every ratio.
- A ratio is *never* displayed alone. Every percentage panel shows `increase(...[window])`
  beneath it, because 99.9% of 30 requests is meaningless.
- Deploy markers on every chart so a budget burn can be attributed.

## 7. Current standing (filled in from the recording rules)

```
Availability (28d): 99.982%   -> budget remaining 36% (7.2 of 20.2 min used)
Latency (28d):      99.31% under 300ms
Correctness (28d):  100.000%
Freshness (7d):     99.7%
Shed rate (7d):     0.004%
Assessment: below the 50% threshold. Reliability work is prioritised this sprint.
```

## 8. Known limitations (state them; a review will find them anyway)

1. `status!~"5.."` treats a 200 with a wrong body as success — hence SLI 3 exists.
2. The 28-day window reacts slowly to a collapse; mitigated by the 5m/1h burn alert.
3. Cards are excluded from SLI 1 (a card decline is a PSP outage, not ours); this is a
   known carve-out with the enterprise contract attached.
4. If the PSP fails, SLI 1 breaches and the budget burns. That is intentional — we are
   still not serving orders — but it means we need a documented "PSP outage" policy
   (§9) for how we handle the budget after an external dependency burns it for us.

## 9. External dependency policy

When a third party (PSP) causes the SLO to be breached:
- Still count it in SLI 1 (users are affected).
- Do not page the whole company; page the owning team with a runbook that names the
  provider and links to their status page.
- After resolution, file an action item to define a **degraded mode** that reduces our
  burn (e.g. queue-and-retry with a 24h SLA instead of failing fast) and re-baseline the
  SLO discussion with the enterprise customer.
- If a single provider caused > 25% of the quarterly budget burn, that becomes a Q-level
  decision: multi-provider, or accept the burn with a documented risk acceptance.

## 10. Review

Quarterly, and after any SEV1. The review answers: is the objective still the right
target (too strict, too loose), are the SLI queries still valid after instrumentation
changes, is the budget policy being followed, and did any action item from a postmortem
change this document.
```

### Verification

```bash
# Every SLI query must return data and be ≤ 5s
for q in service:sli_availability:ratio_rate30d \
         service:sli_latency:ratio_rate30d \
         service:sli_freshness:ratio_rate1d; do
  curl -gs --data-urlencode "query=$q" localhost:9090/api/v1/query \
    | jq -e '.data.result | length > 0' || echo "SLI returns nothing: $q"
done

# The arithmetic must be reproducible
python3 -c "print(0.0005 * 28*24*60)   # 20.16 minutes allowed"

# The release policy must be enforced by the pipeline, not by memory
curl -s "$METRICS/api/v1/query?query=service:error_budget_remaining:ratio28d{service=\"orders\"}" \
  | jq -r '.data.result[0].value[1]'
```

### Interviewer follow-ups

1. **"Why 99.95% when the contract says 99.9%?"** — Because the SLO is an engineering
   target and the SLA is a promise; the 5× gap absorbs measurement error and dependency
   incidents without creating a breach of the contract.
2. **"Your PSP burned 60% of your budget. Now what?"** — Per §9: keep counting it, do not
   silently exclude it, and use the event to justify a degraded mode or multi-provider.
   Excluding external failures from an SLO that users feel is how teams talk themselves
   into 99.99% on a service that is actually 99.5%.
3. **"Who enforces the policy?"** — The pipeline, with named human owners for exceptions.
   A policy nobody enforces is a suggestion, and the first time it is bent is when the
   error budget stops meaning anything.
